That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations until it returns like the old dry palm stalk.﴾ ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; and each is floating in an orbit.﴾ ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship,﴾ ﴿and We created for them of its like that which they ride.﴾ ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to call for help, nor are they rescued,﴾ ﴿except as mercy from Us and enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you, that you may be shown mercy,"﴾ ﴿no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them but that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom God would have fed if He willed? You are only in clear error."﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿They await only a single cry that will seize them while they are disputing.﴾ ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor return to their families.﴾ ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and at once they will rush from the graves to their Lord.﴾ ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place? This is what the Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."﴾ ﴿It will be but one cry, and at once they will all be brought before Us.﴾ ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in anything, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in delight,﴾ ﴿they and their spouses, in shade, reclining on couches.﴾ ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for.﴾ ﴿"Peace!" a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ (p. 322) ﴿"And stand apart today, O guilty ones.﴾ ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you,﴾ ﴿and that you should worship Me? This is a straight path.﴾ ﴿And he had already led astray a great multitude among you. Did you not then use reason?﴾ ﴿This is Hell, which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, and they would race for the path; but how could they see?﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed or return.﴾ ﴿And whomever We let live long, We reverse him in creation. Will they not then understand?﴾ ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it suitable for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an,﴾ ﴿to warn whoever is alive, and that the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have made, cattle, and they are their owners?﴾ ﴿And We have subjected them to them, so some of them they ride and some of them they eat.﴾ ﴿And for them in them are benefits and drinks. Will they not then be thankful?﴾ ﴿And they have taken gods besides God, hoping they might be helped.﴾ ﴿They cannot help them, and they are a mobilized host for them.﴾ ﴿So do not let their saying grieve you. Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ ﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop, and then he is an open adversary?﴾ ﴿And he has struck for Us a parable and forgotten his creation. He said, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knower of all creation.﴾ ﴿He who made for you from the green tree fire, and then you kindle from it."﴾ ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them? Yes, indeed; He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿So glory be to He in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

Qamaḥa al-ba'īru ra'sahu (قَمَحَ البَعِيرُ رَأْسَهُ): he raised his head, after drinking water; the discussion of it will come in full. Al-ʿurjūn (العُرْجُونُ): the stalk of the date cluster, from between the stem to its point of origin on the palm tree. Al-Zajjaj said: it is fuʿlūn, from al-inʿirāj, which is bending. Al-jadath (الجَدَثُ): the grave. It is also heard as jadaf, with the thāʾ replaced by fāʾ, as they said fumm for thumm; and as they replaced fāʾ with thāʾ, they said maʿthūr for maʿfūr. It is a kind of truffle. Al-maskh (المَسْخُ): transformation from one form into a hideous form. Al-ramīm (الرَّمِيمُ): decayed and crumbling.

* *

﴿Ya-Sin.﴾ ﴿By the Qur'an, full of wisdom,﴾ ﴿indeed you are among the messengers,﴾ ﴿upon a straight path.﴾ ﴿It is a revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless.﴾ ﴿The word has certainly come into effect upon most of them, so they do not believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, reaching to the chins, so they are held with their heads raised.﴾ ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and covered them, so they do not see.﴾ ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forth and their traces, and everything We have enumerated in a clear register.﴾.

This surah is Meccan, except that a group claimed that His words ﴿and We record what they have sent forth﴾ and "their traces" were revealed concerning the Banu Salama of the Ansar, when they wanted to leave their homes and move to be near the Mosque of the Messenger; but this claim is not correct. It is also said: except His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47] and the verse that follows.

The discussion of the disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa) has preceded at the beginning of al-Baqara. Ibn Jubayr said here: it is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and its evidence is ﴿indeed you are among the messengers﴾. Sayyid al-Hamawi said:

"O soul, do not purify yourself with love, striving for affection, except for the family of Yasin."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is "O human" in Ethiopian (Habashi). And from him: it is in the dialect of Tayy, for they say īsān meaning insān, and they pluralize it as ayāsīn; so this is from it. Another group said: yā is a vocative particle, and the sīn stands in place of insān, from which a letter was removed and it was placed in its stead. Al-Zamakhshari said: if it is true that its meaning is "O human" in the dialect of Tayy, then its basis is to be ya-unaysīn, and the calling was so frequent on their tongues that they limited it to a part of it, as they said in the oath: mu-llāh and ayman-llāh. End of quote. What is reported from the Arabs in the diminutive of insān is unaysiyān, with a yāʾ followed by an alif, which indicates that its root is unaysān, because diminution returns things to their roots; and we do not know that they said its diminutive as unaysīn. And even on the assumption that it is a remnant of unaysīn, that is not permissible, neither being built on a ḍamma nor remaining pausal; because it is a vocative addressed directly, and also it is not permissible because it is a diminutive, and that is impermissible with regard to the prophethood. His saying "as they said in the oath mu-llāh and ayman-llāh" is one view. Among the grammarians there are those who say that mu is a particle of oath and is not a remnant of ayman.

It was read with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, with its pure imāla (inclination), and between the two pronunciations. The majority read with a sukūn on the nūn, assimilated into the wāw. Among the seven: al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Warsh, and Ibn ʿAmir read it with clear pronunciation, while the rest of the seven read it as assimilated. Ibn Abi Ishaq and ʿIsa read with a fatḥa on the nūn. Qatada said: Yasin is an oath. Abu Hatim said: the analogy of this view is a fatḥa on the nūn, as you say: "Allāh, I will certainly do such-and-such." Al-Zajjaj said: a naṣb, as if he said: "Recite Yasin," and this is according to Sibawayh's view that it is a name for the surah. Al-Kalbi read with a ḍamma on the nūn, and said it is in the dialect of Tayy: "O human." Al-Sammak and Ibn Abi Ishaq also read with a kasra. It was said: the vowel is because of the meeting of two sukūns; the fatḥa is sought for lightness, the ḍamma like ḥaythu, and the kasra is on the basis of their meeting. If it is said that it is an oath, it may be in the naṣb position according to Abu Hatim's view, the rafʿ as a mubtada' (subject), like "the trust of God, I will surely stand," and the jarr by implying a particle of jarr, which is permissible according to the Kufans. (Al-Ḥakīm): either it is faʿīl in the sense of mufʿal, as you say: "I tied the honey, so it is ʿaqīd," meaning maʿqūd; or it is for emphasis from ḥākim; or it is in the sense of cause, that is, possessing wisdom.

﴿Upon a straight path﴾ is a second predicate, or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from him, peace be upon him, or from "the messengers," or it is related to "the messengers." The straight path is the law of Islam.

Talha, al-Ashhab and ʿIsa read, according to the varying reports from them, tanzīla with a naṣb as a verbal noun; Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read tanzīla with a naṣb as a verbal noun; the rest of the seven, Abu Bakr, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, and al-Aʿmash read it with a rafʿ as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is a revelation. Abu Ḥaywa, al-Yazidi, and al-Qursi from Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba read it with a jarr, either as an apposition to "the Qur'an," or as a description by a verbal noun. (Li-tundhira) is related to tanzīl or to arsalnā implied.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 1–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿What their fathers were warned of﴾. Ikrimah said: "mā" means "alladhī" (the one that), i.e., "the thing that their fathers were warned of, of the punishment." Then "mā" is the second object, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ (al-Naba 78:40). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "It is also possible that mā is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), meaning ﴿what their fathers were warned﴾, and the fathers in this case are the earliest of the descendants of Ismaʿil, among whom warning had existed." And "fa-hum" (so they) according to this interpretation means "fa-innahum" (for they). The fāʾ is used to separate one clause from another clause that stands as a relative clause (ṣilah), so it connects to His saying ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾. The phrase "to warn" (li-tundhira) is like when you say: "I sent you to so-and-so to warn him, for he is heedless, or rather he is heedless." Qatadah said: "mā" is a negation, meaning that their fathers were not warned. In this case, "their fathers" are the nearer ones among them, and "mā undhira" is in the position of a qualifier, meaning "whose fathers were not warned." "Fa-hum ghafilūn" (so they are heedless) is connected to the negation, meaning: they were not warned, so they are heedless, since their not being warned is the cause of their heedlessness. By considering the fathers in terms of their antiquity and nearness, the contradiction between warning and its negation disappears.

﴿Indeed, the word has come into effect against most of them﴾. The well-known view is that the word is ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ (Hud 11:119). It was also said: it means that the necessity of punishment was already decreed in His knowledge. And it was said: "the word" (al-qawl) [p. 324] is what God said through the tongue of the messengers, concerning monotheism and other matters, and its proof became clear; so most of them do not believe after that. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles upon their necks﴾ and what follows is that it is literal, not metaphorical (istiʿārah, metaphor). When God, exalted is He, stated that they do not believe, He then informed about some of their conditions in the Hereafter when they enter the Fire. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "His saying ﴿So We covered them, and they cannot see﴾ weakens this view, because the sight of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection is sharp, seeing the ugliness of their state." End of quote. But this does not weaken it. Do you not see His saying ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ (al-Isra 17:97), and His saying ﴿He will say: My Lord, why have You gathered me blind?﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:125)? Or His saying ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾ (Qaf 50:22) may be a kinayah (metonymy, allusion) for his grasp of what he is coming to, as if he sees it. The majority said: that is a metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Ishaq said: it is a metaphor for the state of the disbelievers who intended harm to the Messenger; God made this an example for them in restraining them from him and preventing them from harming him when they plotted against him. Al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Farrāʾ said: it is a metaphor for their withholding from spending in the way of God, as He said ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ (al-Isra 17:29). Ikrimah said: it was revealed when Abu Jahl intended to strike him with a great stone, and in other such occasions, but God prevented him. This is close to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It is narrated that "Abu Jahl carried a stone to throw at the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying, and his hands were bent up to his neck, so that he returned to his companions with the stone stuck in his hand. They could not free it except with great effort. Then he took another stone, but when he approached the Messenger, God blinded his sight so he did not see him. He returned to his companions and could not see them until they called out to him." So the shackle becoming a metaphor refers to the restraint of Abu Jahl and others in this story. And since Abu Jahl's companions were content with what he intended to do, this was attributed to a group. Another group said: it is a metaphor for God's preventing them from faith and His placing a barrier between them and it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is the most preferred of the views, because when God mentioned that they do not believe, due to what had been decreed for them from eternity, He followed this with making for them a restraint and an encompassing wretchedness in which their state is like that of those who are shackled. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an image (tamthīl) of their insistence upon disbelief, and that there is no way to their claim of [being guided], as He made them like the shackled, head-raised (muqmaḥūn), in that they do not turn toward the truth, nor bend their necks toward it, nor lower their heads to it; and like those confined between two barriers, who see neither what is before them nor what is behind them, in that they have no reflection and do not see, meaning they are blind to considering the signs of God, exalted is He. End of quote. In his words there is a hidden trace of Muʿtazilism (dasīsat al-iʿtizāl). Do you not see that the statement of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah, the orthodox majority) is "a metaphor for God's preventing them from faith," while al-Zamakhshari's statement is "an image of their insistence," and he attributes the actions that he counts to them and not to God? The ghull (shackle) is that which surrounds the neck, for the sake of rebuke, constriction, punishment, and captivity. With the neck, both hands or one hand [are bound], for the sake of explanation (taʿlīl). The apparent reference of the pronoun in "fa-hiya" (so they are) is to the shackles, because they are the ones mentioned and spoken of. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: they are broad, reaching the chin with their edges, and the chin is the junction of the two jaws, so the shackled man is compelled to raise his face toward the sky, and that is iqmāḥ (raising the head with lowered gaze), which is close to the meaning of being held with a halter in appearance. Al-Zamakhshari said: the shackles, the origin of which is "up to the chins," are fastened to them. That is because the collar of the shackle, which is around the neck of the shackled one, has at the meeting of its two ends under the chin a ring in which the head of the post sits, passing through the ring up to the chin, so it does not let him lower his head or lay his nape down, so he remains always raising his head. End of quote. Al-Farrāʾ said: qamḥ is that in which one lowers his gaze after raising his head. Al-Zajjaj said something similar, saying: it is said "qamaḥa al-baʿīr raʾsahu ʿan rayy" (the camel raised its head away from water) and "qamaḥa" (it did so). Abu ʿUbayda said: qamaḥa qumūḥan: he raised his head from the pool without drinking, and the plural is qiṣāḥ (camels that raise their heads). From this is the saying of Bishr, describing the death of one of them so that they would bury him:

"We sit around its sides, lowering our gaze like camels with raised heads (qiṣāḥ)."

Al-Layth said: it is the raising of the camel's head when it drinks bad water, then it returns. Al-Zajjaj said: the two months of the winter (al-kānūnayn) are called "shahrā qimāḥ" because when camels come to water they raise their heads because of its extreme coldness. Abu Zayd recited the verse of al-Hudhali:

"A youth, the son of the mighty, when we pass the winter, and provisions are loved in the two months of qimāḥ."

He narrated it with a ḍamma on the qāf, and Ibn al-Sikkit with a kasra, and both are dialects. The two were called "the two months of qimāḥ" because every creature with a liver dislikes drinking water in them. Al-Ḥasan said: al-qāmiḥ is one who raises his gaze toward the place of his foot. Mujahid said: the one raising the head, the one placing his hand over his mouth. Al-Ṭabarī said: the pronoun in "fa-hiya" refers to the hands, even though no mention of them preceded, because its place is clear from the meaning, since the shackle is only on the neck with the two hands, which is why the shackle was named "jāmiʿah" (gatherer), for it gathers the hand and the neck. ʿAli, may God honor his face, saw people raising their heads, so he placed his hands under his jaws and pressed them and raised his head. Al-Zamakhshari said: he made the qimāḥ the result of His saying ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾. If the pronoun referred to the hands, the sense of causation in the qimāḥ would not be apparent; and this placement of a pronoun involves a kind of contrivance and abandoning of the apparent meaning, which the meaning itself calls for, toward falsehood, which turns away from the clear truth toward a confused falsehood. End of quote.

The reading of ʿAbd Allah, Ikrimah, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir and Ḥafṣ is (saddan) with a fatḥa on the sīn in both places (sadd and sadd); the majority read it with a ḍamma. The explanation of sadd was given in al-Kahf. The majority read ﴿fa-aghshaynāhum﴾ with the ghayn dotted; Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Ibn Yaʿmar, Ikrimah, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Sirin, al-Ḥasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Yazid al-Barbari, Yazid ibn al-Muhallab, Abu Ḥanifa and Ibn Miqsam read it with an ʿayn, from ʿashāʾ (night blindness), which is weakness of sight, meaning "We placed upon them a covering."

﴿And it is the same for them﴾ and the verse. Its explanation and grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) were discussed previously in the beginning of al-Baqarah.

﴿You can only warn﴾. ﴿To warn a people﴾ was mentioned earlier, but since it was decreed for them that they would not believe, until He said ﴿and it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾, the warning was of no benefit, since its benefit was absent. So He said ﴿You can only warn﴾, meaning a warning that benefits whoever follows the Reminder (al-dhikr), which is the Qur'an. Qatadah said: or the admonition.

﴿And fears the Most Merciful﴾, meaning the one characterized by mercy. Though mercy may return to hope, yet with his knowledge of His mercy, he fears Him out of fear that He might deprive him of what He has bestowed upon him in the unseen (bi-l-ghayb), meaning in privacy, when the person is absent from the sight of other people. When He instilled warning in him, He gave him good news of forgiveness for what had passed; ﴿and a noble reward﴾ for the righteous deeds he had sent forth, which is Paradise.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the messengership, which is one of the three foundations by which a person becomes a believer, He mentioned the Resurrection, which is another of the three foundations. The third is monotheism (tawḥīd). So He said ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, meaning after their death. Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥak went far in saying that the "reviving of them" means bringing them out of polytheism into faith.

﴿And We record what they have sent forth﴾, is a kinayah (allusion) for recompense, meaning: and We count it. He expressed the encompassing of His knowledge of their deeds by "writing," through which things are preserved. Zirr and Masruq read: "wa-yuktabu mā qaddamū wa-āthārahum" with the yāʾ, in the passive voice, and "what they sent forth" means deeds, and "their traces" means their steps toward the mosques. And it was said: the good and bad practices. It was also said: what they sent forth of bad deeds, and their traces are good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: what they sent forth of righteous deeds other than these, and what they left behind of good effect, such as knowledge they taught, a book they wrote, an endowment they established, or a building they constructed such as a mosque, a hostel, a bridge, or the like, or bad things such as a tax some oppressor imposed on the Muslims, or a coin that he introduced in which people are perplexed, or something he introduced by which people are turned away from the remembrance of God, such as melodies and frivolities. Likewise every good custom or bad custom that is followed, and similar to this is His saying, mighty and majestic, ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forth and left behind﴾ (al-Qiyamah 75:13), from his traces. End of quote. The majority read "wa-kulla shay'in" (and everything) in the accusative, as a case of ishtighāl (the verb governing a pronoun attached to the object, so the noun is put in the accusative). Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative, as a beginning (ibtidāʾ). "The Manifest Imam" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), said by Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Another group said it means the scrolls of deeds.

[p. 321] Surah Ya-Sin, peace be upon him. Makkiyya (Meccan), eighty-three verses.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Ya-Sin.﴾ ﴿By the Qur'an, full of wisdom,﴾ ﴿indeed you are among the messengers,﴾ ﴿upon a straight path.﴾ ﴿It is a revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless.﴾ ﴿The word has certainly come into effect upon most of them, so they do not believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, reaching to the chins, so they are held with their heads raised.﴾ ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and covered them, so they do not see.﴾ ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forth and their traces, and everything We have enumerated in a clear register.﴾ ﴿And present to them a parable: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it,﴾ ﴿when We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened them with a third; and they said, "Indeed, we are messengers sent to you."﴾ ﴿They said, "You are only human beings like us, and the Merciful has revealed nothing. You are only lying."﴾ ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you;﴾ ﴿and our duty is only to deliver the clear message."﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we see you as a bad omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and a painful punishment from us will surely touch you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Your omen is with yourselves. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a transgressing people."﴾ ﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers.﴾ ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and who are guided."﴾ ﴿"And why should I not worship He who created me, and to whom you will be returned?﴾ ﴿Shall I take gods besides Him? If the Merciful intends harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they save me.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I would then be in clear error.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."﴾ ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "Would that my people knew﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."﴾ ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven, nor were We ever to send down [one].﴾ ﴿It was but one cry, and at once they were extinguished.﴾ ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but that they mock him.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾ ﴿And all of them, they will surely be brought before Us.

And a sign for them is the dead earth which We have revived and brought forth from it grain, of which they eat.﴾ ﴿And We made in it gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and caused springs to gush forth from it,﴾ ﴿that they may eat of its fruit, and of what their hands produced. Will they not then be thankful?﴾ ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know.﴾ ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and at once they are in darkness.﴾ ﴿And the sun runs toward its resting place. That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations until it returns like the old dry palm stalk.﴾ ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; and each is floating in an orbit.﴾ ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship,﴾ ﴿and We created for them of its like that which they ride.﴾ ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to call for help, nor are they rescued,﴾ ﴿except as mercy from Us and enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you, that you may be shown mercy,"﴾ ﴿no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them but that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom God would have fed if He willed? You are only in clear error."﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿They await only a single cry that will seize them while they are disputing.﴾ ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor return to their families.﴾ ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and at once they will rush from the graves to their Lord.﴾ ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place? This is what the Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."﴾ ﴿It will be but one cry, and at once they will all be brought before Us.﴾ ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in anything, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in delight,﴾ ﴿they and their spouses, in shade, reclining on couches.﴾ ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they call for.﴾ ﴿"Peace!" a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ (p. 322) ﴿"And stand apart today, O guilty ones.﴾ ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you,﴾ ﴿and that you should worship Me? This is a straight path.﴾ ﴿And he had already led astray a great multitude among you. Did you not then use reason?﴾ ﴿This is Hell, which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, and they would race for the path; but how could they see?﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed or return.﴾ ﴿And whomever We let live long, We reverse him in creation. Will they not then understand?﴾ ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it suitable for him. It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an,﴾ ﴿to warn whoever is alive, and that the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have made, cattle, and they are their owners?﴾ ﴿And We have subjected them to them, so some of them they ride and some of them they eat.﴾ ﴿And for them in them are benefits and drinks. Will they not then be thankful?﴾ ﴿And they have taken gods besides God, hoping they might be helped.﴾ ﴿They cannot help them, and they are a mobilized host for them.﴾ ﴿So do not let their saying grieve you. Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ ﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop, and then he is an open adversary?﴾ ﴿And he has struck for Us a parable and forgotten his creation. He said, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knower of all creation.﴾ ﴿He who made for you from the green tree fire, and then you kindle from it."﴾ ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them? Yes, indeed; He is the All-Creating, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿So glory be to He in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

Qamaḥa al-ba'īru ra'sahu (قَمَحَ البَعِيرُ رَأْسَهُ): he raised his head, after drinking water; the discussion of it will come in full. Al-ʿurjūn (العُرْجُونُ): the stalk of the date cluster, from between the stem to its point of origin on the palm tree. Al-Zajjaj said: it is fuʿlūn, from al-inʿirāj, which is bending. Al-jadath (الجَدَثُ): the grave. It is also heard as jadaf, with the thāʾ replaced by fāʾ, as they said fumm for thumm; and as they replaced fāʾ with thāʾ, they said maʿthūr for maʿfūr. It is a kind of truffle. Al-maskh (المَسْخُ): transformation from one form into a hideous form. Al-ramīm (الرَّمِيمُ): decayed and crumbling.

* *

﴿Ya-Sin.﴾ ﴿By the Qur'an, full of wisdom,﴾ ﴿indeed you are among the messengers,﴾ ﴿upon a straight path.﴾ ﴿It is a revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless.﴾ ﴿The word has certainly come into effect upon most of them, so they do not believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, reaching to the chins, so they are held with their heads raised.﴾ ﴿And We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and covered them, so they do not see.﴾ ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful in the unseen. So give him good tidings of forgiveness and a noble reward.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forth and their traces, and everything We have enumerated in a clear register.﴾.

This surah is Meccan, except that a group claimed that His words ﴿and We record what they have sent forth﴾ and "their traces" were revealed concerning the Banu Salama of the Ansar, when they wanted to leave their homes and move to be near the Mosque of the Messenger; but this claim is not correct. It is also said: except His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47] and the verse that follows.

The discussion of the disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa) has preceded at the beginning of al-Baqara. Ibn Jubayr said here: it is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ), and its evidence is ﴿indeed you are among the messengers﴾. Sayyid al-Hamawi said:

"O soul, do not purify yourself with love, striving for affection, except for the family of Yasin."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is "O human" in Ethiopian (Habashi). And from him: it is in the dialect of Tayy, for they say īsān meaning insān, and they pluralize it as ayāsīn; so this is from it. Another group said: yā is a vocative particle, and the sīn stands in place of insān, from which a letter was removed and it was placed in its stead. Al-Zamakhshari said: if it is true that its meaning is "O human" in the dialect of Tayy, then its basis is to be ya-unaysīn, and the calling was so frequent on their tongues that they limited it to a part of it, as they said in the oath: mu-llāh and ayman-llāh. End of quote. What is reported from the Arabs in the diminutive of insān is unaysiyān, with a yāʾ followed by an alif, which indicates that its root is unaysān, because diminution returns things to their roots; and we do not know that they said its diminutive as unaysīn. And even on the assumption that it is a remnant of unaysīn, that is not permissible, neither being built on a ḍamma nor remaining pausal; because it is a vocative addressed directly, and also it is not permissible because it is a diminutive, and that is impermissible with regard to the prophethood. His saying "as they said in the oath mu-llāh and ayman-llāh" is one view. Among the grammarians there are those who say that mu is a particle of oath and is not a remnant of ayman.

It was read with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, with its pure imāla (inclination), and between the two pronunciations. The majority read with a sukūn on the nūn, assimilated into the wāw. Among the seven: al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, Warsh, and Ibn ʿAmir read it with clear pronunciation, while the rest of the seven read it as assimilated. Ibn Abi Ishaq and ʿIsa read with a fatḥa on the nūn. Qatada said: Yasin is an oath. Abu Hatim said: the analogy of this view is a fatḥa on the nūn, as you say: "Allāh, I will certainly do such-and-such." Al-Zajjaj said: a naṣb, as if he said: "Recite Yasin," and this is according to Sibawayh's view that it is a name for the surah. Al-Kalbi read with a ḍamma on the nūn, and said it is in the dialect of Tayy: "O human." Al-Sammak and Ibn Abi Ishaq also read with a kasra. It was said: the vowel is because of the meeting of two sukūns; the fatḥa is sought for lightness, the ḍamma like ḥaythu, and the kasra is on the basis of their meeting. If it is said that it is an oath, it may be in the naṣb position according to Abu Hatim's view, the rafʿ as a mubtada' (subject), like "the trust of God, I will surely stand," and the jarr by implying a particle of jarr, which is permissible according to the Kufans. (Al-Ḥakīm): either it is faʿīl in the sense of mufʿal, as you say: "I tied the honey, so it is ʿaqīd," meaning maʿqūd; or it is for emphasis from ḥākim; or it is in the sense of cause, that is, possessing wisdom.

﴿Upon a straight path﴾ is a second predicate, or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from him, peace be upon him, or from "the messengers," or it is related to "the messengers." The straight path is the law of Islam.

Talha, al-Ashhab and ʿIsa read, according to the varying reports from them, tanzīla with a naṣb as a verbal noun; Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read tanzīla with a naṣb as a verbal noun; the rest of the seven, Abu Bakr, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Hasan, al-Aʿraj, and al-Aʿmash read it with a rafʿ as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is a revelation. Abu Ḥaywa, al-Yazidi, and al-Qursi from Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba read it with a jarr, either as an apposition to "the Qur'an," or as a description by a verbal noun. (Li-tundhira) is related to tanzīl or to arsalnā implied.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 1–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿What their fathers were warned of﴾. Ikrimah said: "mā" means "alladhī" (the one that), i.e., "the thing that their fathers were warned of, of the punishment." Then "mā" is the second object, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ (al-Naba 78:40). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "It is also possible that mā is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), meaning ﴿what their fathers were warned﴾, and the fathers in this case are the earliest of the descendants of Ismaʿil, among whom warning had existed." And "fa-hum" (so they) according to this interpretation means "fa-innahum" (for they). The fāʾ is used to separate one clause from another clause that stands as a relative clause (ṣilah), so it connects to His saying ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾. The phrase "to warn" (li-tundhira) is like when you say: "I sent you to so-and-so to warn him, for he is heedless, or rather he is heedless." Qatadah said: "mā" is a negation, meaning that their fathers were not warned. In this case, "their fathers" are the nearer ones among them, and "mā undhira" is in the position of a qualifier, meaning "whose fathers were not warned." "Fa-hum ghafilūn" (so they are heedless) is connected to the negation, meaning: they were not warned, so they are heedless, since their not being warned is the cause of their heedlessness. By considering the fathers in terms of their antiquity and nearness, the contradiction between warning and its negation disappears.

﴿Indeed, the word has come into effect against most of them﴾. The well-known view is that the word is ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ (Hud 11:119). It was also said: it means that the necessity of punishment was already decreed in His knowledge. And it was said: "the word" (al-qawl) [p. 324] is what God said through the tongue of the messengers, concerning monotheism and other matters, and its proof became clear; so most of them do not believe after that. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles upon their necks﴾ and what follows is that it is literal, not metaphorical (istiʿārah, metaphor). When God, exalted is He, stated that they do not believe, He then informed about some of their conditions in the Hereafter when they enter the Fire. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "His saying ﴿So We covered them, and they cannot see﴾ weakens this view, because the sight of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection is sharp, seeing the ugliness of their state." End of quote. But this does not weaken it. Do you not see His saying ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ (al-Isra 17:97), and His saying ﴿He will say: My Lord, why have You gathered me blind?﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:125)? Or His saying ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾ (Qaf 50:22) may be a kinayah (metonymy, allusion) for his grasp of what he is coming to, as if he sees it. The majority said: that is a metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Ishaq said: it is a metaphor for the state of the disbelievers who intended harm to the Messenger; God made this an example for them in restraining them from him and preventing them from harming him when they plotted against him. Al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Farrāʾ said: it is a metaphor for their withholding from spending in the way of God, as He said ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ (al-Isra 17:29). Ikrimah said: it was revealed when Abu Jahl intended to strike him with a great stone, and in other such occasions, but God prevented him. This is close to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It is narrated that "Abu Jahl carried a stone to throw at the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying, and his hands were bent up to his neck, so that he returned to his companions with the stone stuck in his hand. They could not free it except with great effort. Then he took another stone, but when he approached the Messenger, God blinded his sight so he did not see him. He returned to his companions and could not see them until they called out to him." So the shackle becoming a metaphor refers to the restraint of Abu Jahl and others in this story. And since Abu Jahl's companions were content with what he intended to do, this was attributed to a group. Another group said: it is a metaphor for God's preventing them from faith and His placing a barrier between them and it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is the most preferred of the views, because when God mentioned that they do not believe, due to what had been decreed for them from eternity, He followed this with making for them a restraint and an encompassing wretchedness in which their state is like that of those who are shackled. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an image (tamthīl) of their insistence upon disbelief, and that there is no way to their claim of [being guided], as He made them like the shackled, head-raised (muqmaḥūn), in that they do not turn toward the truth, nor bend their necks toward it, nor lower their heads to it; and like those confined between two barriers, who see neither what is before them nor what is behind them, in that they have no reflection and do not see, meaning they are blind to considering the signs of God, exalted is He. End of quote. In his words there is a hidden trace of Muʿtazilism (dasīsat al-iʿtizāl). Do you not see that the statement of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah, the orthodox majority) is "a metaphor for God's preventing them from faith," while al-Zamakhshari's statement is "an image of their insistence," and he attributes the actions that he counts to them and not to God? The ghull (shackle) is that which surrounds the neck, for the sake of rebuke, constriction, punishment, and captivity. With the neck, both hands or one hand [are bound], for the sake of explanation (taʿlīl). The apparent reference of the pronoun in "fa-hiya" (so they are) is to the shackles, because they are the ones mentioned and spoken of. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: they are broad, reaching the chin with their edges, and the chin is the junction of the two jaws, so the shackled man is compelled to raise his face toward the sky, and that is iqmāḥ (raising the head with lowered gaze), which is close to the meaning of being held with a halter in appearance. Al-Zamakhshari said: the shackles, the origin of which is "up to the chins," are fastened to them. That is because the collar of the shackle, which is around the neck of the shackled one, has at the meeting of its two ends under the chin a ring in which the head of the post sits, passing through the ring up to the chin, so it does not let him lower his head or lay his nape down, so he remains always raising his head. End of quote. Al-Farrāʾ said: qamḥ is that in which one lowers his gaze after raising his head. Al-Zajjaj said something similar, saying: it is said "qamaḥa al-baʿīr raʾsahu ʿan rayy" (the camel raised its head away from water) and "qamaḥa" (it did so). Abu ʿUbayda said: qamaḥa qumūḥan: he raised his head from the pool without drinking, and the plural is qiṣāḥ (camels that raise their heads). From this is the saying of Bishr, describing the death of one of them so that they would bury him:

"We sit around its sides, lowering our gaze like camels with raised heads (qiṣāḥ)."

Al-Layth said: it is the raising of the camel's head when it drinks bad water, then it returns. Al-Zajjaj said: the two months of the winter (al-kānūnayn) are called "shahrā qimāḥ" because when camels come to water they raise their heads because of its extreme coldness. Abu Zayd recited the verse of al-Hudhali:

"A youth, the son of the mighty, when we pass the winter, and provisions are loved in the two months of qimāḥ."

He narrated it with a ḍamma on the qāf, and Ibn al-Sikkit with a kasra, and both are dialects. The two were called "the two months of qimāḥ" because every creature with a liver dislikes drinking water in them. Al-Ḥasan said: al-qāmiḥ is one who raises his gaze toward the place of his foot. Mujahid said: the one raising the head, the one placing his hand over his mouth. Al-Ṭabarī said: the pronoun in "fa-hiya" refers to the hands, even though no mention of them preceded, because its place is clear from the meaning, since the shackle is only on the neck with the two hands, which is why the shackle was named "jāmiʿah" (gatherer), for it gathers the hand and the neck. ʿAli, may God honor his face, saw people raising their heads, so he placed his hands under his jaws and pressed them and raised his head. Al-Zamakhshari said: he made the qimāḥ the result of His saying ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾. If the pronoun referred to the hands, the sense of causation in the qimāḥ would not be apparent; and this placement of a pronoun involves a kind of contrivance and abandoning of the apparent meaning, which the meaning itself calls for, toward falsehood, which turns away from the clear truth toward a confused falsehood. End of quote.

The reading of ʿAbd Allah, Ikrimah, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir and Ḥafṣ is (saddan) with a fatḥa on the sīn in both places (sadd and sadd); the majority read it with a ḍamma. The explanation of sadd was given in al-Kahf. The majority read ﴿fa-aghshaynāhum﴾ with the ghayn dotted; Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Ibn Yaʿmar, Ikrimah, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Sirin, al-Ḥasan, Abu Rajaʾ, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Yazid al-Barbari, Yazid ibn al-Muhallab, Abu Ḥanifa and Ibn Miqsam read it with an ʿayn, from ʿashāʾ (night blindness), which is weakness of sight, meaning "We placed upon them a covering."

﴿And it is the same for them﴾ and the verse. Its explanation and grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) were discussed previously in the beginning of al-Baqarah.

﴿You can only warn﴾. ﴿To warn a people﴾ was mentioned earlier, but since it was decreed for them that they would not believe, until He said ﴿and it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾, the warning was of no benefit, since its benefit was absent. So He said ﴿You can only warn﴾, meaning a warning that benefits whoever follows the Reminder (al-dhikr), which is the Qur'an. Qatadah said: or the admonition.

﴿And fears the Most Merciful﴾, meaning the one characterized by mercy. Though mercy may return to hope, yet with his knowledge of His mercy, he fears Him out of fear that He might deprive him of what He has bestowed upon him in the unseen (bi-l-ghayb), meaning in privacy, when the person is absent from the sight of other people. When He instilled warning in him, He gave him good news of forgiveness for what had passed; ﴿and a noble reward﴾ for the righteous deeds he had sent forth, which is Paradise.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the messengership, which is one of the three foundations by which a person becomes a believer, He mentioned the Resurrection, which is another of the three foundations. The third is monotheism (tawḥīd). So He said ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾, meaning after their death. Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥak went far in saying that the "reviving of them" means bringing them out of polytheism into faith.

﴿And We record what they have sent forth﴾, is a kinayah (allusion) for recompense, meaning: and We count it. He expressed the encompassing of His knowledge of their deeds by "writing," through which things are preserved. Zirr and Masruq read: "wa-yuktabu mā qaddamū wa-āthārahum" with the yāʾ, in the passive voice, and "what they sent forth" means deeds, and "their traces" means their steps toward the mosques. And it was said: the good and bad practices. It was also said: what they sent forth of bad deeds, and their traces are good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari said: what they sent forth of righteous deeds other than these, and what they left behind of good effect, such as knowledge they taught, a book they wrote, an endowment they established, or a building they constructed such as a mosque, a hostel, a bridge, or the like, or bad things such as a tax some oppressor imposed on the Muslims, or a coin that he introduced in which people are perplexed, or something he introduced by which people are turned away from the remembrance of God, such as melodies and frivolities. Likewise every good custom or bad custom that is followed, and similar to this is His saying, mighty and majestic, ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forth and left behind﴾ (al-Qiyamah 75:13), from his traces. End of quote. The majority read "wa-kulla shay'in" (and everything) in the accusative, as a case of ishtighāl (the verb governing a pronoun attached to the object, so the noun is put in the accusative). Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative, as a beginning (ibtidāʾ). "The Manifest Imam" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), said by Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Another group said it means the scrolls of deeds.

[p. 326]

﴿And strike for them an example: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it.﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:13] ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, and they said, "Indeed we are messengers to you."﴾ [36:14] ﴿They said, "You are only humans like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ [36:15] ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you."﴾ [36:16] ﴿And we are not [responsible] except for clear notification.﴾ [36:17] ﴿They said, "Indeed we consider you a bad omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and painful punishment will surely touch you from us."﴾ [36:18] ﴿They said, "Your omen is with you. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a people who transgress."﴾ [36:19] ﴿And there came from the far end of the city a man running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ [36:20] ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and they are guided.﴾ ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me and to whom you will be returned?﴾ ﴿Shall I take other than Him as gods? If the Most Merciful intends me harm, their intercession will not benefit me at all, nor can they save me.﴾ ﴿Indeed I would then be in clear error.﴾ ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "I wish my people knew﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."﴾.

The discussion of ﴿وَاضْرِبْ﴾ (wa-ḍrib, "and strike") together with "the example" has already been covered in His saying ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [2:26]. "The town" is Antioch (Antakiya), and there is no disagreement about the story of the companions of the town.

﴿When the messengers came to it﴾ [36:13]: they were three, and He grouped them together in the coming, although they differed about the time of the coming.

﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [36:14]: The apparent meaning of "We sent" is that they were prophets whom God sent, and what the sent ones said to them, ﴿You are only humans like us﴾ [36:15], supports this. This kind of exchange happens only with someone whom God has sent. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ka'b. Qatada and others among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) said: Jesus, peace be upon him, sent them after he had been raised and the one upon whom the likeness was cast had been crucified, and the disciples then scattered throughout the regions. God then recounted the story of those who went to Antioch, whose people were worshippers of idols. This is the view of Wahb and Ka'b al-Ahbar. Al-Naqqash ibn Sam'an reported: "Yuhanna." Muqatil said: "Tuman" and "Yunus." (fa-kadhdhabūhumā) means: they called them to God, and the two informed them that they were messengers of God, ﴿but they denied them﴾. ﴿So We strengthened [them] with a third﴾ [36:14]: that is, We made [them] strong and firm. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Qutayba, who said: it is said "ta'azzaza lahm al-naqa" (the camel's meat became firm) when it hardened. Others said: it is said that rain "yu'azziz" the land when it packs and firms it, and hard ground is called "al-qur'ān." This is according to the reading with the doubled zāy (fa-azzaznā with shadda), which is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, and Aban read it with a light (unstressed) zāy. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: "fa-ghalabnā" (so We overcame). He said: this comes from their saying "man 'azzanī" (whoever overpowers me), and from His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [38:23]. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read [p. 327] "bi-l-thālith" with the definite article (alif and lām), and "al-thālith" is Shim'un al-Safa, according to Ibn Abbas. Ka'b and Wahb said: Shalum; and it was said: Yunus. The object of fa-azzaznā with doubling is omitted, meaning: We strengthened the two with a third. With the unstressed form, the meaning is: We overcame them, that is, by the argument of a third and what is gently conveyed through reaching the call to God, even to the king, as is mentioned in their story, and this (or part of it) will come, God willing.

[The word] "messengers" (mursalūn) came first without the lām because it is the beginning of an announcement, and so it does not need emphasis after the exchange. "Indeed we are messengers to you" (la-mursalūn) has the emphatic lām because it is an answer to a denial. This was a community that denied prophethood by its saying ﴿the Most Merciful has sent down nothing﴾ [36:15]. The messengers answered them by referring knowledge to God and being content with His knowledge, and informed them that they were responsible only for conveying [the message], and that they were not responsible for their guidance or their misguidance. There is a warning in this for them. The conveyance is described as "clear" (al-mubīn), meaning clear with signs that witness to the truth of the sending, such as the miracles mentioned in this story: healing the blind-born and the leper and reviving the dead.

﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾ [36:18]: that is, we consider you ill-omened (tashā'amnā). Muqatil said: the rain was withheld from them. Another said: leprosy spread among them when they denied the messengers. Ibn Atiyya said: The apparent meaning is that their taking of omens was the cause of what entered among them of division of word and temptation of people. This is like the omen-taking of the Quraysh regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and like what Moses, peace be upon him, was addressed with. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is because they disliked their religion and their souls recoiled from it. It is the habit of the ignorant to attribute blessings to everything they incline toward, desire, and whose nature accepts, and to consider ill omen in what they recoil from and dislike. If good fortune or affliction befalls them, they say: "This is by the blessing of such-and-such, and this is by the ill omen of such-and-such," as God related about the Copts: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they take omen from Moses and those with him﴾ [7:131], and about the polytheists of Mecca: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say: "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [4:78]. End of quotation. Qatada said: "If something befalls us, it is because of you." (la-narjumannahum) means: we will stone them with stones, as Qatada said.

﴿a painful punishment﴾ [36:18] is the burning.

﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19]: that is, your share (ḥaẓẓ) and what has come to you of good or evil is with you, that is, from your own actions. It is not because of us; rather, it is because of your disbelief. Al-Hasan, Ibn Hurmuz, Amr ibn Ubayd, and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read ṭayrukum with a silent yā' after the ṭā'. It was reported that al-Hasan read ittayyurukum, the verbal noun (maṣdar) of ittayyara, whose original form is tatayyara, in which the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā', so a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) was introduced in the past tense and in the verbal noun. The majority read ṭā'irukum on the pattern fā'il.

The majority read ﴿Is it because you were reminded?﴾ [36:19] with two hamzas: the first is the interrogative hamza, and the second is the hamza of the conditional particle in (in). The Kufans and Ibn Amir softened it, and the rest of the Seven (Readers) made it intermediate (sahhalahā). Zirr read it with two open hamzas, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far and Talha, except that the second is pronounced between-between (bayn bayn). A poet, in its realization, said:

"Ara-in kunta Dāwūda ibna Aḥwā mar-ḥalan / fa-lastu bi-dā'in li-ibni ʿammika maḥramā"

[Translator's note: a line of poetry; retained as given.]

Al-Majishuni, who is Abu Salama Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Salama al-Madani, read it with one open hamza. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra-ha (hā' with kasra). Abu ʿAmr in one transmission, and Zirr also, read it with a madda (lengthening) before the open hamza, having found the juxtaposition of the two heavy, so he separated them with an alif. Abu Ja'far also, al-Hasan also, Qatada, Isa al-Hamdani, and al-A'mash read ʾayna with an open hamza, a silent yā', and an open nūn, as a adverb of place (ẓarf makān). This was also reported from Isa al-Thaqafi.

The first reading means: "If you are reminded, you take omens," with the omitted element being made the focus of the interrogation, according to the view of Sibawayh; or making it a conditional, according to the view of Yunus. If you posit it as a present (verb), it would be jussive (majzūm). The second reading means: "Because you were reminded, did you take omens?" Here in is an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlihi, object of cause). The same applies to the single open hamza and the one with a madda before the open hamza. Reading the kasra-ed hamza alone, the in is a conditional particle with the meaning of an announcement: "If you are reminded, you take omens." The last reading, with ayna, has a conditional adverb whose answer is omitted for indication, and its estimate is: "Wherever you are reminded, your omen accompanies you," which is indicated by His saying ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19]. Whoever permits placing the answer (jazāʾ) before the condition (sharṭ), namely the Kufans, Abu Zayd, and al-Mubarrad, may hold that the answer is ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19], and its original form was: "Wherever you are reminded, then your omen is with you," and when it was placed first the fā' was omitted. The majority read dhukkirtum with a doubled kāf. Abu Ja'far, Khalid ibn Iyas, Talha, al-Hasan, and Qatada, Abu Haywa, al-A'mash through the route of Zā'ida, and al-Asma'i from Nafi' read it with the light form.

﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [36:19]: exceeding the limit in your misguidance, and therefore the misfortune has come to you.

﴿And there came from the far end of the city a man running﴾ [36:20]: his name is Habib, according to Ibn Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Mujahid, and Muqatil. It was said: he was the son of Isra'il, and he was a launderer. It was also said: a cobbler. It was said: he used to carve idols, and it is possible that he combined these trades. ﴿From the far end of the city﴾ [36:20] means: from the most distant of its places. It was said: he was outside the city tending his crop. It was said: he was in a cave worshipping his Lord. It was said: he was a leper, and the farthest of the gates of the city was assigned to him, and he worshipped idols for seventy years, calling them to remove his affliction. When the messengers called him to the worship of God, he said: "Is there a sign?" They said: "Yes, we call upon our Lord, the Capable, who will relieve you of what afflicts you." He said: "This is wondrous! For seventy years I have called upon these gods and they could not do it. Will your Lord relieve it in a single morning?" They said: "Yes, our Lord is capable of whatever He wills, and these [idols] benefit nothing and harm nothing." So he believed. They called upon their Lord, and God removed what was on him, as if there had never been any affliction in him. He then turned to earning a living, and whenever he walked, he gave away his earnings: half for his dependents, and half he gave as food [to others]. When his people resolved to kill the messengers, he came to them and said: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾ [36:20]. This Habib was among those who believed in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and between them were six hundred years, just as Tubba' al-Akbar believed in him, and Waraqa ibn Nawfal and others. No one believed in any prophet other than him except after his appearance.

Ibn Abi Layla said: the foremost of the nations are three, who never disbelieved for the blink of an eye: ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, the companion of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of Pharaoh's family. Al-Zamakhshari cited the saying of Ibn Abi Layla as a ḥadīth from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was mentioned before that his condition was that he was a leper, who worshipped idols for seventy years, and God knows best. Here ﴿from the far end of the city﴾ [36:20] came first, while in the narratives it came later, and this is one of the variations of eloquence (tafannun fī al-balāgha).

﴿A man running﴾ [36:20] means walking on his two feet.

﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ [36:20]. The apparent meaning is that he did not say this after his belief had preceded, as was mentioned in a previous story. It was also said: Jesus came and heard their saying and understood it in what he understood. It is reported that he followed up their matter and tested them by saying to them: "Do you ask for a wage for this call of yours?" They said: "No." Then he called his people to follow them and to believe in them, and argued against them with his words: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and they are guided﴾ [36:21], that is, they are guided by God. He first commanded them to follow the messengers, that is, they are God's messengers to you, so follow them. Then he commanded them a second time with a comprehensive sentence in encouragement: that they do not ask for any of the worldly goods of theirs, and that they are guided by their guidance, so that they combine the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Some grammarians have permitted that man (whoever) be an apposition (badal) to "the messengers," in which the governing element appears, as it appears when it is a preposition, as in His saying ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾ [43:33]. The majority do not parse as an apposition anything in which the raising or governing element is explicitly stated; rather, they make that restricted to the preposition. When the raising and governing element is through following (tatbī', i.e., the adjective-like attribution), not through apposition. In His saying ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾ there is evidence for the deficiency of one who takes a wage for something from the acts of the Law that are obligatory upon him, such as prayer.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 21–27 (part 2 of 2):

When He had commanded them to follow the messengers, he began to present the proof for following them and for worshipping God. He presented it in the form of counsel to himself, while he actually intended it as counsel to them, so as to be gentle with them and to win them over. This is more effective in sincere advice, since he wants for them only what he wants for himself. So he placed his statement, ﴿And why should I not worship the One who originated me?﴾, in the place of: "And why should you not worship the One who originated you?" That is why he said, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. Had he not intended this, he would have said, "And to Him I will return."

Then he continued the speech in the same manner, addressing himself, saying, ﴿Shall I take gods besides Him?﴾, which are powerless in everything, neither benefiting nor harming. If the Most Merciful should intend harm for me, their intercession would not avail, and they could not rescue me from it. He first expressed the lack of standing, that their intercession would not benefit, and then the lack of power. He expressed the absence of rescue, since it is its consequence. (p. 329)

Regarding the ya' of the speaker in (yuridni), Talhah al-Sammān read it with a fatha, as in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, the readers are Talhah ibn Musarrif, 'Isa al-Hamadhani, and Abu Ja'far, and it is also transmitted from Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was read as ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ meaning: 'if He makes me one who brings harm upon myself.'" End of quote. This, God knows best, is an opinion in the books of qira'at (canonical and variant recitations). The reading yuridni with a fatha on the ya' led him to suppose that it is the prefixed ya' of the imperfect (ya' al-mudara'ah), so he made the verb transitive by means of the ya' that causes transitivity, like the hamza, and therefore he added to it the causative hamza (hamzat al-ta'diyah) and governed two objects with it. What is found in the books of the shadh (irregular, non-canonical) readers is that it is the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah) which is deleted both in writing and in pronunciation because of the meeting of two sukun (unvocalized letters). In the book of Ibn Khalawayh he says: "with a fatha on the ya' of possession." In al-Lawami' he says: "in ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ with the fatha, which is the original form of the ya' according to the Basrans, but this one is deleted, meaning the Basran one, i.e., the one affirmed by the Barbari script, visible to the eye, because it is written, unlike the one deleted both in writing and in pronunciation, which is not seen by the eye." (Inni idhan) — if I do not worship the One who originated me and take gods besides Him, I would be in clear error, evident to anyone with sound intellect.

Then he openly declared his faith and proclaimed the truth, addressing his people, saying: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord﴾, that is, the One you disbelieved in, ﴿so listen to me﴾, that is, listen to my words and obey me. I have alerted you to the truth, that worship is only for the One from whom your origin is and to whom your return is. The apparent sense is that the address with the kaf and the mim and the waw is to his people, and the command is meant as emphasis and alerting. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b, and Wahb. It was also said: by His words ﴿so listen to me﴾ he addressed the messengers, as a way of calling them to witness and entrusting the matter to them. It was also said: the address in (bi-Rabbikum) and in (fasma'uni) is to the messengers. When he advised his people, they began to stone him, so he hastened toward the messengers before he could be killed and said that, that is, "Listen to my faith and bear witness for me to it."

﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is a genuine command. It was also said: its meaning is "Paradise has become obligatory for you," so it is a report that he has deserved to enter it, and this will not happen except after resurrection. The Qur'an does not state that he was killed. Al-Hasan said: when his people wanted to kill him, God raised him to heaven, so he is in Paradise, not dying until the heavens perish and Paradise is destroyed; when God restores Paradise, he will enter it. It was also said: when he said that, they lifted him to the king, and he prolonged the speech with them to occupy them from killing the messengers, until he openly declared his faith to them. They then rushed upon him and killed him by trampling with their feet until his heart came out from his back, and he was thrown into a well, which is al-Rass. Al-Suddi said: they pelted him with stones while he was saying, "O God, guide my people," until he died. Al-Kalbi said: they threw him into a pit and cast earth upon him, and he died. From al-Hasan: they burned him with fire, hung him at the gate of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. It was also said: they sawed him with saws until it came out between his legs. From Qatadah: God admitted him into Paradise while he was in it alive and provided for, referring to His words, ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169], rejoicing.

In the copy of the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah that we consulted, there is the following text: The majority read ﴿fasma'una﴾ with a fatha on the nun. Abu Hatim said: "This is an error and is not permitted, because it is a command, so either the nun must be dropped, or it must be kasra as a fixed ending (bina'). End of quote," meaning the ya' of the speaker, and the nun is the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah). His statement "the majority read" is a gross error, and it cannot be, God knows best, except from the copyist. Rather, as far as I know, the readers, all seven of them and the shadh ones, agree on the kasra of the nun, except what is transmitted from 'Ismah from 'Asim with the fatha on the nun, mentioned in al-Kamil of the author Abu al-Qasim al-Hudhali. Perhaps this is an error from 'Ismah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Here there is an omitted element, which the traditions and reports have transmitted continuously, namely that they killed him, and it was said to him at his death, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ This happened, God knows best, when his station in it was shown to him and he was assured that he was among its inhabitants, so he saw what gladdened his eye. When this happened, he wished that his people would know of it." End of quote. The saying ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ seems to be an answer to someone asking about his condition at meeting his Lord after that steadfastness in his religion, so it was said, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ The construction "It was said to him" was not used, because it is known that he is the one addressed. His wish that his people would know of this is connected to an assumed question about what he had said at that moment, as a sign of advice and sincerity toward them, meaning: if they knew that, they would believe in God. In a hadith: "He advised his people while alive and dead." (p. 330) It was also said: he wished for that so that they would know that they had been in error regarding his matter, while he was right, so they would regret, be grieved by that, and be given glad tidings of it. It is naturally found in human temperament that whoever attains good outside his homeland wishes that his neighbors and peers among whom he grew up would know of it. We have been told that the vizier Dhink al-Din al-Masiri, who was a vizier to the king of Egypt, went to his village from which he came, which is Masir, one of the smallest villages of Egypt. He was asked about that, and he said: "I wanted the old women of Masir to see me in this state I am in." The poet said:

Honor is sought and sought after,
and the dearest of it is what is attained in one's homeland.

The apparent meaning of what is in His words ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ is that it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). They allowed that it could mean "that which" (alladhi), with a returning pronoun omitted, its estimated form being: "with that which my Lord has forgiven me of sins." This is not good, because it would lead to a wish that they know about the forgiven sins, whereas what is fitting is a wish that they know about the forgiveness of his sins and that he was made one of the honored. Al-Farra' permitted that it be an interrogative (istifham). Al-Kisa'i said: "If this were correct, meaning the interrogative, it would say bima without an alif." Al-Farra' said: "It is permissible to say bima with the alif," and he cited verses for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be interrogative, meaning: 'for what reason has my Lord forgiven me?' He means what he had done with them of steadfastness in exalting the religion of God, to the point that it was said that your saying ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ with the alif dropped is better, although keeping it is permissible, so he said: 'I have known by what I did this, and by what I did.'" End of quote. The well-known view is that keeping the alif in the interrogative ma, when a preposition has come before it, is restricted to poetic necessity, as in the saying:

Upon what did the vile one revile me,
like a pig rolling in ashes?

Its omission is the more common form in speech, as in the saying:

Upon what does the spear keep weighing on my shoulder
when I do not thrust, when the horses charge?

And it was read: ﴿among the honored﴾, with a shadda on the ra' and a fatha on the kaf; the majority read it with a sukun on the kaf and a light ra'.

[p. 326]

﴿And strike for them an example: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it.﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:13] ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, and they said, "Indeed we are messengers to you."﴾ [36:14] ﴿They said, "You are only humans like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ [36:15] ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you."﴾ [36:16] ﴿And we are not [responsible] except for clear notification.﴾ [36:17] ﴿They said, "Indeed we consider you a bad omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and painful punishment will surely touch you from us."﴾ [36:18] ﴿They said, "Your omen is with you. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a people who transgress."﴾ [36:19] ﴿And there came from the far end of the city a man running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ [36:20] ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and they are guided.﴾ ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me and to whom you will be returned?﴾ ﴿Shall I take other than Him as gods? If the Most Merciful intends me harm, their intercession will not benefit me at all, nor can they save me.﴾ ﴿Indeed I would then be in clear error.﴾ ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "I wish my people knew﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."﴾.

The discussion of ﴿وَاضْرِبْ﴾ (wa-ḍrib, "and strike") together with "the example" has already been covered in His saying ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [2:26]. "The town" is Antioch (Antakiya), and there is no disagreement about the story of the companions of the town.

﴿When the messengers came to it﴾ [36:13]: they were three, and He grouped them together in the coming, although they differed about the time of the coming.

﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [36:14]: The apparent meaning of "We sent" is that they were prophets whom God sent, and what the sent ones said to them, ﴿You are only humans like us﴾ [36:15], supports this. This kind of exchange happens only with someone whom God has sent. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ka'b. Qatada and others among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) said: Jesus, peace be upon him, sent them after he had been raised and the one upon whom the likeness was cast had been crucified, and the disciples then scattered throughout the regions. God then recounted the story of those who went to Antioch, whose people were worshippers of idols. This is the view of Wahb and Ka'b al-Ahbar. Al-Naqqash ibn Sam'an reported: "Yuhanna." Muqatil said: "Tuman" and "Yunus." (fa-kadhdhabūhumā) means: they called them to God, and the two informed them that they were messengers of God, ﴿but they denied them﴾. ﴿So We strengthened [them] with a third﴾ [36:14]: that is, We made [them] strong and firm. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Qutayba, who said: it is said "ta'azzaza lahm al-naqa" (the camel's meat became firm) when it hardened. Others said: it is said that rain "yu'azziz" the land when it packs and firms it, and hard ground is called "al-qur'ān." This is according to the reading with the doubled zāy (fa-azzaznā with shadda), which is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, and Aban read it with a light (unstressed) zāy. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: "fa-ghalabnā" (so We overcame). He said: this comes from their saying "man 'azzanī" (whoever overpowers me), and from His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [38:23]. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read [p. 327] "bi-l-thālith" with the definite article (alif and lām), and "al-thālith" is Shim'un al-Safa, according to Ibn Abbas. Ka'b and Wahb said: Shalum; and it was said: Yunus. The object of fa-azzaznā with doubling is omitted, meaning: We strengthened the two with a third. With the unstressed form, the meaning is: We overcame them, that is, by the argument of a third and what is gently conveyed through reaching the call to God, even to the king, as is mentioned in their story, and this (or part of it) will come, God willing.

[The word] "messengers" (mursalūn) came first without the lām because it is the beginning of an announcement, and so it does not need emphasis after the exchange. "Indeed we are messengers to you" (la-mursalūn) has the emphatic lām because it is an answer to a denial. This was a community that denied prophethood by its saying ﴿the Most Merciful has sent down nothing﴾ [36:15]. The messengers answered them by referring knowledge to God and being content with His knowledge, and informed them that they were responsible only for conveying [the message], and that they were not responsible for their guidance or their misguidance. There is a warning in this for them. The conveyance is described as "clear" (al-mubīn), meaning clear with signs that witness to the truth of the sending, such as the miracles mentioned in this story: healing the blind-born and the leper and reviving the dead.

﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾ [36:18]: that is, we consider you ill-omened (tashā'amnā). Muqatil said: the rain was withheld from them. Another said: leprosy spread among them when they denied the messengers. Ibn Atiyya said: The apparent meaning is that their taking of omens was the cause of what entered among them of division of word and temptation of people. This is like the omen-taking of the Quraysh regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and like what Moses, peace be upon him, was addressed with. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is because they disliked their religion and their souls recoiled from it. It is the habit of the ignorant to attribute blessings to everything they incline toward, desire, and whose nature accepts, and to consider ill omen in what they recoil from and dislike. If good fortune or affliction befalls them, they say: "This is by the blessing of such-and-such, and this is by the ill omen of such-and-such," as God related about the Copts: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they take omen from Moses and those with him﴾ [7:131], and about the polytheists of Mecca: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say: "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [4:78]. End of quotation. Qatada said: "If something befalls us, it is because of you." (la-narjumannahum) means: we will stone them with stones, as Qatada said.

﴿a painful punishment﴾ [36:18] is the burning.

﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19]: that is, your share (ḥaẓẓ) and what has come to you of good or evil is with you, that is, from your own actions. It is not because of us; rather, it is because of your disbelief. Al-Hasan, Ibn Hurmuz, Amr ibn Ubayd, and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read ṭayrukum with a silent yā' after the ṭā'.
