In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, the readers are Talhah ibn Musarrif, 'Isa al-Hamadhani, and Abu Ja'far, and it is also transmitted from Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was read as ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ meaning: 'if He makes me one who brings harm upon myself.'" End of quote. This, God knows best, is an opinion in the books of qira'at (canonical and variant recitations). The reading yuridni with a fatha on the ya' led him to suppose that it is the prefixed ya' of the imperfect (ya' al-mudara'ah), so he made the verb transitive by means of the ya' that causes transitivity, like the hamza, and therefore he added to it the causative hamza (hamzat al-ta'diyah) and governed two objects with it. What is found in the books of the shadh (irregular, non-canonical) readers is that it is the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah) which is deleted both in writing and in pronunciation because of the meeting of two sukun (unvocalized letters). In the book of Ibn Khalawayh he says: "with a fatha on the ya' of possession." In al-Lawami' he says: "in ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ with the fatha, which is the original form of the ya' according to the Basrans, but this one is deleted, meaning the Basran one, i.e., the one affirmed by the Barbari script, visible to the eye, because it is written, unlike the one deleted both in writing and in pronunciation, which is not seen by the eye." (Inni idhan) — if I do not worship the One who originated me and take gods besides Him, I would be in clear error, evident to anyone with sound intellect.

Then he openly declared his faith and proclaimed the truth, addressing his people, saying: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord﴾, that is, the One you disbelieved in, ﴿so listen to me﴾, that is, listen to my words and obey me. I have alerted you to the truth, that worship is only for the One from whom your origin is and to whom your return is. The apparent sense is that the address with the kaf and the mim and the waw is to his people, and the command is meant as emphasis and alerting. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b, and Wahb. It was also said: by His words ﴿so listen to me﴾ he addressed the messengers, as a way of calling them to witness and entrusting the matter to them. It was also said: the address in (bi-Rabbikum) and in (fasma'uni) is to the messengers. When he advised his people, they began to stone him, so he hastened toward the messengers before he could be killed and said that, that is, "Listen to my faith and bear witness for me to it."

﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is a genuine command. It was also said: its meaning is "Paradise has become obligatory for you," so it is a report that he has deserved to enter it, and this will not happen except after resurrection. The Qur'an does not state that he was killed. Al-Hasan said: when his people wanted to kill him, God raised him to heaven, so he is in Paradise, not dying until the heavens perish and Paradise is destroyed; when God restores Paradise, he will enter it. It was also said: when he said that, they lifted him to the king, and he prolonged the speech with them to occupy them from killing the messengers, until he openly declared his faith to them. They then rushed upon him and killed him by trampling with their feet until his heart came out from his back, and he was thrown into a well, which is al-Rass. Al-Suddi said: they pelted him with stones while he was saying, "O God, guide my people," until he died. Al-Kalbi said: they threw him into a pit and cast earth upon him, and he died. From al-Hasan: they burned him with fire, hung him at the gate of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. It was also said: they sawed him with saws until it came out between his legs. From Qatadah: God admitted him into Paradise while he was in it alive and provided for, referring to His words, ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169], rejoicing.

In the copy of the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah that we consulted, there is the following text: The majority read ﴿fasma'una﴾ with a fatha on the nun. Abu Hatim said: "This is an error and is not permitted, because it is a command, so either the nun must be dropped, or it must be kasra as a fixed ending (bina'). End of quote," meaning the ya' of the speaker, and the nun is the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah). His statement "the majority read" is a gross error, and it cannot be, God knows best, except from the copyist. Rather, as far as I know, the readers, all seven of them and the shadh ones, agree on the kasra of the nun, except what is transmitted from 'Ismah from 'Asim with the fatha on the nun, mentioned in al-Kamil of the author Abu al-Qasim al-Hudhali. Perhaps this is an error from 'Ismah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Here there is an omitted element, which the traditions and reports have transmitted continuously, namely that they killed him, and it was said to him at his death, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ This happened, God knows best, when his station in it was shown to him and he was assured that he was among its inhabitants, so he saw what gladdened his eye. When this happened, he wished that his people would know of it." End of quote. The saying ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ seems to be an answer to someone asking about his condition at meeting his Lord after that steadfastness in his religion, so it was said, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ The construction "It was said to him" was not used, because it is known that he is the one addressed. His wish that his people would know of this is connected to an assumed question about what he had said at that moment, as a sign of advice and sincerity toward them, meaning: if they knew that, they would believe in God. In a hadith: "He advised his people while alive and dead." (p. 330) It was also said: he wished for that so that they would know that they had been in error regarding his matter, while he was right, so they would regret, be grieved by that, and be given glad tidings of it. It is naturally found in human temperament that whoever attains good outside his homeland wishes that his neighbors and peers among whom he grew up would know of it. We have been told that the vizier Dhink al-Din al-Masiri, who was a vizier to the king of Egypt, went to his village from which he came, which is Masir, one of the smallest villages of Egypt. He was asked about that, and he said: "I wanted the old women of Masir to see me in this state I am in." The poet said:

Honor is sought and sought after,
and the dearest of it is what is attained in one's homeland.

The apparent meaning of what is in His words ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ is that it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). They allowed that it could mean "that which" (alladhi), with a returning pronoun omitted, its estimated form being: "with that which my Lord has forgiven me of sins." This is not good, because it would lead to a wish that they know about the forgiven sins, whereas what is fitting is a wish that they know about the forgiveness of his sins and that he was made one of the honored. Al-Farra' permitted that it be an interrogative (istifham). Al-Kisa'i said: "If this were correct, meaning the interrogative, it would say bima without an alif." Al-Farra' said: "It is permissible to say bima with the alif," and he cited verses for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be interrogative, meaning: 'for what reason has my Lord forgiven me?' He means what he had done with them of steadfastness in exalting the religion of God, to the point that it was said that your saying ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ with the alif dropped is better, although keeping it is permissible, so he said: 'I have known by what I did this, and by what I did.'" End of quote. The well-known view is that keeping the alif in the interrogative ma, when a preposition has come before it, is restricted to poetic necessity, as in the saying:

Upon what did the vile one revile me,
like a pig rolling in ashes?

Its omission is the more common form in speech, as in the saying:

Upon what does the spear keep weighing on my shoulder
when I do not thrust, when the horses charge?

And it was read: ﴿among the honored﴾, with a shadda on the ra' and a fatha on the kaf; the majority read it with a sukun on the kaf and a light ra'.

[p. 326]

﴿And strike for them an example: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it.﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:13] ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, and they said, "Indeed we are messengers to you."﴾ [36:14] ﴿They said, "You are only humans like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ [36:15] ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you."﴾ [36:16] ﴿And we are not [responsible] except for clear notification.﴾ [36:17] ﴿They said, "Indeed we consider you a bad omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and painful punishment will surely touch you from us."﴾ [36:18] ﴿They said, "Your omen is with you. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a people who transgress."﴾ [36:19] ﴿And there came from the far end of the city a man running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ [36:20] ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and they are guided.﴾ ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me and to whom you will be returned?﴾ ﴿Shall I take other than Him as gods? If the Most Merciful intends me harm, their intercession will not benefit me at all, nor can they save me.﴾ ﴿Indeed I would then be in clear error.﴾ ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "I wish my people knew﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."﴾.

The discussion of ﴿وَاضْرِبْ﴾ (wa-ḍrib, "and strike") together with "the example" has already been covered in His saying ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [2:26]. "The town" is Antioch (Antakiya), and there is no disagreement about the story of the companions of the town.

﴿When the messengers came to it﴾ [36:13]: they were three, and He grouped them together in the coming, although they differed about the time of the coming.

﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [36:14]: The apparent meaning of "We sent" is that they were prophets whom God sent, and what the sent ones said to them, ﴿You are only humans like us﴾ [36:15], supports this. This kind of exchange happens only with someone whom God has sent. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ka'b. Qatada and others among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) said: Jesus, peace be upon him, sent them after he had been raised and the one upon whom the likeness was cast had been crucified, and the disciples then scattered throughout the regions. God then recounted the story of those who went to Antioch, whose people were worshippers of idols. This is the view of Wahb and Ka'b al-Ahbar. Al-Naqqash ibn Sam'an reported: "Yuhanna." Muqatil said: "Tuman" and "Yunus." (fa-kadhdhabūhumā) means: they called them to God, and the two informed them that they were messengers of God, ﴿but they denied them﴾. ﴿So We strengthened [them] with a third﴾ [36:14]: that is, We made [them] strong and firm. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Qutayba, who said: it is said "ta'azzaza lahm al-naqa" (the camel's meat became firm) when it hardened. Others said: it is said that rain "yu'azziz" the land when it packs and firms it, and hard ground is called "al-qur'ān." This is according to the reading with the doubled zāy (fa-azzaznā with shadda), which is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, and Aban read it with a light (unstressed) zāy. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: "fa-ghalabnā" (so We overcame). He said: this comes from their saying "man 'azzanī" (whoever overpowers me), and from His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [38:23]. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read [p. 327] "bi-l-thālith" with the definite article (alif and lām), and "al-thālith" is Shim'un al-Safa, according to Ibn Abbas. Ka'b and Wahb said: Shalum; and it was said: Yunus. The object of fa-azzaznā with doubling is omitted, meaning: We strengthened the two with a third. With the unstressed form, the meaning is: We overcame them, that is, by the argument of a third and what is gently conveyed through reaching the call to God, even to the king, as is mentioned in their story, and this (or part of it) will come, God willing.

[The word] "messengers" (mursalūn) came first without the lām because it is the beginning of an announcement, and so it does not need emphasis after the exchange. "Indeed we are messengers to you" (la-mursalūn) has the emphatic lām because it is an answer to a denial. This was a community that denied prophethood by its saying ﴿the Most Merciful has sent down nothing﴾ [36:15]. The messengers answered them by referring knowledge to God and being content with His knowledge, and informed them that they were responsible only for conveying [the message], and that they were not responsible for their guidance or their misguidance. There is a warning in this for them. The conveyance is described as "clear" (al-mubīn), meaning clear with signs that witness to the truth of the sending, such as the miracles mentioned in this story: healing the blind-born and the leper and reviving the dead.

﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾ [36:18]: that is, we consider you ill-omened (tashā'amnā). Muqatil said: the rain was withheld from them. Another said: leprosy spread among them when they denied the messengers. Ibn Atiyya said: The apparent meaning is that their taking of omens was the cause of what entered among them of division of word and temptation of people. This is like the omen-taking of the Quraysh regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and like what Moses, peace be upon him, was addressed with. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is because they disliked their religion and their souls recoiled from it. It is the habit of the ignorant to attribute blessings to everything they incline toward, desire, and whose nature accepts, and to consider ill omen in what they recoil from and dislike. If good fortune or affliction befalls them, they say: "This is by the blessing of such-and-such, and this is by the ill omen of such-and-such," as God related about the Copts: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they take omen from Moses and those with him﴾ [7:131], and about the polytheists of Mecca: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say: "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [4:78]. End of quotation. Qatada said: "If something befalls us, it is because of you." (la-narjumannahum) means: we will stone them with stones, as Qatada said.

﴿a painful punishment﴾ [36:18] is the burning.

﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19]: that is, your share (ḥaẓẓ) and what has come to you of good or evil is with you, that is, from your own actions. It is not because of us; rather, it is because of your disbelief. Al-Hasan, Ibn Hurmuz, Amr ibn Ubayd, and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read ṭayrukum with a silent yā' after the ṭā'. It was reported that al-Hasan read ittayyurukum, the verbal noun (maṣdar) of ittayyara, whose original form is tatayyara, in which the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā', so a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) was introduced in the past tense and in the verbal noun. The majority read ṭā'irukum on the pattern fā'il.

The majority read ﴿Is it because you were reminded?﴾ [36:19] with two hamzas: the first is the interrogative hamza, and the second is the hamza of the conditional particle in (in). The Kufans and Ibn Amir softened it, and the rest of the Seven (Readers) made it intermediate (sahhalahā). Zirr read it with two open hamzas, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far and Talha, except that the second is pronounced between-between (bayn bayn). A poet, in its realization, said:

"Ara-in kunta Dāwūda ibna Aḥwā mar-ḥalan / fa-lastu bi-dā'in li-ibni ʿammika maḥramā"

[Translator's note: a line of poetry; retained as given.]

Al-Majishuni, who is Abu Salama Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Salama al-Madani, read it with one open hamza. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra-ha (hā' with kasra). Abu ʿAmr in one transmission, and Zirr also, read it with a madda (lengthening) before the open hamza, having found the juxtaposition of the two heavy, so he separated them with an alif. Abu Ja'far also, al-Hasan also, Qatada, Isa al-Hamdani, and al-A'mash read ʾayna with an open hamza, a silent yā', and an open nūn, as a adverb of place (ẓarf makān). This was also reported from Isa al-Thaqafi.

The first reading means: "If you are reminded, you take omens," with the omitted element being made the focus of the interrogation, according to the view of Sibawayh; or making it a conditional, according to the view of Yunus. If you posit it as a present (verb), it would be jussive (majzūm). The second reading means: "Because you were reminded, did you take omens?" Here in is an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlihi, object of cause). The same applies to the single open hamza and the one with a madda before the open hamza. Reading the kasra-ed hamza alone, the in is a conditional particle with the meaning of an announcement: "If you are reminded, you take omens." The last reading, with ayna, has a conditional adverb whose answer is omitted for indication, and its estimate is: "Wherever you are reminded, your omen accompanies you," which is indicated by His saying ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19]. Whoever permits placing the answer (jazāʾ) before the condition (sharṭ), namely the Kufans, Abu Zayd, and al-Mubarrad, may hold that the answer is ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19], and its original form was: "Wherever you are reminded, then your omen is with you," and when it was placed first the fā' was omitted. The majority read dhukkirtum with a doubled kāf. Abu Ja'far, Khalid ibn Iyas, Talha, al-Hasan, and Qatada, Abu Haywa, al-A'mash through the route of Zā'ida, and al-Asma'i from Nafi' read it with the light form.

﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [36:19]: exceeding the limit in your misguidance, and therefore the misfortune has come to you.

﴿And there came from the far end of the city a man running﴾ [36:20]: his name is Habib, according to Ibn Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Mujahid, and Muqatil. It was said: he was the son of Isra'il, and he was a launderer. It was also said: a cobbler. It was said: he used to carve idols, and it is possible that he combined these trades. ﴿From the far end of the city﴾ [36:20] means: from the most distant of its places. It was said: he was outside the city tending his crop. It was said: he was in a cave worshipping his Lord. It was said: he was a leper, and the farthest of the gates of the city was assigned to him, and he worshipped idols for seventy years, calling them to remove his affliction. When the messengers called him to the worship of God, he said: "Is there a sign?" They said: "Yes, we call upon our Lord, the Capable, who will relieve you of what afflicts you." He said: "This is wondrous! For seventy years I have called upon these gods and they could not do it. Will your Lord relieve it in a single morning?" They said: "Yes, our Lord is capable of whatever He wills, and these [idols] benefit nothing and harm nothing." So he believed. They called upon their Lord, and God removed what was on him, as if there had never been any affliction in him. He then turned to earning a living, and whenever he walked, he gave away his earnings: half for his dependents, and half he gave as food [to others]. When his people resolved to kill the messengers, he came to them and said: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾ [36:20]. This Habib was among those who believed in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and between them were six hundred years, just as Tubba' al-Akbar believed in him, and Waraqa ibn Nawfal and others. No one believed in any prophet other than him except after his appearance.

Ibn Abi Layla said: the foremost of the nations are three, who never disbelieved for the blink of an eye: ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, the companion of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of Pharaoh's family. Al-Zamakhshari cited the saying of Ibn Abi Layla as a ḥadīth from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was mentioned before that his condition was that he was a leper, who worshipped idols for seventy years, and God knows best. Here ﴿from the far end of the city﴾ [36:20] came first, while in the narratives it came later, and this is one of the variations of eloquence (tafannun fī al-balāgha).

﴿A man running﴾ [36:20] means walking on his two feet.

﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ [36:20]. The apparent meaning is that he did not say this after his belief had preceded, as was mentioned in a previous story. It was also said: Jesus came and heard their saying and understood it in what he understood. It is reported that he followed up their matter and tested them by saying to them: "Do you ask for a wage for this call of yours?" They said: "No." Then he called his people to follow them and to believe in them, and argued against them with his words: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and they are guided﴾ [36:21], that is, they are guided by God. He first commanded them to follow the messengers, that is, they are God's messengers to you, so follow them. Then he commanded them a second time with a comprehensive sentence in encouragement: that they do not ask for any of the worldly goods of theirs, and that they are guided by their guidance, so that they combine the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Some grammarians have permitted that man (whoever) be an apposition (badal) to "the messengers," in which the governing element appears, as it appears when it is a preposition, as in His saying ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾ [43:33]. The majority do not parse as an apposition anything in which the raising or governing element is explicitly stated; rather, they make that restricted to the preposition. When the raising and governing element is through following (tatbī', i.e., the adjective-like attribution), not through apposition. In His saying ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾ there is evidence for the deficiency of one who takes a wage for something from the acts of the Law that are obligatory upon him, such as prayer.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 21–27 (part 2 of 2):

When He had commanded them to follow the messengers, he began to present the proof for following them and for worshipping God. He presented it in the form of counsel to himself, while he actually intended it as counsel to them, so as to be gentle with them and to win them over. This is more effective in sincere advice, since he wants for them only what he wants for himself. So he placed his statement, ﴿And why should I not worship the One who originated me?﴾, in the place of: "And why should you not worship the One who originated you?" That is why he said, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. Had he not intended this, he would have said, "And to Him I will return."

Then he continued the speech in the same manner, addressing himself, saying, ﴿Shall I take gods besides Him?﴾, which are powerless in everything, neither benefiting nor harming. If the Most Merciful should intend harm for me, their intercession would not avail, and they could not rescue me from it. He first expressed the lack of standing, that their intercession would not benefit, and then the lack of power. He expressed the absence of rescue, since it is its consequence. (p. 329)

Regarding the ya' of the speaker in (yuridni), Talhah al-Sammān read it with a fatha, as in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, the readers are Talhah ibn Musarrif, 'Isa al-Hamadhani, and Abu Ja'far, and it is also transmitted from Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was read as ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ meaning: 'if He makes me one who brings harm upon myself.'" End of quote. This, God knows best, is an opinion in the books of qira'at (canonical and variant recitations). The reading yuridni with a fatha on the ya' led him to suppose that it is the prefixed ya' of the imperfect (ya' al-mudara'ah), so he made the verb transitive by means of the ya' that causes transitivity, like the hamza, and therefore he added to it the causative hamza (hamzat al-ta'diyah) and governed two objects with it. What is found in the books of the shadh (irregular, non-canonical) readers is that it is the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah) which is deleted both in writing and in pronunciation because of the meeting of two sukun (unvocalized letters). In the book of Ibn Khalawayh he says: "with a fatha on the ya' of possession." In al-Lawami' he says: "in ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ with the fatha, which is the original form of the ya' according to the Basrans, but this one is deleted, meaning the Basran one, i.e., the one affirmed by the Barbari script, visible to the eye, because it is written, unlike the one deleted both in writing and in pronunciation, which is not seen by the eye." (Inni idhan) — if I do not worship the One who originated me and take gods besides Him, I would be in clear error, evident to anyone with sound intellect.

Then he openly declared his faith and proclaimed the truth, addressing his people, saying: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord﴾, that is, the One you disbelieved in, ﴿so listen to me﴾, that is, listen to my words and obey me. I have alerted you to the truth, that worship is only for the One from whom your origin is and to whom your return is. The apparent sense is that the address with the kaf and the mim and the waw is to his people, and the command is meant as emphasis and alerting. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b, and Wahb. It was also said: by His words ﴿so listen to me﴾ he addressed the messengers, as a way of calling them to witness and entrusting the matter to them. It was also said: the address in (bi-Rabbikum) and in (fasma'uni) is to the messengers. When he advised his people, they began to stone him, so he hastened toward the messengers before he could be killed and said that, that is, "Listen to my faith and bear witness for me to it."

﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is a genuine command. It was also said: its meaning is "Paradise has become obligatory for you," so it is a report that he has deserved to enter it, and this will not happen except after resurrection. The Qur'an does not state that he was killed. Al-Hasan said: when his people wanted to kill him, God raised him to heaven, so he is in Paradise, not dying until the heavens perish and Paradise is destroyed; when God restores Paradise, he will enter it. It was also said: when he said that, they lifted him to the king, and he prolonged the speech with them to occupy them from killing the messengers, until he openly declared his faith to them. They then rushed upon him and killed him by trampling with their feet until his heart came out from his back, and he was thrown into a well, which is al-Rass. Al-Suddi said: they pelted him with stones while he was saying, "O God, guide my people," until he died. Al-Kalbi said: they threw him into a pit and cast earth upon him, and he died. From al-Hasan: they burned him with fire, hung him at the gate of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. It was also said: they sawed him with saws until it came out between his legs. From Qatadah: God admitted him into Paradise while he was in it alive and provided for, referring to His words, ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169], rejoicing.

In the copy of the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah that we consulted, there is the following text: The majority read ﴿fasma'una﴾ with a fatha on the nun. Abu Hatim said: "This is an error and is not permitted, because it is a command, so either the nun must be dropped, or it must be kasra as a fixed ending (bina'). End of quote," meaning the ya' of the speaker, and the nun is the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah). His statement "the majority read" is a gross error, and it cannot be, God knows best, except from the copyist. Rather, as far as I know, the readers, all seven of them and the shadh ones, agree on the kasra of the nun, except what is transmitted from 'Ismah from 'Asim with the fatha on the nun, mentioned in al-Kamil of the author Abu al-Qasim al-Hudhali. Perhaps this is an error from 'Ismah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Here there is an omitted element, which the traditions and reports have transmitted continuously, namely that they killed him, and it was said to him at his death, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ This happened, God knows best, when his station in it was shown to him and he was assured that he was among its inhabitants, so he saw what gladdened his eye. When this happened, he wished that his people would know of it." End of quote. The saying ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ seems to be an answer to someone asking about his condition at meeting his Lord after that steadfastness in his religion, so it was said, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ The construction "It was said to him" was not used, because it is known that he is the one addressed. His wish that his people would know of this is connected to an assumed question about what he had said at that moment, as a sign of advice and sincerity toward them, meaning: if they knew that, they would believe in God. In a hadith: "He advised his people while alive and dead." (p. 330) It was also said: he wished for that so that they would know that they had been in error regarding his matter, while he was right, so they would regret, be grieved by that, and be given glad tidings of it. It is naturally found in human temperament that whoever attains good outside his homeland wishes that his neighbors and peers among whom he grew up would know of it. We have been told that the vizier Dhink al-Din al-Masiri, who was a vizier to the king of Egypt, went to his village from which he came, which is Masir, one of the smallest villages of Egypt. He was asked about that, and he said: "I wanted the old women of Masir to see me in this state I am in." The poet said:

Honor is sought and sought after,
and the dearest of it is what is attained in one's homeland.

The apparent meaning of what is in His words ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ is that it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). They allowed that it could mean "that which" (alladhi), with a returning pronoun omitted, its estimated form being: "with that which my Lord has forgiven me of sins." This is not good, because it would lead to a wish that they know about the forgiven sins, whereas what is fitting is a wish that they know about the forgiveness of his sins and that he was made one of the honored. Al-Farra' permitted that it be an interrogative (istifham). Al-Kisa'i said: "If this were correct, meaning the interrogative, it would say bima without an alif." Al-Farra' said: "It is permissible to say bima with the alif," and he cited verses for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be interrogative, meaning: 'for what reason has my Lord forgiven me?' He means what he had done with them of steadfastness in exalting the religion of God, to the point that it was said that your saying ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ with the alif dropped is better, although keeping it is permissible, so he said: 'I have known by what I did this, and by what I did.'" End of quote. The well-known view is that keeping the alif in the interrogative ma, when a preposition has come before it, is restricted to poetic necessity, as in the saying:

Upon what did the vile one revile me,
like a pig rolling in ashes?

Its omission is the more common form in speech, as in the saying:

Upon what does the spear keep weighing on my shoulder
when I do not thrust, when the horses charge?

And it was read: ﴿among the honored﴾, with a shadda on the ra' and a fatha on the kaf; the majority read it with a sukun on the kaf and a light ra'.

[p. 326]

﴿And strike for them an example: the companions of the town, when the messengers came to it.﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:13] ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, and they said, "Indeed we are messengers to you."﴾ [36:14] ﴿They said, "You are only humans like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing. You are only lying."﴾ [36:15] ﴿They said, "Our Lord knows that we are indeed messengers to you."﴾ [36:16] ﴿And we are not [responsible] except for clear notification.﴾ [36:17] ﴿They said, "Indeed we consider you a bad omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and painful punishment will surely touch you from us."﴾ [36:18] ﴿They said, "Your omen is with you. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a people who transgress."﴾ [36:19] ﴿And there came from the far end of the city a man running. He said, "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ [36:20] ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and they are guided.﴾ ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me and to whom you will be returned?﴾ ﴿Shall I take other than Him as gods? If the Most Merciful intends me harm, their intercession will not benefit me at all, nor can they save me.﴾ ﴿Indeed I would then be in clear error.﴾ ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise." He said, "I wish my people knew﴾ ﴿of how my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."﴾.

The discussion of ﴿وَاضْرِبْ﴾ (wa-ḍrib, "and strike") together with "the example" has already been covered in His saying ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [2:26]. "The town" is Antioch (Antakiya), and there is no disagreement about the story of the companions of the town.

﴿When the messengers came to it﴾ [36:13]: they were three, and He grouped them together in the coming, although they differed about the time of the coming.

﴿When We sent to them two﴾ [36:14]: The apparent meaning of "We sent" is that they were prophets whom God sent, and what the sent ones said to them, ﴿You are only humans like us﴾ [36:15], supports this. This kind of exchange happens only with someone whom God has sent. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ka'b. Qatada and others among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) said: Jesus, peace be upon him, sent them after he had been raised and the one upon whom the likeness was cast had been crucified, and the disciples then scattered throughout the regions. God then recounted the story of those who went to Antioch, whose people were worshippers of idols. This is the view of Wahb and Ka'b al-Ahbar. Al-Naqqash ibn Sam'an reported: "Yuhanna." Muqatil said: "Tuman" and "Yunus." (fa-kadhdhabūhumā) means: they called them to God, and the two informed them that they were messengers of God, ﴿but they denied them﴾. ﴿So We strengthened [them] with a third﴾ [36:14]: that is, We made [them] strong and firm. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Qutayba, who said: it is said "ta'azzaza lahm al-naqa" (the camel's meat became firm) when it hardened. Others said: it is said that rain "yu'azziz" the land when it packs and firms it, and hard ground is called "al-qur'ān." This is according to the reading with the doubled zāy (fa-azzaznā with shadda), which is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, and Aban read it with a light (unstressed) zāy. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: "fa-ghalabnā" (so We overcame). He said: this comes from their saying "man 'azzanī" (whoever overpowers me), and from His saying ﴿and he overpowered me in the speech﴾ [38:23]. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read [p. 327] "bi-l-thālith" with the definite article (alif and lām), and "al-thālith" is Shim'un al-Safa, according to Ibn Abbas. Ka'b and Wahb said: Shalum; and it was said: Yunus. The object of fa-azzaznā with doubling is omitted, meaning: We strengthened the two with a third. With the unstressed form, the meaning is: We overcame them, that is, by the argument of a third and what is gently conveyed through reaching the call to God, even to the king, as is mentioned in their story, and this (or part of it) will come, God willing.

[The word] "messengers" (mursalūn) came first without the lām because it is the beginning of an announcement, and so it does not need emphasis after the exchange. "Indeed we are messengers to you" (la-mursalūn) has the emphatic lām because it is an answer to a denial. This was a community that denied prophethood by its saying ﴿the Most Merciful has sent down nothing﴾ [36:15]. The messengers answered them by referring knowledge to God and being content with His knowledge, and informed them that they were responsible only for conveying [the message], and that they were not responsible for their guidance or their misguidance. There is a warning in this for them. The conveyance is described as "clear" (al-mubīn), meaning clear with signs that witness to the truth of the sending, such as the miracles mentioned in this story: healing the blind-born and the leper and reviving the dead.

﴿We consider you a bad omen﴾ [36:18]: that is, we consider you ill-omened (tashā'amnā). Muqatil said: the rain was withheld from them. Another said: leprosy spread among them when they denied the messengers. Ibn Atiyya said: The apparent meaning is that their taking of omens was the cause of what entered among them of division of word and temptation of people. This is like the omen-taking of the Quraysh regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and like what Moses, peace be upon him, was addressed with. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is because they disliked their religion and their souls recoiled from it. It is the habit of the ignorant to attribute blessings to everything they incline toward, desire, and whose nature accepts, and to consider ill omen in what they recoil from and dislike. If good fortune or affliction befalls them, they say: "This is by the blessing of such-and-such, and this is by the ill omen of such-and-such," as God related about the Copts: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they take omen from Moses and those with him﴾ [7:131], and about the polytheists of Mecca: ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say: "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [4:78]. End of quotation. Qatada said: "If something befalls us, it is because of you." (la-narjumannahum) means: we will stone them with stones, as Qatada said.

﴿a painful punishment﴾ [36:18] is the burning.

﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19]: that is, your share (ḥaẓẓ) and what has come to you of good or evil is with you, that is, from your own actions. It is not because of us; rather, it is because of your disbelief. Al-Hasan, Ibn Hurmuz, Amr ibn Ubayd, and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read ṭayrukum with a silent yā' after the ṭā'. It was reported that al-Hasan read ittayyurukum, the verbal noun (maṣdar) of ittayyara, whose original form is tatayyara, in which the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā', so a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) was introduced in the past tense and in the verbal noun. The majority read ṭā'irukum on the pattern fā'il.

The majority read ﴿Is it because you were reminded?﴾ [36:19] with two hamzas: the first is the interrogative hamza, and the second is the hamza of the conditional particle in (in). The Kufans and Ibn Amir softened it, and the rest of the Seven (Readers) made it intermediate (sahhalahā). Zirr read it with two open hamzas, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far and Talha, except that the second is pronounced between-between (bayn bayn). A poet, in its realization, said:

"Ara-in kunta Dāwūda ibna Aḥwā mar-ḥalan / fa-lastu bi-dā'in li-ibni ʿammika maḥramā"

[Translator's note: a line of poetry; retained as given.]

Al-Majishuni, who is Abu Salama Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Salama al-Madani, read it with one open hamza. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra-ha (hā' with kasra). Abu ʿAmr in one transmission, and Zirr also, read it with a madda (lengthening) before the open hamza, having found the juxtaposition of the two heavy, so he separated them with an alif. Abu Ja'far also, al-Hasan also, Qatada, Isa al-Hamdani, and al-A'mash read ʾayna with an open hamza, a silent yā', and an open nūn, as a adverb of place (ẓarf makān). This was also reported from Isa al-Thaqafi.

The first reading means: "If you are reminded, you take omens," with the omitted element being made the focus of the interrogation, according to the view of Sibawayh; or making it a conditional, according to the view of Yunus. If you posit it as a present (verb), it would be jussive (majzūm). The second reading means: "Because you were reminded, did you take omens?" Here in is an object of purpose (maf'ūl min ajlihi, object of cause). The same applies to the single open hamza and the one with a madda before the open hamza. Reading the kasra-ed hamza alone, the in is a conditional particle with the meaning of an announcement: "If you are reminded, you take omens." The last reading, with ayna, has a conditional adverb whose answer is omitted for indication, and its estimate is: "Wherever you are reminded, your omen accompanies you," which is indicated by His saying ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19]. Whoever permits placing the answer (jazāʾ) before the condition (sharṭ), namely the Kufans, Abu Zayd, and al-Mubarrad, may hold that the answer is ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ [36:19], and its original form was: "Wherever you are reminded, then your omen is with you," and when it was placed first the fā' was omitted. The majority read dhukkirtum with a doubled kāf. Abu Ja'far, Khalid ibn Iyas, Talha, al-Hasan, and Qatada, Abu Haywa, al-A'mash through the route of Zā'ida, and al-Asma'i from Nafi' read it with the light form.

﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [36:19]: exceeding the limit in your misguidance, and therefore the misfortune has come to you.

﴿And there came from the far end of the city a man running﴾ [36:20]: his name is Habib, according to Ibn Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Mujahid, and Muqatil. It was said: he was the son of Isra'il, and he was a launderer. It was also said: a cobbler. It was said: he used to carve idols, and it is possible that he combined these trades. ﴿From the far end of the city﴾ [36:20] means: from the most distant of its places. It was said: he was outside the city tending his crop. It was said: he was in a cave worshipping his Lord. It was said: he was a leper, and the farthest of the gates of the city was assigned to him, and he worshipped idols for seventy years, calling them to remove his affliction. When the messengers called him to the worship of God, he said: "Is there a sign?" They said: "Yes, we call upon our Lord, the Capable, who will relieve you of what afflicts you." He said: "This is wondrous! For seventy years I have called upon these gods and they could not do it. Will your Lord relieve it in a single morning?" They said: "Yes, our Lord is capable of whatever He wills, and these [idols] benefit nothing and harm nothing." So he believed. They called upon their Lord, and God removed what was on him, as if there had never been any affliction in him. He then turned to earning a living, and whenever he walked, he gave away his earnings: half for his dependents, and half he gave as food [to others]. When his people resolved to kill the messengers, he came to them and said: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾ [36:20]. This Habib was among those who believed in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and between them were six hundred years, just as Tubba' al-Akbar believed in him, and Waraqa ibn Nawfal and others. No one believed in any prophet other than him except after his appearance.

Ibn Abi Layla said: the foremost of the nations are three, who never disbelieved for the blink of an eye: ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib, the companion of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of Pharaoh's family. Al-Zamakhshari cited the saying of Ibn Abi Layla as a ḥadīth from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was mentioned before that his condition was that he was a leper, who worshipped idols for seventy years, and God knows best. Here ﴿from the far end of the city﴾ [36:20] came first, while in the narratives it came later, and this is one of the variations of eloquence (tafannun fī al-balāgha).

﴿A man running﴾ [36:20] means walking on his two feet.

﴿He said, "O my people, follow the messengers"﴾ [36:20]. The apparent meaning is that he did not say this after his belief had preceded, as was mentioned in a previous story. It was also said: Jesus came and heard their saying and understood it in what he understood. It is reported that he followed up their matter and tested them by saying to them: "Do you ask for a wage for this call of yours?" They said: "No." Then he called his people to follow them and to believe in them, and argued against them with his words: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward, and they are guided﴾ [36:21], that is, they are guided by God. He first commanded them to follow the messengers, that is, they are God's messengers to you, so follow them. Then he commanded them a second time with a comprehensive sentence in encouragement: that they do not ask for any of the worldly goods of theirs, and that they are guided by their guidance, so that they combine the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Some grammarians have permitted that man (whoever) be an apposition (badal) to "the messengers," in which the governing element appears, as it appears when it is a preposition, as in His saying ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾ [43:33]. The majority do not parse as an apposition anything in which the raising or governing element is explicitly stated; rather, they make that restricted to the preposition. When the raising and governing element is through following (tatbī', i.e., the adjective-like attribution), not through apposition. In His saying ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾ there is evidence for the deficiency of one who takes a wage for something from the acts of the Law that are obligatory upon him, such as prayer.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 21–27 (part 2 of 2):

When He had commanded them to follow the messengers, he began to present the proof for following them and for worshipping God. He presented it in the form of counsel to himself, while he actually intended it as counsel to them, so as to be gentle with them and to win them over. This is more effective in sincere advice, since he wants for them only what he wants for himself. So he placed his statement, ﴿And why should I not worship the One who originated me?﴾, in the place of: "And why should you not worship the One who originated you?" That is why he said, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. Had he not intended this, he would have said, "And to Him I will return."

Then he continued the speech in the same manner, addressing himself, saying, ﴿Shall I take gods besides Him?﴾, which are powerless in everything, neither benefiting nor harming. If the Most Merciful should intend harm for me, their intercession would not avail, and they could not rescue me from it. He first expressed the lack of standing, that their intercession would not benefit, and then the lack of power. He expressed the absence of rescue, since it is its consequence. (p. 329)

Regarding the ya' of the speaker in (yuridni), Talhah al-Sammān read it with a fatha, as in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, the readers are Talhah ibn Musarrif, 'Isa al-Hamadhani, and Abu Ja'far, and it is also transmitted from Nafi', 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was read as ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ meaning: 'if He makes me one who brings harm upon myself.'" End of quote. This, God knows best, is an opinion in the books of qira'at (canonical and variant recitations). The reading yuridni with a fatha on the ya' led him to suppose that it is the prefixed ya' of the imperfect (ya' al-mudara'ah), so he made the verb transitive by means of the ya' that causes transitivity, like the hamza, and therefore he added to it the causative hamza (hamzat al-ta'diyah) and governed two objects with it. What is found in the books of the shadh (irregular, non-canonical) readers is that it is the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah) which is deleted both in writing and in pronunciation because of the meeting of two sukun (unvocalized letters). In the book of Ibn Khalawayh he says: "with a fatha on the ya' of possession." In al-Lawami' he says: "in ﴿if the Most Merciful should cause me harm﴾ with the fatha, which is the original form of the ya' according to the Basrans, but this one is deleted, meaning the Basran one, i.e., the one affirmed by the Barbari script, visible to the eye, because it is written, unlike the one deleted both in writing and in pronunciation, which is not seen by the eye." (Inni idhan) — if I do not worship the One who originated me and take gods besides Him, I would be in clear error, evident to anyone with sound intellect.

Then he openly declared his faith and proclaimed the truth, addressing his people, saying: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord﴾, that is, the One you disbelieved in, ﴿so listen to me﴾, that is, listen to my words and obey me. I have alerted you to the truth, that worship is only for the One from whom your origin is and to whom your return is. The apparent sense is that the address with the kaf and the mim and the waw is to his people, and the command is meant as emphasis and alerting. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b, and Wahb. It was also said: by His words ﴿so listen to me﴾ he addressed the messengers, as a way of calling them to witness and entrusting the matter to them. It was also said: the address in (bi-Rabbikum) and in (fasma'uni) is to the messengers. When he advised his people, they began to stone him, so he hastened toward the messengers before he could be killed and said that, that is, "Listen to my faith and bear witness for me to it."

﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is a genuine command. It was also said: its meaning is "Paradise has become obligatory for you," so it is a report that he has deserved to enter it, and this will not happen except after resurrection. The Qur'an does not state that he was killed. Al-Hasan said: when his people wanted to kill him, God raised him to heaven, so he is in Paradise, not dying until the heavens perish and Paradise is destroyed; when God restores Paradise, he will enter it. It was also said: when he said that, they lifted him to the king, and he prolonged the speech with them to occupy them from killing the messengers, until he openly declared his faith to them. They then rushed upon him and killed him by trampling with their feet until his heart came out from his back, and he was thrown into a well, which is al-Rass. Al-Suddi said: they pelted him with stones while he was saying, "O God, guide my people," until he died. Al-Kalbi said: they threw him into a pit and cast earth upon him, and he died. From al-Hasan: they burned him with fire, hung him at the gate of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. It was also said: they sawed him with saws until it came out between his legs. From Qatadah: God admitted him into Paradise while he was in it alive and provided for, referring to His words, ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169], rejoicing.

In the copy of the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah that we consulted, there is the following text: The majority read ﴿fasma'una﴾ with a fatha on the nun. Abu Hatim said: "This is an error and is not permitted, because it is a command, so either the nun must be dropped, or it must be kasra as a fixed ending (bina'). End of quote," meaning the ya' of the speaker, and the nun is the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah). His statement "the majority read" is a gross error, and it cannot be, God knows best, except from the copyist. Rather, as far as I know, the readers, all seven of them and the shadh ones, agree on the kasra of the nun, except what is transmitted from 'Ismah from 'Asim with the fatha on the nun, mentioned in al-Kamil of the author Abu al-Qasim al-Hudhali. Perhaps this is an error from 'Ismah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Here there is an omitted element, which the traditions and reports have transmitted continuously, namely that they killed him, and it was said to him at his death, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ This happened, God knows best, when his station in it was shown to him and he was assured that he was among its inhabitants, so he saw what gladdened his eye. When this happened, he wished that his people would know of it." End of quote. The saying ﴿It was said, "Enter Paradise."﴾ seems to be an answer to someone asking about his condition at meeting his Lord after that steadfastness in his religion, so it was said, ﴿Enter Paradise.﴾ The construction "It was said to him" was not used, because it is known that he is the one addressed. His wish that his people would know of this is connected to an assumed question about what he had said at that moment, as a sign of advice and sincerity toward them, meaning: if they knew that, they would believe in God. In a hadith: "He advised his people while alive and dead." (p. 330) It was also said: he wished for that so that they would know that they had been in error regarding his matter, while he was right, so they would regret, be grieved by that, and be given glad tidings of it. It is naturally found in human temperament that whoever attains good outside his homeland wishes that his neighbors and peers among whom he grew up would know of it. We have been told that the vizier Dhink al-Din al-Masiri, who was a vizier to the king of Egypt, went to his village from which he came, which is Masir, one of the smallest villages of Egypt. He was asked about that, and he said: "I wanted the old women of Masir to see me in this state I am in." The poet said:

Honor is sought and sought after,
and the dearest of it is what is attained in one's homeland.

The apparent meaning of what is in His words ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ is that it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). They allowed that it could mean "that which" (alladhi), with a returning pronoun omitted, its estimated form being: "with that which my Lord has forgiven me of sins." This is not good, because it would lead to a wish that they know about the forgiven sins, whereas what is fitting is a wish that they know about the forgiveness of his sins and that he was made one of the honored. Al-Farra' permitted that it be an interrogative (istifham). Al-Kisa'i said: "If this were correct, meaning the interrogative, it would say bima without an alif." Al-Farra' said: "It is permissible to say bima with the alif," and he cited verses for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be interrogative, meaning: 'for what reason has my Lord forgiven me?' He means what he had done with them of steadfastness in exalting the religion of God, to the point that it was said that your saying ﴿for what my Lord has forgiven me﴾ with the alif dropped is better, although keeping it is permissible, so he said: 'I have known by what I did this, and by what I did.'" End of quote. The well-known view is that keeping the alif in the interrogative ma, when a preposition has come before it, is restricted to poetic necessity, as in the saying:

Upon what did the vile one revile me,
like a pig rolling in ashes?

Its omission is the more common form in speech, as in the saying:

Upon what does the spear keep weighing on my shoulder
when I do not thrust, when the horses charge?

And it was read: ﴿among the honored﴾, with a shadda on the ra' and a fatha on the kaf; the majority read it with a sukun on the kaf and a light ra'.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Ya-Sin, verses 28–44 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Nor did We send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down.﴾ ﴿It was but one Cry, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾ ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾ ﴿And all of them, without exception, will be brought before Us.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is the dead earth: We gave it life and brought forth from it grain, of which they eat.﴾ ﴿And We made in it gardens of palms and vines, and caused springs to gush forth in it.﴾ ﴿That they may eat of its fruit, and of what their hands have made. Will they not then give thanks?﴾ ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of what they do not know.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place; that is the decree of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations, until it returns like the old withered palm-stalk.﴾ ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outrun the day; each floats in an orbit.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾ ﴿And We created for them of its like what they ride.﴾ ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry for them, nor are they rescued.﴾ ﴿Except as mercy from Us and enjoyment for a time.﴾

(p-331) He, may He be exalted, informed of the destruction of the people of Habib by one single Cry, which Jibril shouted at them. In this there is a warning to Quraysh that what befell them may befall them too, since they are the ones for whom the parable was struck. He, may He be exalted, also informed that He did not send down against them for their destruction any host from heaven, such as stones, wind, or other things, and they were too insignificant for Him. His saying "after him" (min ba'dihi) indicates the starting point of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning that He did not send a messenger to them, nor did He reproach them after killing him, but hastened their destruction. The apparent reading is that the ma in His saying ﴿وما كُنّا مُنْزِلِينَ﴾ is a negation, so the meaning is close to that of the sentence before it: "It was not valid in Our judgment that We should send down against them a host from heaven for their destruction, because He, may He be exalted, ordained the destruction of every people in some respects and not others, as He said ﴿فَكُلًّا أخَذْنا بِذَنْبِهِ﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 40], and so on." A group said that ma is a noun (ism) conjoined to jund (host). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "That is, a host, and from (p-332) that which We were sending down upon the nations like them." End of quote. This is an unsound interpretation, because the min in min jund is extra (za'idah). According to the Basrans, other than al-Akhfash, the extra min has two conditions: first, that it be preceded by a negation, a prohibition, or an interrogative; second, that it be followed by an indefinite noun. Even if this is so, the conjoined noun after an indefinite cannot be definite. It is not permitted to say: "I did not strike any man, nor Zayd," and it is not permitted to say: "nor from Zayd." Ibn ʿAtiyya took the conjoined word as meaning "the one" (alladhi), which is definite, so it cannot be conjoined to an indefinite noun governed by the extra min. Abu al-Baqa said: "It is permissible for ma to be extra, that is, 'and indeed We were sending down,'" but this is not correct.

He read ﴿إنْ كانَتْ إلّا صَيْحَةً﴾ with the accusative on Sayhah, with kana as a defective (naqisah) verb whose subject (ism) is a pronoun, meaning: "If the seizure or punishment was" (in kanat al-akhdhah aw al-ʿuqubah). Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, and Muʿadh ibn al-Harith al-Qari read sayhatun with the nominative in both places, taking kanat as complete (tammah), meaning: "What happened or occurred was only one Cry." The original rule is that the verb should not take the feminine ending (ta'), because when the verb is attributed to a feminine noun that follows illa, the sign of feminine gender is not attached. One says: "No one stood up but Hind," and it is not permitted to say: "No one stood up but Hind" with the feminine ending attached, according to our companions (the Basran grammarians), except in poetry. Some permitted it in ordinary speech, though rarely. Similar is the reading of al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu Rajaʾ, al-Jahdari, Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, and Abu Bahriyyah: ﴿لا تُرى إلّا مَساكِنُهم﴾ with the ta'. The well-known reading is with the ya'. Also the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

And nothing remained but the ribs, heaving.

And the saying of another:

She is free of suspicion and blame in our war, except the daughters of our paternal uncles.

Abu Hatim and many grammarians rejected this reading because of the attachment of the feminine ending.

﴿فَإذا هم خامِدُونَ﴾: that is, extinction overtook them immediately after the Cry, without delay. He used "extinguished" (khumud) as a metaphor for their silence after their life, like a fire that dies down after it blazed. The address "Alas" (ya hasrah) in this sense means: "This is the time of your presence and manifestation," a supposed address, like this one, according to Sibawayh, and it is an indefinite vocative according to the reading of the majority. Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and al-Hasan read: ﴿يا حَسْرَةَ العِبادِ﴾ with the annexation (idafah). So the regret may be from them over what they missed, and it may be the regret of others over them, for what they missed of following the messengers when they were brought forth for punishment. Human nature is moved when witnessing the punishment of others and grieves over them.

Abu al-Zinad, ʿAbdullah ibn Dhakwan al-Madani, Ibn Hurmuz, and Ibn Jundub read ﴿يا حَسْرَهْ عَلى العِبادِ﴾ with the ha' silent in both states, treating connection like pause, and they paused on the ha' for emphasis in regret, since the ha' contains a sigh like the ta'awwuh (groan). Then they connected in that same state, as stated by the author of al-Lawami. Ibn Khalawayh said: "Ya hasrata ʿala al-ʿibad without tanwin," as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Its basis is that he dispensed with the fatha in place of the alif, which replaces the ya' of the speaker in vocatives, just as he dispensed with the kasra in place of the ya'. It has also been read: ﴿يا حَسْرَتا﴾ with the alif, meaning "O my regret," and it may be from God in the sense of metaphor, to magnify what they committed against themselves, and to express strong denial and wonder at it. The apparent meaning is that the servants are those who denied the messengers, and the angels grieved over them, as said by al-Dahhak. Al-Dahhak also said: the meaning is "Alas, O regret of the angels over Our servants, the messengers, when faith no longer benefits them." Abu al-ʿAliyah said: the servants here refer to the three messengers, and this regret was from the disbelievers when they saw God's punishment and lamented what they had missed. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "His saying ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ (no messenger comes to them) refutes this interpretation." End of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: al-hasrah is a state that overtakes a person from excessive regret over what has no end, until he remains exhausted (hasir). It was said: the one addressed is omitted, and ḥasratan is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar), meaning "O people, grieve with grief." It was also said that ﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلى العِبادِ﴾ is the words of the man who came from the farthest part of the city running, when the people rushed to kill him. It was said: it is the words of the three messengers, who said this when they were killed, and the punishment came down upon them, saying: "Alas for these people," as if they wished that they had believed. End of quote. The alif and lam (in al-ʿibad) are for a known reference (al-ʿahd) if we say the servants meant are the three messengers, or those to whom they were sent, who perished because of their disbelief and denial of them. The apparent meaning is that the definite article here defines the category of the denying disbelievers. In summary, the one who grieves is: the angels, or God, or the believers, or the three messengers, or that man, these are the sayings.

﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ up to the end of the verse: this is an illustration addressed to Quraysh, who are the people to whom the pronoun in His words ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed﴾ refers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Kam (how many) here is khabariyya (the informative kam), and anna-hum (that they) is a badal (substitute, apposition) for it, and the seeing is ocular seeing." End of quotation. This is not correct, because if it is khabariyya, it is in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by ahlaknā (We destroyed), and nothing else is permissible for it. Given this, it is impossible for anna-hum to be a badal of it, because the badal (substitution) is intended to repeat the governing verb, and if ahlaknā were made to govern anna-hum, it would not be sound. Do you not see that if you said "We destroyed the cessation of their return" or "We destroyed their not returning," it would not be a sentence? But Ibn 'Atiyya imagined that yaraw (they see) has kam as its object, so he imagined that their saying "that they do not return" is a badal, because it is permissible for it to be governed by it, so you say: "Have they not seen that they do not return?" This and its like is evidence of his weakness in the science of Arabic grammar.

al-Zajjaj said: it is a badal from the clause, and the meaning is: "Have they not seen that the generations We destroyed do not return to them? Because non-return and destruction have the meaning of prohibition." What al-Zajjaj said is nothing, because it is not a grammatical badal; he only explained the meaning and did not observe the technical rule of grammar (sina'at al-nahw).

Abu al-Baqa' said: anna-hum ilayhim (that they to them). End of quotation. This is nothing, because kam is not a mu'mal (governed element) of yaraw.

It is transmitted from al-Farra' that he makes yaraw govern in both clauses without badal. His saying "in both clauses" is permissible, because anna-hum and what follows it is not a clause. He did not explain how this governing works.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ألم يروا﴾ means "Have they not known?" It is mu'allaq (suspended) from governing kam, because kam is not governed by a verb preceding it, whether it is interrogative or informative, since its origin is interrogation, except that its meaning permeates the sentence, as it permeates in your saying: "Have they not seen that Zayd is indeed departing?" even though you did not govern its wording. And ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ is a badal from (ahlaknā) according to the meaning, not according to the wording. Its estimate: "Have they not seen the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they are not returning to them?" End of quotation.

So he made yaraw mean ya'lamu (they know) and suspended it from governing kam. His saying "because kam is not governed by what precedes it, whether it is interrogative or informative" is not absolute, because if the governing element is a harf al-jarr (preposition) or a mudaf (construct noun), it is permissible for it to govern kam, as in: "On how many a trunk is your house built?" "Where is the leader of how many you accompanied?" "For how many a poor person did you give charity? I hope for the reward." "Where is the martyr of how many in the way of God that you did good to?" His saying "or informative" — the informative kam has two dialects: the eloquent one, as he mentioned, is not preceded by any governing element except those we have mentioned, namely the preposition; and the other dialect, transmitted by al-Akhfash, says: "malaktu kam ghulām" (I owned how many boys), meaning: "I owned many boys." So just as the governing element may precede kathīr (many), likewise it may precede kam because it has its meaning.

His saying "because its origin is interrogation" is not correct; its origin is not interrogation, rather each of the two kinds is a basis in its own category, but it is a shared word between interrogation and information. His saying "except that its meaning permeates the sentence" means that the meaning of yaraw permeates the sentence, because he made it suspended, and explained yaraw as ya'lamu. His saying "as in your saying: 'Have they not seen that Zayd is indeed departing?'" — the clause "Zayd is indeed departing" is governed according to meaning by yaraw; if it were governed according to wording, the lam (emphatic lam) would not enter, and anna would be fatha-vowelled. Anna with lam in its predicate is among the particles that suspend verbs of the heart.

His saying: "and ﴿that they do not return﴾ [al-Anbiya 95] to the end of his speech" is not correct as a badal, neither according to wording nor according to meaning. As for according to wording, he claimed that yaraw is suspended, so kam would be interrogative, and it would be the object of ahlaknā, and ahlaknā does not govern ﴿that they to them do not return﴾, and this was mentioned earlier. As for according to meaning, it is also not correct, because he said its estimate, that is, according to meaning: "Have they not seen the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they are not returning to them?" Then their being not-so-and-so is not the multitude of destruction, so it is not a badal of kull from kull (whole from whole), nor a badal of part from destruction, nor a badal of part from whole, nor a badal al-ishtimal (badal of inclusion), because badal al-ishtimal is correct when it can be idafa-ed (made construct) to what it substitutes for, and likewise badal of part from whole, and this is not correct here. You do not say: "Have they not seen the cessation of the return of the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them." In badal al-ishtimal, as in: "The girl pleased me her beauty," and "Zayd was robbed of his garment," it is correct to say: "The beauty of the girl pleased me," and "The garment of Zayd was stolen." The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of such a sentence has already preceded us in His words: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-An'am 6], in the surah of al-An'am.

What the discipline of Arabic grammar requires is that anna-hum is governed by an elided verb, which the meaning indicates, and its estimate: "We decided" or "We ruled" ﴿that they to them do not return﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited: innahum, with a kasra on the hamza, as a new sentence (isti'naf) and a cutting of the clause from what precedes it in terms of i'rab. This indicates that the fath (fatha) reading is also cut from what precedes it in terms of i'rab, so that the two readings agree and do not differ.

The pronoun in anna-hum refers to the meaning of kam, namely the generations, and ilayhim refers to the one to whom yaraw is attributed, namely Quraysh. So the meaning is: "They do not return to anyone in this world."

It has been said: the pronoun in anna-hum refers to the one to whom yaraw is attributed, and the pronoun in ilayhim refers to the destroyed ones. The meaning is: the remaining ones do not return to the destroyed ones by lineage or by birth; that is, We destroyed them and cut off their offspring, and destruction together with the cutting off of offspring is more complete and more general.

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited: "Have they not seen whom We destroyed," and anna-hum according to this is a badal al-ishtimal. In their saying "that they do not return" there is a refutation of those who believe in the return (raj'a). It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Some people claim that 'Ali will be raised before the Day of Resurrection." He said: "Those people are not us, when we married his wives and divided his inheritance."

'Asim, Hamza and Ibn 'Amir recited: with the heavy pronunciation of lamma (lammā); the rest of the seven read it with the light pronunciation. As for the one who makes it heavy, lamma is in his view with the meaning of illa (except), and in (in) is negative, meaning: "There is not all of them except that all of them are brought before Us," that is, gathered, as Qatada said. Ibn Salam said: "punished." It has also been said: the estimate is "for whom" (li-man ma) and this is nothing.

As for the one who makes lamma light, he takes in (in) as the light form of the heavy one, and ma as an extra element (za'ida). That is: "Indeed all of them, certainly all are brought before Us." This is according to the school of the Basrans.

As for the Kufans, in (in) in their view is negative, the lam is with the meaning of illa (except), and ma is extra, and lamma with the heavy mim is with the meaning of illa, established in the language of the Arabs by the transmission of trustworthy narrators, so the claim of al-Kisa'i that he does not know this should not be considered.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: regarding the meaning of lamma as illa there is a suitable sense, which is that lamma is as if it were both negative particles together, namely lam and ma, so the negation is emphasized; and illa is as if it were two negative particles, in and la, so one of them is used in place of the other. End of quotation. He took this from the saying of al-Farra' regarding illa in exception, that it is composed of in and la, except that al-Farra' made the light in (in) from the heavy one and ma extra, meaning: "In all of them are certainly brought before Us." This is according to the school of the Basrans. As for the Kufans, in (in) in their view is negative, the lam is with the meaning of illa, ma is extra, and lamma with the heavy mim is with the meaning of illa, established as a negative particle. This is a view rejected by the grammarians, weak, and what is composed from it and adds distortion is weaker than it. Kull (all) has the meaning of encompassing, and jami' (all) is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and it indicates collectivity. Jami' muhdarun (brought before Us) here is according to the meaning, just as mun-tasir (victorious) was made singular according to the wording, and both after jami' are observed in terms of the verse-endings (fawasil).

This sentence came after the mention of destruction to make clear that the One Most High does not leave whoever He destroys unattended; rather, after their destruction there is gathering, reckoning, reward and punishment. For this reason He followed this with what indicates the Gathering (hashr), in His words: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth: We gave it life﴾ and what follows it of signs. He began with the earth because it is their dwelling place, in motion and stillness, life and death. The death of the earth is its barrenness, and its reviving is by rain.

The pronoun in lahum refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and those who are like them in denying the Gathering. "Ahyaynāhā" (We gave it life) is a new sentence of explanation for the dead earth being a sign, and likewise ﴿We strip off﴾ [yaslakh]. It has been said: ahyaynāhā is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element of it is "āyah" (sign) with what it contains of the meaning of informing, and "āyah" would be a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and "the dead earth" would be the subject (mubtada'). So the intention with "āyah" is delay, and the estimate is: "And the dead earth is a sign for them, revived," like your saying: "Standing is Zayd, hastening," that is, "Zayd is standing, hastening." And "for them" is connected to "āyah," not a qualifier.

al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible for the earth and the night to be described by a verb, because by them is meant the two kinds in an absolute sense, not a particular earth and night, by their being revived, so they are treated like indefinite nouns in being described by verbs and the like:
"And indeed I pass by the base man who abuses me"
End of quotation. This demolishes what has been established among the leading grammarians, that an indefinite noun is only qualified by an indefinite noun, and a definite noun is only qualified by a definite noun, and there is no evidence for those who went to that view. As for "yasubbuni" (who abuses me), it is a circumstantial clause (hal), that is, "abbing me." Al-Zamakhshari followed Ibn Malik in this in his book al-Tashil.

In these sentences there is a multiplicity: indeed, reviving it so that it becomes green, delighting the soul and the eye; and bringing forth grain from it so that what they live on is in the place where they are settled, not in the sky or in the air. He made the grains (habbāt) because they eat from the grain, and perhaps the soul yearns for a change, so the earth yields grain, and the tree yields fruit, and the gushing of springs produces dependence on the cultivation of crops and fruit, and if it came from the sky it would not be known where it is planted nor where the rain falls.

Jinah ibn Hubaysh recited "wa-fajarnā" (and We caused to gush) with the light pronunciation, while the majority read it with the heavy pronunciation. "Min thamarih" (of its fruit) with two fathas; Talha, Ibn Wathab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with two dammas; al-A'mash read it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. The pronoun in thamarihi refers to the water. It has been said: because the springs indicate it, and because it is by elision of an idafa, that is, "of the water of the springs." It has been said: it refers to the palm trees, and it suffices with that because of the knowledge of the sharing of the kinds in what the palm is attached to, namely eating its fruit. Or it is meant: "of the fruit of what was mentioned," which is the gardens, as the poet said:
"In it are lines of black and white,
as if on its skin is the pattern of leprosy (bahaq)."
It was said to him: "How did you say 'springs,' when it seems that what preceded is lines?" He said: "Arat said that." It has been said: it refers to the gushing that is indicated by "We caused to gush," and the verse "and We caused to gush" is the nearest mentioned thing. He meant by its fruit its benefits, as you say: "The fruit of trade is profit."

al-Zamakhshari said: and its origin is "min thamarinā" (of Our fruit), as He said "and We made" and "and We caused to gush," so he moved the speech from the first person to the third person by way of iltifat (shift of person). The meaning is: "that they may eat of what God created of fruit, and of what their hands made of planting, watering, wells and other works, until the fruit reached its end, and its produce appeared." That is, the fruit in itself is the act and creation of God, and in it are traces of the toil of the sons of Adam. It is also permissible that "ma" be negative, so that the fruit is the creation of God, and human hands did not make it, nor are they able to create it.

The majority read ﴿wa-mā ʿamilathu﴾ with the pronoun. If "mā" is a relative pronoun, the pronoun refers to it; if it is negative, the pronoun refers to the fruit. Talha, 'Isa, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it without a pronoun, with the object of "ʿamilat" omitted in both estimates. In this reading it is permitted that "mā" be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), that is, "and the work of their hands," and this is a verbal noun used to mean the thing made, so it returns to the sense of the relative pronoun.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 28–44 (part 3 of 4):

When God enumerated these blessings, He urged gratitude, saying: ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ Then God declared Himself far above everything that a heretic might ascribe to Him or that a polytheist might associate with Him.
