He mentioned the creation of pairs (*azwaj*), which are the kinds of all things: ﴿of what the earth produces﴾, such as palm trees, trees, crops, fruits and other things. Every kind is a pair, differing in color, taste, shape, and in being small or large. ﴿And of themselves﴾, meaning males and females. ﴿And of what they do not know﴾, meaning kinds of things they do not know. They were informed of their existence but did not know what they are, since their knowledge does not extend to their essence, and this is not something needed for religion or for worldly life. In informing them of the multitude of His creatures there is evidence of the vastness of His dominion and the greatness of His power.

When God mentioned reasoning from the conditions of the earth, which is the universal place (*al-makan al-kulli*), He mentioned reasoning from the night and the day, which is the universal time (*al-zaman al-kulli*). There is a connection between them: substances cannot do without place, and accidents (*a'rad*) cannot do without time, since every accident is in a time. A similar statement occurs in His words: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37], and then after it: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾ [Fussilat: 39], and so on. There He began with time, because the aim was to establish the oneness of God by the proof of His words: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37], and then the resurrection by His words: ﴿Indeed, He who gave it life is the One who will give life to the dead﴾ [Fussilat: 39]. Here the aim is the resurrection first, because mention of it is more frequent there, while mention of tawhid is more frequent in Fussilat, as evidenced by His words: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth﴾ [Fussilat: 9]. The end of the quotation, which is from the words of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi, with some abridgment.

*Naslakhu* (﴿نَسْلَخُ﴾) means we strip off and peel away. It is a metaphor for removing the light and uncovering it from the place of the night. *Muzlimun* (﴿مُظْلِمُونَ﴾) means entering into darkness, [p. 336] just as one says: *a'attamna* and *as'harna*, meaning we entered the time of 'atama (late night) and of sahar (pre-dawn). Some people have used this to argue that the night is the origin and the day is a later addition to it. They also argued that the sun's resting place is before the Throne, where it prostrates every night after it sets, as occurs in the hadith of Abu Dharr: "It is said to it: Rise from where you rose. When its rising is from its setting, it is said to it: Rise from where you set. That is the time when faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or did not earn good through its faith." Ibn 'Abbas said: When it sets and reaches the place beyond which it does not pass, it stands beneath the Throne until it rises. Al-Hasan said: The sun has three hundred and sixty rising-points in the year. It descends each day to a rising-point and then does not descend again until the year turns, while it runs in the orbit of the mansions (*falak al-manazil*), or until the Day of Resurrection, or its disappearance (ghaybubatuha), because it runs at every moment to a specific limit where it sets. Or [the resting place is] one of its rising-points at the two solstices (*al-munqalabayn*), because they are the extremes of its rising-points; when it reaches them it turns back. Otherwise, it would not come to rest from its motion even for the blink of an eye. Ibn Qutayba inclined to this view. Or [the resting place is] its standing at midday each day, and the evidence of its standing is that shadow stands still at that time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *li-mustaqarr lahā* means: a fixed, predetermined limit, at which its orbit ends at the end of the year. It is likened to the resting place of a traveler when he has completed his journey. Or it is like the final point for it among the risings and settings, because it traverses them rising point by rising point and setting point by setting point until it reaches the farthest point, and then returns. Therefore, that is its limit and its resting place, since it does not exceed it, or since no one from its course reaches beyond it each day in the sight of our eyes, which is the sunset. It was also said: its resting place is the place where God fixed its course, so that it came to rest there, and that is the end of the year. It was also said: it is the time at which it comes to rest and its motion ceases, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: Regarding the resting place there are several views, in time and in place. In time it is the night, or the year, or the Day of Resurrection. In place it is the furthest point of its ascent in summer and its descent in winter, and it runs to that point and then returns; or it is the furthest of its rising-points, so that each day it has a rising-point, for six months, and then it returns to those arches (*al-muqantarat*). This is what was mentioned above regarding height, since the difference in rising-points is the cause of the difference in height. Or [it means] its arrival at its house in Leo (*al-Asad*), or the circle on which its motion takes place, where it does not deviate from the zodiac (*mintaqat al-buruj*) as the sun passes along it. It may be said: it runs in the manner of its resting place, since the astronomers (*ashab al-hay'a*) said: the sun is in an orbit, and the orbit revolves, turning the sun, so the sun runs in the manner of its resting place. End of quotation.

It is also read as *ila mustaqarrihā* (﴿إلى مُسْتَقَرِّها﴾). 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud], Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' ibn Rabah, Zayn al-'Abidin, al-Baqir and his son al-Sadiq, and Ibn Abi 'Abda read it as *la mustaqarra lahā* (﴿لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها﴾), a negation built on the fatha, which implies the negation of every resting place, and that is in this world; that is, it runs constantly in it and never comes to rest. Only Ibn Abi 'Abla read *mustaqarrun* with a raised and nunated ending, treating *la* as working like *laysa* (in its action), as in the words of the poet:

"Be strong, for nothing on earth remains, nor does any burden of what God has decreed protect."

The reference in *dhalika* (﴿ذَلِكَ﴾) is to the running of the sun: that running is according to that measure and that precise calculation.

﴿The decree of the Mighty﴾: the Dominant with His power over every thing that can be decreed, the All-Encompassing in knowledge of every thing known. The two Harams (the Meccan and Medinan readers), Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin, and al-Hasan, in one report from him, read *wal-qamaru* with a raised ending as a beginning (*ibtida'*). The rest of the seven read it with a fatha as an object of an implied verb (*ishtighal*). *Qaddarnāhu* (﴿قَدَّرْناهُ﴾) is with an elided modifier, meaning: we decreed its course. *Manāzila* (﴿مَنازِلَ﴾) is an adverb of place, meaning: its mansions. It was also said: we decreed its light in mansions, so the amount of light increases each day in the conjunction mansions and decreases in the opposition mansions. It was also said: we decreed it, meaning we made its motion the reverse of the mansions of the sun's lights, and this does not require omitting a preposition of description, since the body of the moon is dark, and light settles in it because it accepts the reverse of the sun's brightness, like a polished mirror when a ray is directed at it.

These mansions are well known among the Arabs. They are twenty-eight mansions, and the moon descends each night into one of them, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it, according to an even measure without variation. It runs through them from the night of the new moon to the twenty-eighth, and then it runs for two nights when the month has only twenty-nine days. These mansions are the positions of the stars to which the Arabs attributed the rain-bringing seasons (*al-anwa' al-mustamtira*), and they are: al-Sharatan, al-Batin, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Hab'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Dabra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, al-'Afr, al-Zubana, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, the front of the bucket (Far' al-Dalw al-Muqaddam), the back of the bucket (Far' al-Dalw al-Mu'akhkhar), and Batn al-Hut, which is also called al-Rishā'. When it reaches the end of its mansions, it becomes thin, bends like a bow, and turns yellow, so it is likened to an old palm-stalk (*'urjun qadim*) in three respects, except for one. Sulayman al-Taymi read *ka-l-'irjawn* with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the jim, while the majority read it with a damma. Both are dialectal forms, like *al-biryun*. *Qadim* (﴿القَدِيمِ﴾) means that over which a long time has passed. It was said: the minimum period for something to be described as old (*qadim*) is one year. So if a man said: "Every slave of mine is old, so he is free," or wrote that in a will, those who had been with him for a year or more would be freed. End of quotation. Antiquity is a relative matter, and it may be applied to something that has not lasted a year or two, so one does not say that the world is ancient (*qadim*); rather, custom is taken into account in such matters.

﴿Nor is it for the sun to overtake the moon﴾: *yanbaghi lahā* (﴿يَنْبَغِي لَها﴾) is used of what cannot be otherwise, meaning that He did not give it the power to do so. This overtaking that is not fitting is, as al-Zamakhshari said: God assigned to each of the night and the day and their two signs a portion of time, and set for it a known limit, and arranged their affairs in succession. So it is not fitting for the sun that it should not begin for it, nor that it be valid or proper, because the arrangement is based on the outcome. If each of the two luminaries had an authority of its own, so that it could overtake the moon, they would coincide at the same time and the sun would enter into the moon's authority and obliterate its light. Nor would the night outrun the day, meaning the sign of the night would not outrun the sign of the day; these are the two luminaries. The matter remains in this order until God voids what He has arranged and diminishes what He has joined, so that the sun and moon are brought together and the sun rises from its west. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: when the sun rises, the moon has no light, and when the moon rises, the sun has no light. Mujahid said: the light of one of them is not like the light of the other. Qatada said: each has a limit that it does not exceed and does not fall short of; when the authority of this one comes, the other departs. Ibn 'Abbas also said: when they meet in the sky, one of them is in front of the other, in mansions where they do not share. Al-Hasan said: they do not meet in the sky on the night of the crescent specifically, meaning the sun does not remain until dawn, but when it sets, the moon rises. Yahya ibn Sallam said: it does not overtake it on the night of the full moon specifically, because the moon sets before the sun rises. It was also said: it cannot overtake it in its swiftness, because the orbit of the moon's sphere is inside the sphere of Mercury, the sphere of Mercury is inside the sphere of Venus, and the sphere of Venus is inside the sphere of the sun. So when the path of the sun is farther away, the moon traverses all parts of its sphere, meaning the twelve zodiacal signs, in the time that the sun takes to traverse one of them. Al-Nahhas said: what is said about it, and the clearest of it, is that the moon's course is swift, and the sun cannot overtake it in its course. End of quotation. This is a summary of the view stated before:

﴿Nor does the night outrun the day﴾. It does not contradict His words: ﴿He covers the night over the day, seeking it urgently﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], because the apparent meaning of *yatlubuhu hathithan* (﴿يَطْلُبُهُ حَثِيثًا﴾) is that the day is also ahead, which agrees with the apparent meaning. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi understood from *yatlubuhu hathithan* that the day seeks the night, and the night precedes it. From His words ﴿nor does the night outrun the day﴾ he understood that the night is overtaken, not overtaking, and so he raised it as an objection, saying: How can the night be both overtaking and overtaken? He answered that the night here means the authority of the night, which is the moon, and it does not overtake the sun in its swift daily motion. The night there means the night itself, and each of them, since it comes after the other, is seeking it. End of quotation. This question arose for him because he took the subject pronoun in *yatlubuhu* as referring to the day, and the object pronoun as referring to the night. The apparent meaning is that the subject pronoun refers to what is the grammatical subject in meaning, which is the night, because before the transitivizing hamza [in *yughshi*] it was: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], and the object pronoun refers to the day, because it was the object before and after the transitive form.

'Imara ibn 'Aqil ibn Bilal ibn Jarir al-Khatafi read *sabiqu* without tanwin and *al-nahara* with a fatha. Al-Mubarrad said: I heard him recite it, and I said: What is this? He said: I meant *sabiq al-nahar*, and I dropped the tanwin because it is lighter. End of quotation. He dropped the tanwin because of the meeting of two unvoweled consonants.

The explanation of ﴿And each is in an orbit, swimming﴾ has already been given in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The apparent meaning of "dhurriyyah" is the children and whoever among them grows up. It has also been said that the word applies to both fathers and children; this was reported from Abu Uthman. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is confusion, and this usage is not known in the language." The discussion of *dhurriyyah* has already been covered in Surat Al 'Imran.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *lahum* ("for them") and in *dhurriyyatihim* ("their offspring") refers to the same thing. The meaning is that God carried the offspring of these people, that is, their earliest ancestors, in the ship of Nuh (peace be upon him). This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of others. Similar to this is that the ships that exist among the children of Adam until the Day of Resurrection are included. Alternatively, the phrase *dhurriyyatihim* may involve an omitted noun, meaning "the offspring of their kind," and *dhurriyyah* may refer to those who cannot walk or ride among the offspring and the weak. Then *al-fulk* is a collective noun, and God bestowed favour upon them by this. That *al-fulk* is meant in a generic sense was also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi. Similar to this is the camel and everything else that is ridden.

It has also been said that the two pronouns refer to different things: the *dhurriyyah* of the past generations. This was reported from 'Ali ibn Sulayman, and it was a sign for these people, since they are the offspring of that *dhurriyyah*.

It has also been said that *dhurriyyah* means sperm drops, and *al-fulk al-mashhun* ("the laden ship") means the wombs of women. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. This cannot be correct, because it belongs to the type of esoteric (Batiniyyah) and extreme Sufi *tafsir* (interpretation of the Qur'an), which interprets God's Book in a way that the wording does not indicate by any of the modes of indication, thus "distorting words from their places."

That the apparent sense of *al-fulk* is intended is shown by His saying ﴿And We created for them of the like thereof that which they ride﴾, meaning camels, horses, mules and donkeys. The likeness lies in the fact that each is a means of riding that carries people to their lands, and this applies when *al-fulk* is taken generically. If, however, it refers to the ship of Nuh, the likeness lies in its being ships like it, which exist among the children of Adam.

The view of those who say that "the offspring in the ship" are the people of Nuh in his ship, and that "the like" means the term and what is ridden, is far-fetched, because His saying ﴿And if We will, We shall drown them﴾ refutes it.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-A'mash, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Aban ibn 'Uthman read *dhurriyyatihim* in the plural. Zayd and Aban read the *dhal* with a kasra. The rest of the seven readers, along with Talhah and 'Isa, read it in the singular.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *dhurriyyatahum* means their children and those whose carrying concerns them. It has also been said that the term *dhurriyyah* applies to women, since they are its fields. In a hadith it is reported that he (ﷺ) forbade killing the *dharari*, meaning women.

﴿Of the like thereof﴾: of the like of the ship, ﴿that which they ride﴾: of the camels, which are the ships of the land. It has been said that ﴿al-fulk al-mashhun﴾ is the ship of Nuh. The meaning of God carrying their offspring in it is that their earliest ancestors were carried in it, and their offspring were in their loins. He mentioned their offspring rather than themselves because it is more eloquent in terms of favour upon them, and more fitting for wonder at His power in carrying their descendants until the Day of Resurrection in the ship of Nuh. ﴿Of the like thereof﴾: of the like of that ship, ﴿that which they ride﴾: of the ships. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: He singled out the offspring for mention because those who existed were disbelievers, and there was no benefit in their existence. That is, the carrying was not a carrying of them, but a carrying of what was in their loins of the believers. He also said: The pronoun in *wa-ayah lahum* ("and a sign for them") refers to the servants in His saying ﴿Alas for the servants﴾. Then He said after this ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth which We revived﴾, ﴿and a sign for them is the night﴾, ﴿and a sign for them that We carried their offspring﴾, meaning the offspring of the servants. It is not necessary that the pronoun in both places refer to two different meanings. This is like His saying ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [an-Nisa 29], which means: none of you should kill one another. That is the sense here.

﴿And a sign for them﴾: that is, the sign of each one of them, ﴿that We carried﴾: the offspring of each one of them, or the offspring of some of them. End of quotation.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿And We created﴾ is that creating and originating are intended, so the reference is to camels and what is ridden. Here *min* is explanatory. Although what a human makes may sometimes be attributed to God as creation, the more common usage is what we have mentioned. When the ships are intended, *min* is partitive. The apparent reference of *lahum* is to what it referred to in ﴿And a sign for them﴾, because it is the subject being spoken of. It is also permitted that it refer to the offspring. The apparent reference of the pronoun in *mithlihi* is to (p-339) the ship. It has been said that it refers to something known though not mentioned, and its implied sense is: of the like of what We mentioned of the created things in His saying ﴿Glory be to the One who created all the pairs of what the earth produces﴾, just as they said concerning His saying ﴿of its fruit﴾, meaning of the fruit of what We mentioned.

Al-Hasan read *nughargqihum* with shaddah; the majority read it without shaddah. *Al-sarikh* is an *fa'il* form meaning "one who cries out," that is, one who seeks help, and also meaning "one who gives help," that is, one who relieves. This is its meaning here, that is, there is no one to relieve them and no one to assist them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ means there is no rescue for them. End of quotation. It appears that he took it as a verbal noun from *af'ala*, and this requires a transmitted report that *sarikh* can be a verbal noun meaning *sirakh* (crying out).

The apparent sense of His saying ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ is: there is no helper for those whom God wills to drown, ﴿nor are they rescued﴾: that is, they are not saved from death by drowning. He first negated the *sarikh*, which is specific, and then negated their being rescued by a *sarikh* or by anything else.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ is a resumed statement of information about those who travel at sea, whether they are saved or drowned. In this state they have no salvation except by the mercy of God. His saying ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ is not tied to those who are drowned, although it may be tied to them, and the first is better, so consider it. End of quotation. This is not good, nor is it better.

The *fa'* in ﴿so there is no sarikh for them﴾ connects the sentence to what precedes it with clear linkage and binds it to it with evident tie. Deliverance from the punishment is in two respects: what prevents it from its origin, which is negated by His saying ﴿there is no sarikh for them﴾, and what lifts it after it occurs, which is negated by His saying ﴿nor are they rescued﴾.

The word *rahmatan* ("mercy") is in the accusative as an exception with the object of purpose omitted, meaning: for a mercy from Us. Al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: ﴿until a time﴾ means until the time of death, as reported by Qatadah. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is either for a mercy from Us, and that they may enjoy life until a term, that is, until an appointed time at which they must die after salvation from drowning. End of quotation. He said "they must die after salvation from drowning" because He said ﴿And if We will﴾, that is, to drown them, ﴿We shall drown them﴾, so whoever God wills to drown must die by drowning.

The apparent sense is that ﴿from Us and as enjoyment until a time﴾ applies to those who are rescued, so it does not imply permanence. Rather, God rescues him out of mercy, lets him enjoy life for a time, and then makes him die. It has also been said that there is a division in this: except for mercy toward one whom He knows will believe, so God rescues him out of mercy, and whoever He knows will not believe, He withholds [death] for a time, and he increases in sin.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Ya-Sin, verses 28–44 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Nor did We send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down.﴾ ﴿It was but one Cry, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾ ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾ ﴿And all of them, without exception, will be brought before Us.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is the dead earth: We gave it life and brought forth from it grain, of which they eat.﴾ ﴿And We made in it gardens of palms and vines, and caused springs to gush forth in it.﴾ ﴿That they may eat of its fruit, and of what their hands have made. Will they not then give thanks?﴾ ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of what they do not know.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place; that is the decree of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations, until it returns like the old withered palm-stalk.﴾ ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outrun the day; each floats in an orbit.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾ ﴿And We created for them of its like what they ride.﴾ ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry for them, nor are they rescued.﴾ ﴿Except as mercy from Us and enjoyment for a time.﴾

(p-331) He, may He be exalted, informed of the destruction of the people of Habib by one single Cry, which Jibril shouted at them. In this there is a warning to Quraysh that what befell them may befall them too, since they are the ones for whom the parable was struck. He, may He be exalted, also informed that He did not send down against them for their destruction any host from heaven, such as stones, wind, or other things, and they were too insignificant for Him. His saying "after him" (min ba'dihi) indicates the starting point of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning that He did not send a messenger to them, nor did He reproach them after killing him, but hastened their destruction. The apparent reading is that the ma in His saying ﴿وما كُنّا مُنْزِلِينَ﴾ is a negation, so the meaning is close to that of the sentence before it: "It was not valid in Our judgment that We should send down against them a host from heaven for their destruction, because He, may He be exalted, ordained the destruction of every people in some respects and not others, as He said ﴿فَكُلًّا أخَذْنا بِذَنْبِهِ﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 40], and so on." A group said that ma is a noun (ism) conjoined to jund (host). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "That is, a host, and from (p-332) that which We were sending down upon the nations like them." End of quote. This is an unsound interpretation, because the min in min jund is extra (za'idah). According to the Basrans, other than al-Akhfash, the extra min has two conditions: first, that it be preceded by a negation, a prohibition, or an interrogative; second, that it be followed by an indefinite noun. Even if this is so, the conjoined noun after an indefinite cannot be definite. It is not permitted to say: "I did not strike any man, nor Zayd," and it is not permitted to say: "nor from Zayd." Ibn ʿAtiyya took the conjoined word as meaning "the one" (alladhi), which is definite, so it cannot be conjoined to an indefinite noun governed by the extra min. Abu al-Baqa said: "It is permissible for ma to be extra, that is, 'and indeed We were sending down,'" but this is not correct.

He read ﴿إنْ كانَتْ إلّا صَيْحَةً﴾ with the accusative on Sayhah, with kana as a defective (naqisah) verb whose subject (ism) is a pronoun, meaning: "If the seizure or punishment was" (in kanat al-akhdhah aw al-ʿuqubah). Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, and Muʿadh ibn al-Harith al-Qari read sayhatun with the nominative in both places, taking kanat as complete (tammah), meaning: "What happened or occurred was only one Cry." The original rule is that the verb should not take the feminine ending (ta'), because when the verb is attributed to a feminine noun that follows illa, the sign of feminine gender is not attached. One says: "No one stood up but Hind," and it is not permitted to say: "No one stood up but Hind" with the feminine ending attached, according to our companions (the Basran grammarians), except in poetry. Some permitted it in ordinary speech, though rarely. Similar is the reading of al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu Rajaʾ, al-Jahdari, Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, and Abu Bahriyyah: ﴿لا تُرى إلّا مَساكِنُهم﴾ with the ta'. The well-known reading is with the ya'. Also the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

And nothing remained but the ribs, heaving.

And the saying of another:

She is free of suspicion and blame in our war, except the daughters of our paternal uncles.

Abu Hatim and many grammarians rejected this reading because of the attachment of the feminine ending.

﴿فَإذا هم خامِدُونَ﴾: that is, extinction overtook them immediately after the Cry, without delay. He used "extinguished" (khumud) as a metaphor for their silence after their life, like a fire that dies down after it blazed. The address "Alas" (ya hasrah) in this sense means: "This is the time of your presence and manifestation," a supposed address, like this one, according to Sibawayh, and it is an indefinite vocative according to the reading of the majority. Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and al-Hasan read: ﴿يا حَسْرَةَ العِبادِ﴾ with the annexation (idafah). So the regret may be from them over what they missed, and it may be the regret of others over them, for what they missed of following the messengers when they were brought forth for punishment. Human nature is moved when witnessing the punishment of others and grieves over them.

Abu al-Zinad, ʿAbdullah ibn Dhakwan al-Madani, Ibn Hurmuz, and Ibn Jundub read ﴿يا حَسْرَهْ عَلى العِبادِ﴾ with the ha' silent in both states, treating connection like pause, and they paused on the ha' for emphasis in regret, since the ha' contains a sigh like the ta'awwuh (groan). Then they connected in that same state, as stated by the author of al-Lawami. Ibn Khalawayh said: "Ya hasrata ʿala al-ʿibad without tanwin," as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Its basis is that he dispensed with the fatha in place of the alif, which replaces the ya' of the speaker in vocatives, just as he dispensed with the kasra in place of the ya'. It has also been read: ﴿يا حَسْرَتا﴾ with the alif, meaning "O my regret," and it may be from God in the sense of metaphor, to magnify what they committed against themselves, and to express strong denial and wonder at it. The apparent meaning is that the servants are those who denied the messengers, and the angels grieved over them, as said by al-Dahhak. Al-Dahhak also said: the meaning is "Alas, O regret of the angels over Our servants, the messengers, when faith no longer benefits them." Abu al-ʿAliyah said: the servants here refer to the three messengers, and this regret was from the disbelievers when they saw God's punishment and lamented what they had missed. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "His saying ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ (no messenger comes to them) refutes this interpretation." End of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: al-hasrah is a state that overtakes a person from excessive regret over what has no end, until he remains exhausted (hasir). It was said: the one addressed is omitted, and ḥasratan is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar), meaning "O people, grieve with grief." It was also said that ﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلى العِبادِ﴾ is the words of the man who came from the farthest part of the city running, when the people rushed to kill him. It was said: it is the words of the three messengers, who said this when they were killed, and the punishment came down upon them, saying: "Alas for these people," as if they wished that they had believed. End of quote. The alif and lam (in al-ʿibad) are for a known reference (al-ʿahd) if we say the servants meant are the three messengers, or those to whom they were sent, who perished because of their disbelief and denial of them. The apparent meaning is that the definite article here defines the category of the denying disbelievers. In summary, the one who grieves is: the angels, or God, or the believers, or the three messengers, or that man, these are the sayings.

﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ up to the end of the verse: this is an illustration addressed to Quraysh, who are the people to whom the pronoun in His words ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed﴾ refers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Kam (how many) here is khabariyya (the informative kam), and anna-hum (that they) is a badal (substitute, apposition) for it, and the seeing is ocular seeing." End of quotation. This is not correct, because if it is khabariyya, it is in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by ahlaknā (We destroyed), and nothing else is permissible for it. Given this, it is impossible for anna-hum to be a badal of it, because the badal (substitution) is intended to repeat the governing verb, and if ahlaknā were made to govern anna-hum, it would not be sound. Do you not see that if you said "We destroyed the cessation of their return" or "We destroyed their not returning," it would not be a sentence? But Ibn 'Atiyya imagined that yaraw (they see) has kam as its object, so he imagined that their saying "that they do not return" is a badal, because it is permissible for it to be governed by it, so you say: "Have they not seen that they do not return?" This and its like is evidence of his weakness in the science of Arabic grammar.

al-Zajjaj said: it is a badal from the clause, and the meaning is: "Have they not seen that the generations We destroyed do not return to them? Because non-return and destruction have the meaning of prohibition." What al-Zajjaj said is nothing, because it is not a grammatical badal; he only explained the meaning and did not observe the technical rule of grammar (sina'at al-nahw).

Abu al-Baqa' said: anna-hum ilayhim (that they to them). End of quotation. This is nothing, because kam is not a mu'mal (governed element) of yaraw.

It is transmitted from al-Farra' that he makes yaraw govern in both clauses without badal. His saying "in both clauses" is permissible, because anna-hum and what follows it is not a clause. He did not explain how this governing works.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ألم يروا﴾ means "Have they not known?" It is mu'allaq (suspended) from governing kam, because kam is not governed by a verb preceding it, whether it is interrogative or informative, since its origin is interrogation, except that its meaning permeates the sentence, as it permeates in your saying: "Have they not seen that Zayd is indeed departing?" even though you did not govern its wording. And ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ is a badal from (ahlaknā) according to the meaning, not according to the wording. Its estimate: "Have they not seen the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they are not returning to them?" End of quotation.

So he made yaraw mean ya'lamu (they know) and suspended it from governing kam. His saying "because kam is not governed by what precedes it, whether it is interrogative or informative" is not absolute, because if the governing element is a harf al-jarr (preposition) or a mudaf (construct noun), it is permissible for it to govern kam, as in: "On how many a trunk is your house built?" "Where is the leader of how many you accompanied?" "For how many a poor person did you give charity? I hope for the reward." "Where is the martyr of how many in the way of God that you did good to?" His saying "or informative" — the informative kam has two dialects: the eloquent one, as he mentioned, is not preceded by any governing element except those we have mentioned, namely the preposition; and the other dialect, transmitted by al-Akhfash, says: "malaktu kam ghulām" (I owned how many boys), meaning: "I owned many boys." So just as the governing element may precede kathīr (many), likewise it may precede kam because it has its meaning.

His saying "because its origin is interrogation" is not correct; its origin is not interrogation, rather each of the two kinds is a basis in its own category, but it is a shared word between interrogation and information. His saying "except that its meaning permeates the sentence" means that the meaning of yaraw permeates the sentence, because he made it suspended, and explained yaraw as ya'lamu. His saying "as in your saying: 'Have they not seen that Zayd is indeed departing?'" — the clause "Zayd is indeed departing" is governed according to meaning by yaraw; if it were governed according to wording, the lam (emphatic lam) would not enter, and anna would be fatha-vowelled. Anna with lam in its predicate is among the particles that suspend verbs of the heart.

His saying: "and ﴿that they do not return﴾ [al-Anbiya 95] to the end of his speech" is not correct as a badal, neither according to wording nor according to meaning. As for according to wording, he claimed that yaraw is suspended, so kam would be interrogative, and it would be the object of ahlaknā, and ahlaknā does not govern ﴿that they to them do not return﴾, and this was mentioned earlier. As for according to meaning, it is also not correct, because he said its estimate, that is, according to meaning: "Have they not seen the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they are not returning to them?" Then their being not-so-and-so is not the multitude of destruction, so it is not a badal of kull from kull (whole from whole), nor a badal of part from destruction, nor a badal of part from whole, nor a badal al-ishtimal (badal of inclusion), because badal al-ishtimal is correct when it can be idafa-ed (made construct) to what it substitutes for, and likewise badal of part from whole, and this is not correct here. You do not say: "Have they not seen the cessation of the return of the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them." In badal al-ishtimal, as in: "The girl pleased me her beauty," and "Zayd was robbed of his garment," it is correct to say: "The beauty of the girl pleased me," and "The garment of Zayd was stolen." The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of such a sentence has already preceded us in His words: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-An'am 6], in the surah of al-An'am.

What the discipline of Arabic grammar requires is that anna-hum is governed by an elided verb, which the meaning indicates, and its estimate: "We decided" or "We ruled" ﴿that they to them do not return﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited: innahum, with a kasra on the hamza, as a new sentence (isti'naf) and a cutting of the clause from what precedes it in terms of i'rab. This indicates that the fath (fatha) reading is also cut from what precedes it in terms of i'rab, so that the two readings agree and do not differ.

The pronoun in anna-hum refers to the meaning of kam, namely the generations, and ilayhim refers to the one to whom yaraw is attributed, namely Quraysh. So the meaning is: "They do not return to anyone in this world."

It has been said: the pronoun in anna-hum refers to the one to whom yaraw is attributed, and the pronoun in ilayhim refers to the destroyed ones. The meaning is: the remaining ones do not return to the destroyed ones by lineage or by birth; that is, We destroyed them and cut off their offspring, and destruction together with the cutting off of offspring is more complete and more general.

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited: "Have they not seen whom We destroyed," and anna-hum according to this is a badal al-ishtimal. In their saying "that they do not return" there is a refutation of those who believe in the return (raj'a). It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Some people claim that 'Ali will be raised before the Day of Resurrection." He said: "Those people are not us, when we married his wives and divided his inheritance."

'Asim, Hamza and Ibn 'Amir recited: with the heavy pronunciation of lamma (lammā); the rest of the seven read it with the light pronunciation. As for the one who makes it heavy, lamma is in his view with the meaning of illa (except), and in (in) is negative, meaning: "There is not all of them except that all of them are brought before Us," that is, gathered, as Qatada said. Ibn Salam said: "punished." It has also been said: the estimate is "for whom" (li-man ma) and this is nothing.

As for the one who makes lamma light, he takes in (in) as the light form of the heavy one, and ma as an extra element (za'ida). That is: "Indeed all of them, certainly all are brought before Us." This is according to the school of the Basrans.

As for the Kufans, in (in) in their view is negative, the lam is with the meaning of illa (except), and ma is extra, and lamma with the heavy mim is with the meaning of illa, established in the language of the Arabs by the transmission of trustworthy narrators, so the claim of al-Kisa'i that he does not know this should not be considered.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: regarding the meaning of lamma as illa there is a suitable sense, which is that lamma is as if it were both negative particles together, namely lam and ma, so the negation is emphasized; and illa is as if it were two negative particles, in and la, so one of them is used in place of the other. End of quotation. He took this from the saying of al-Farra' regarding illa in exception, that it is composed of in and la, except that al-Farra' made the light in (in) from the heavy one and ma extra, meaning: "In all of them are certainly brought before Us." This is according to the school of the Basrans. As for the Kufans, in (in) in their view is negative, the lam is with the meaning of illa, ma is extra, and lamma with the heavy mim is with the meaning of illa, established as a negative particle. This is a view rejected by the grammarians, weak, and what is composed from it and adds distortion is weaker than it. Kull (all) has the meaning of encompassing, and jami' (all) is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and it indicates collectivity. Jami' muhdarun (brought before Us) here is according to the meaning, just as mun-tasir (victorious) was made singular according to the wording, and both after jami' are observed in terms of the verse-endings (fawasil).

This sentence came after the mention of destruction to make clear that the One Most High does not leave whoever He destroys unattended; rather, after their destruction there is gathering, reckoning, reward and punishment. For this reason He followed this with what indicates the Gathering (hashr), in His words: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth: We gave it life﴾ and what follows it of signs. He began with the earth because it is their dwelling place, in motion and stillness, life and death. The death of the earth is its barrenness, and its reviving is by rain.

The pronoun in lahum refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and those who are like them in denying the Gathering. "Ahyaynāhā" (We gave it life) is a new sentence of explanation for the dead earth being a sign, and likewise ﴿We strip off﴾ [yaslakh]. It has been said: ahyaynāhā is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element of it is "āyah" (sign) with what it contains of the meaning of informing, and "āyah" would be a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and "the dead earth" would be the subject (mubtada'). So the intention with "āyah" is delay, and the estimate is: "And the dead earth is a sign for them, revived," like your saying: "Standing is Zayd, hastening," that is, "Zayd is standing, hastening." And "for them" is connected to "āyah," not a qualifier.

al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible for the earth and the night to be described by a verb, because by them is meant the two kinds in an absolute sense, not a particular earth and night, by their being revived, so they are treated like indefinite nouns in being described by verbs and the like:
"And indeed I pass by the base man who abuses me"
End of quotation. This demolishes what has been established among the leading grammarians, that an indefinite noun is only qualified by an indefinite noun, and a definite noun is only qualified by a definite noun, and there is no evidence for those who went to that view. As for "yasubbuni" (who abuses me), it is a circumstantial clause (hal), that is, "abbing me." Al-Zamakhshari followed Ibn Malik in this in his book al-Tashil.

In these sentences there is a multiplicity: indeed, reviving it so that it becomes green, delighting the soul and the eye; and bringing forth grain from it so that what they live on is in the place where they are settled, not in the sky or in the air. He made the grains (habbāt) because they eat from the grain, and perhaps the soul yearns for a change, so the earth yields grain, and the tree yields fruit, and the gushing of springs produces dependence on the cultivation of crops and fruit, and if it came from the sky it would not be known where it is planted nor where the rain falls.

Jinah ibn Hubaysh recited "wa-fajarnā" (and We caused to gush) with the light pronunciation, while the majority read it with the heavy pronunciation. "Min thamarih" (of its fruit) with two fathas; Talha, Ibn Wathab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with two dammas; al-A'mash read it with a damma on the tha' and a sukun on the mim. The pronoun in thamarihi refers to the water. It has been said: because the springs indicate it, and because it is by elision of an idafa, that is, "of the water of the springs." It has been said: it refers to the palm trees, and it suffices with that because of the knowledge of the sharing of the kinds in what the palm is attached to, namely eating its fruit. Or it is meant: "of the fruit of what was mentioned," which is the gardens, as the poet said:
"In it are lines of black and white,
as if on its skin is the pattern of leprosy (bahaq)."
It was said to him: "How did you say 'springs,' when it seems that what preceded is lines?" He said: "Arat said that." It has been said: it refers to the gushing that is indicated by "We caused to gush," and the verse "and We caused to gush" is the nearest mentioned thing. He meant by its fruit its benefits, as you say: "The fruit of trade is profit."

al-Zamakhshari said: and its origin is "min thamarinā" (of Our fruit), as He said "and We made" and "and We caused to gush," so he moved the speech from the first person to the third person by way of iltifat (shift of person). The meaning is: "that they may eat of what God created of fruit, and of what their hands made of planting, watering, wells and other works, until the fruit reached its end, and its produce appeared." That is, the fruit in itself is the act and creation of God, and in it are traces of the toil of the sons of Adam. It is also permissible that "ma" be negative, so that the fruit is the creation of God, and human hands did not make it, nor are they able to create it.

The majority read ﴿wa-mā ʿamilathu﴾ with the pronoun. If "mā" is a relative pronoun, the pronoun refers to it; if it is negative, the pronoun refers to the fruit. Talha, 'Isa, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it without a pronoun, with the object of "ʿamilat" omitted in both estimates. In this reading it is permitted that "mā" be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), that is, "and the work of their hands," and this is a verbal noun used to mean the thing made, so it returns to the sense of the relative pronoun.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 28–44 (part 3 of 4):

When God enumerated these blessings, He urged gratitude, saying: ﴿Will they not then give thanks?﴾ Then God declared Himself far above everything that a heretic might ascribe to Him or that a polytheist might associate with Him. He mentioned the creation of pairs (*azwaj*), which are the kinds of all things: ﴿of what the earth produces﴾, such as palm trees, trees, crops, fruits and other things. Every kind is a pair, differing in color, taste, shape, and in being small or large. ﴿And of themselves﴾, meaning males and females. ﴿And of what they do not know﴾, meaning kinds of things they do not know. They were informed of their existence but did not know what they are, since their knowledge does not extend to their essence, and this is not something needed for religion or for worldly life. In informing them of the multitude of His creatures there is evidence of the vastness of His dominion and the greatness of His power.

When God mentioned reasoning from the conditions of the earth, which is the universal place (*al-makan al-kulli*), He mentioned reasoning from the night and the day, which is the universal time (*al-zaman al-kulli*). There is a connection between them: substances cannot do without place, and accidents (*a'rad*) cannot do without time, since every accident is in a time. A similar statement occurs in His words: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37], and then after it: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾ [Fussilat: 39], and so on. There He began with time, because the aim was to establish the oneness of God by the proof of His words: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ [Fussilat: 37], and then the resurrection by His words: ﴿Indeed, He who gave it life is the One who will give life to the dead﴾ [Fussilat: 39]. Here the aim is the resurrection first, because mention of it is more frequent there, while mention of tawhid is more frequent in Fussilat, as evidenced by His words: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth﴾ [Fussilat: 9]. The end of the quotation, which is from the words of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi, with some abridgment.

*Naslakhu* (﴿نَسْلَخُ﴾) means we strip off and peel away. It is a metaphor for removing the light and uncovering it from the place of the night. *Muzlimun* (﴿مُظْلِمُونَ﴾) means entering into darkness, [p. 336] just as one says: *a'attamna* and *as'harna*, meaning we entered the time of 'atama (late night) and of sahar (pre-dawn). Some people have used this to argue that the night is the origin and the day is a later addition to it. They also argued that the sun's resting place is before the Throne, where it prostrates every night after it sets, as occurs in the hadith of Abu Dharr: "It is said to it: Rise from where you rose. When its rising is from its setting, it is said to it: Rise from where you set. That is the time when faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or did not earn good through its faith." Ibn 'Abbas said: When it sets and reaches the place beyond which it does not pass, it stands beneath the Throne until it rises. Al-Hasan said: The sun has three hundred and sixty rising-points in the year. It descends each day to a rising-point and then does not descend again until the year turns, while it runs in the orbit of the mansions (*falak al-manazil*), or until the Day of Resurrection, or its disappearance (ghaybubatuha), because it runs at every moment to a specific limit where it sets. Or [the resting place is] one of its rising-points at the two solstices (*al-munqalabayn*), because they are the extremes of its rising-points; when it reaches them it turns back. Otherwise, it would not come to rest from its motion even for the blink of an eye. Ibn Qutayba inclined to this view. Or [the resting place is] its standing at midday each day, and the evidence of its standing is that shadow stands still at that time.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *li-mustaqarr lahā* means: a fixed, predetermined limit, at which its orbit ends at the end of the year. It is likened to the resting place of a traveler when he has completed his journey. Or it is like the final point for it among the risings and settings, because it traverses them rising point by rising point and setting point by setting point until it reaches the farthest point, and then returns. Therefore, that is its limit and its resting place, since it does not exceed it, or since no one from its course reaches beyond it each day in the sight of our eyes, which is the sunset. It was also said: its resting place is the place where God fixed its course, so that it came to rest there, and that is the end of the year. It was also said: it is the time at which it comes to rest and its motion ceases, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: Regarding the resting place there are several views, in time and in place. In time it is the night, or the year, or the Day of Resurrection. In place it is the furthest point of its ascent in summer and its descent in winter, and it runs to that point and then returns; or it is the furthest of its rising-points, so that each day it has a rising-point, for six months, and then it returns to those arches (*al-muqantarat*). This is what was mentioned above regarding height, since the difference in rising-points is the cause of the difference in height. Or [it means] its arrival at its house in Leo (*al-Asad*), or the circle on which its motion takes place, where it does not deviate from the zodiac (*mintaqat al-buruj*) as the sun passes along it. It may be said: it runs in the manner of its resting place, since the astronomers (*ashab al-hay'a*) said: the sun is in an orbit, and the orbit revolves, turning the sun, so the sun runs in the manner of its resting place. End of quotation.

It is also read as *ila mustaqarrihā* (﴿إلى مُسْتَقَرِّها﴾). 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud], Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' ibn Rabah, Zayn al-'Abidin, al-Baqir and his son al-Sadiq, and Ibn Abi 'Abda read it as *la mustaqarra lahā* (﴿لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها﴾), a negation built on the fatha, which implies the negation of every resting place, and that is in this world; that is, it runs constantly in it and never comes to rest. Only Ibn Abi 'Abla read *mustaqarrun* with a raised and nunated ending, treating *la* as working like *laysa* (in its action), as in the words of the poet:

"Be strong, for nothing on earth remains, nor does any burden of what God has decreed protect."

The reference in *dhalika* (﴿ذَلِكَ﴾) is to the running of the sun: that running is according to that measure and that precise calculation.

﴿The decree of the Mighty﴾: the Dominant with His power over every thing that can be decreed, the All-Encompassing in knowledge of every thing known. The two Harams (the Meccan and Medinan readers), Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin, and al-Hasan, in one report from him, read *wal-qamaru* with a raised ending as a beginning (*ibtida'*). The rest of the seven read it with a fatha as an object of an implied verb (*ishtighal*). *Qaddarnāhu* (﴿قَدَّرْناهُ﴾) is with an elided modifier, meaning: we decreed its course. *Manāzila* (﴿مَنازِلَ﴾) is an adverb of place, meaning: its mansions. It was also said: we decreed its light in mansions, so the amount of light increases each day in the conjunction mansions and decreases in the opposition mansions. It was also said: we decreed it, meaning we made its motion the reverse of the mansions of the sun's lights, and this does not require omitting a preposition of description, since the body of the moon is dark, and light settles in it because it accepts the reverse of the sun's brightness, like a polished mirror when a ray is directed at it.

These mansions are well known among the Arabs. They are twenty-eight mansions, and the moon descends each night into one of them, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it, according to an even measure without variation. It runs through them from the night of the new moon to the twenty-eighth, and then it runs for two nights when the month has only twenty-nine days. These mansions are the positions of the stars to which the Arabs attributed the rain-bringing seasons (*al-anwa' al-mustamtira*), and they are: al-Sharatan, al-Batin, al-Thurayya, al-Dabaran, al-Hab'a, al-Han'a, al-Dhira', al-Nathra, al-Tarf, al-Jabha, al-Dabra, al-Sarfa, al-'Awwa', al-Simak, al-'Afr, al-Zubana, al-Iklil, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhabih, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, Sa'd al-Akhbiya, the front of the bucket (Far' al-Dalw al-Muqaddam), the back of the bucket (Far' al-Dalw al-Mu'akhkhar), and Batn al-Hut, which is also called al-Rishā'. When it reaches the end of its mansions, it becomes thin, bends like a bow, and turns yellow, so it is likened to an old palm-stalk (*'urjun qadim*) in three respects, except for one. Sulayman al-Taymi read *ka-l-'irjawn* with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the jim, while the majority read it with a damma. Both are dialectal forms, like *al-biryun*. *Qadim* (﴿القَدِيمِ﴾) means that over which a long time has passed. It was said: the minimum period for something to be described as old (*qadim*) is one year. So if a man said: "Every slave of mine is old, so he is free," or wrote that in a will, those who had been with him for a year or more would be freed. End of quotation. Antiquity is a relative matter, and it may be applied to something that has not lasted a year or two, so one does not say that the world is ancient (*qadim*); rather, custom is taken into account in such matters.

﴿Nor is it for the sun to overtake the moon﴾: *yanbaghi lahā* (﴿يَنْبَغِي لَها﴾) is used of what cannot be otherwise, meaning that He did not give it the power to do so. This overtaking that is not fitting is, as al-Zamakhshari said: God assigned to each of the night and the day and their two signs a portion of time, and set for it a known limit, and arranged their affairs in succession. So it is not fitting for the sun that it should not begin for it, nor that it be valid or proper, because the arrangement is based on the outcome. If each of the two luminaries had an authority of its own, so that it could overtake the moon, they would coincide at the same time and the sun would enter into the moon's authority and obliterate its light. Nor would the night outrun the day, meaning the sign of the night would not outrun the sign of the day; these are the two luminaries. The matter remains in this order until God voids what He has arranged and diminishes what He has joined, so that the sun and moon are brought together and the sun rises from its west. End of quotation.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: when the sun rises, the moon has no light, and when the moon rises, the sun has no light. Mujahid said: the light of one of them is not like the light of the other. Qatada said: each has a limit that it does not exceed and does not fall short of; when the authority of this one comes, the other departs. Ibn 'Abbas also said: when they meet in the sky, one of them is in front of the other, in mansions where they do not share. Al-Hasan said: they do not meet in the sky on the night of the crescent specifically, meaning the sun does not remain until dawn, but when it sets, the moon rises. Yahya ibn Sallam said: it does not overtake it on the night of the full moon specifically, because the moon sets before the sun rises. It was also said: it cannot overtake it in its swiftness, because the orbit of the moon's sphere is inside the sphere of Mercury, the sphere of Mercury is inside the sphere of Venus, and the sphere of Venus is inside the sphere of the sun. So when the path of the sun is farther away, the moon traverses all parts of its sphere, meaning the twelve zodiacal signs, in the time that the sun takes to traverse one of them. Al-Nahhas said: what is said about it, and the clearest of it, is that the moon's course is swift, and the sun cannot overtake it in its course. End of quotation. This is a summary of the view stated before:

﴿Nor does the night outrun the day﴾. It does not contradict His words: ﴿He covers the night over the day, seeking it urgently﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], because the apparent meaning of *yatlubuhu hathithan* (﴿يَطْلُبُهُ حَثِيثًا﴾) is that the day is also ahead, which agrees with the apparent meaning. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi understood from *yatlubuhu hathithan* that the day seeks the night, and the night precedes it. From His words ﴿nor does the night outrun the day﴾ he understood that the night is overtaken, not overtaking, and so he raised it as an objection, saying: How can the night be both overtaking and overtaken? He answered that the night here means the authority of the night, which is the moon, and it does not overtake the sun in its swift daily motion. The night there means the night itself, and each of them, since it comes after the other, is seeking it. End of quotation. This question arose for him because he took the subject pronoun in *yatlubuhu* as referring to the day, and the object pronoun as referring to the night. The apparent meaning is that the subject pronoun refers to what is the grammatical subject in meaning, which is the night, because before the transitivizing hamza [in *yughshi*] it was: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], and the object pronoun refers to the day, because it was the object before and after the transitive form.

'Imara ibn 'Aqil ibn Bilal ibn Jarir al-Khatafi read *sabiqu* without tanwin and *al-nahara* with a fatha. Al-Mubarrad said: I heard him recite it, and I said: What is this? He said: I meant *sabiq al-nahar*, and I dropped the tanwin because it is lighter. End of quotation. He dropped the tanwin because of the meeting of two unvoweled consonants.

The explanation of ﴿And each is in an orbit, swimming﴾ has already been given in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The apparent meaning of "dhurriyyah" is the children and whoever among them grows up. It has also been said that the word applies to both fathers and children; this was reported from Abu Uthman. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is confusion, and this usage is not known in the language." The discussion of *dhurriyyah* has already been covered in Surat Al 'Imran.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in *lahum* ("for them") and in *dhurriyyatihim* ("their offspring") refers to the same thing. The meaning is that God carried the offspring of these people, that is, their earliest ancestors, in the ship of Nuh (peace be upon him). This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of others. Similar to this is that the ships that exist among the children of Adam until the Day of Resurrection are included. Alternatively, the phrase *dhurriyyatihim* may involve an omitted noun, meaning "the offspring of their kind," and *dhurriyyah* may refer to those who cannot walk or ride among the offspring and the weak. Then *al-fulk* is a collective noun, and God bestowed favour upon them by this. That *al-fulk* is meant in a generic sense was also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi. Similar to this is the camel and everything else that is ridden.

It has also been said that the two pronouns refer to different things: the *dhurriyyah* of the past generations. This was reported from 'Ali ibn Sulayman, and it was a sign for these people, since they are the offspring of that *dhurriyyah*.

It has also been said that *dhurriyyah* means sperm drops, and *al-fulk al-mashhun* ("the laden ship") means the wombs of women. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. This cannot be correct, because it belongs to the type of esoteric (Batiniyyah) and extreme Sufi *tafsir* (interpretation of the Qur'an), which interprets God's Book in a way that the wording does not indicate by any of the modes of indication, thus "distorting words from their places."

That the apparent sense of *al-fulk* is intended is shown by His saying ﴿And We created for them of the like thereof that which they ride﴾, meaning camels, horses, mules and donkeys. The likeness lies in the fact that each is a means of riding that carries people to their lands, and this applies when *al-fulk* is taken generically. If, however, it refers to the ship of Nuh, the likeness lies in its being ships like it, which exist among the children of Adam.

The view of those who say that "the offspring in the ship" are the people of Nuh in his ship, and that "the like" means the term and what is ridden, is far-fetched, because His saying ﴿And if We will, We shall drown them﴾ refutes it.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-A'mash, Zayd ibn 'Ali and Aban ibn 'Uthman read *dhurriyyatihim* in the plural. Zayd and Aban read the *dhal* with a kasra. The rest of the seven readers, along with Talhah and 'Isa, read it in the singular.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *dhurriyyatahum* means their children and those whose carrying concerns them. It has also been said that the term *dhurriyyah* applies to women, since they are its fields. In a hadith it is reported that he (ﷺ) forbade killing the *dharari*, meaning women.

﴿Of the like thereof﴾: of the like of the ship, ﴿that which they ride﴾: of the camels, which are the ships of the land. It has been said that ﴿al-fulk al-mashhun﴾ is the ship of Nuh. The meaning of God carrying their offspring in it is that their earliest ancestors were carried in it, and their offspring were in their loins. He mentioned their offspring rather than themselves because it is more eloquent in terms of favour upon them, and more fitting for wonder at His power in carrying their descendants until the Day of Resurrection in the ship of Nuh. ﴿Of the like thereof﴾: of the like of that ship, ﴿that which they ride﴾: of the ships. End of quotation.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: He singled out the offspring for mention because those who existed were disbelievers, and there was no benefit in their existence. That is, the carrying was not a carrying of them, but a carrying of what was in their loins of the believers. He also said: The pronoun in *wa-ayah lahum* ("and a sign for them") refers to the servants in His saying ﴿Alas for the servants﴾. Then He said after this ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth which We revived﴾, ﴿and a sign for them is the night﴾, ﴿and a sign for them that We carried their offspring﴾, meaning the offspring of the servants. It is not necessary that the pronoun in both places refer to two different meanings. This is like His saying ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [an-Nisa 29], which means: none of you should kill one another. That is the sense here.

﴿And a sign for them﴾: that is, the sign of each one of them, ﴿that We carried﴾: the offspring of each one of them, or the offspring of some of them. End of quotation.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿And We created﴾ is that creating and originating are intended, so the reference is to camels and what is ridden. Here *min* is explanatory. Although what a human makes may sometimes be attributed to God as creation, the more common usage is what we have mentioned. When the ships are intended, *min* is partitive. The apparent reference of *lahum* is to what it referred to in ﴿And a sign for them﴾, because it is the subject being spoken of. It is also permitted that it refer to the offspring. The apparent reference of the pronoun in *mithlihi* is to (p-339) the ship. It has been said that it refers to something known though not mentioned, and its implied sense is: of the like of what We mentioned of the created things in His saying ﴿Glory be to the One who created all the pairs of what the earth produces﴾, just as they said concerning His saying ﴿of its fruit﴾, meaning of the fruit of what We mentioned.

Al-Hasan read *nughargqihum* with shaddah; the majority read it without shaddah. *Al-sarikh* is an *fa'il* form meaning "one who cries out," that is, one who seeks help, and also meaning "one who gives help," that is, one who relieves. This is its meaning here, that is, there is no one to relieve them and no one to assist them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ means there is no rescue for them. End of quotation. It appears that he took it as a verbal noun from *af'ala*, and this requires a transmitted report that *sarikh* can be a verbal noun meaning *sirakh* (crying out).

The apparent sense of His saying ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ is: there is no helper for those whom God wills to drown, ﴿nor are they rescued﴾: that is, they are not saved from death by drowning. He first negated the *sarikh*, which is specific, and then negated their being rescued by a *sarikh* or by anything else.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ is a resumed statement of information about those who travel at sea, whether they are saved or drowned. In this state they have no salvation except by the mercy of God. His saying ﴿There is no sarikh for them﴾ is not tied to those who are drowned, although it may be tied to them, and the first is better, so consider it. End of quotation. This is not good, nor is it better.

The *fa'* in ﴿so there is no sarikh for them﴾ connects the sentence to what precedes it with clear linkage and binds it to it with evident tie. Deliverance from the punishment is in two respects: what prevents it from its origin, which is negated by His saying ﴿there is no sarikh for them﴾, and what lifts it after it occurs, which is negated by His saying ﴿nor are they rescued﴾.

The word *rahmatan* ("mercy") is in the accusative as an exception with the object of purpose omitted, meaning: for a mercy from Us. Al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: ﴿until a time﴾ means until the time of death, as reported by Qatadah. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is either for a mercy from Us, and that they may enjoy life until a term, that is, until an appointed time at which they must die after salvation from drowning. End of quotation. He said "they must die after salvation from drowning" because He said ﴿And if We will﴾, that is, to drown them, ﴿We shall drown them﴾, so whoever God wills to drown must die by drowning.

The apparent sense is that ﴿from Us and as enjoyment until a time﴾ applies to those who are rescued, so it does not imply permanence. Rather, God rescues him out of mercy, lets him enjoy life for a time, and then makes him die. It has also been said that there is a division in this: except for mercy toward one whom He knows will believe, so God rescues him out of mercy, and whoever He knows will not believe, He withholds [death] for a time, and he increases in sin.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah Ya-Sin, verses 28–44 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Nor did We send down upon his people after him any host from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down.﴾ ﴿It was but one Cry, and behold, they were extinguished.﴾ ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾ ﴿And all of them, without exception, will be brought before Us.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is the dead earth: We gave it life and brought forth from it grain, of which they eat.﴾ ﴿And We made in it gardens of palms and vines, and caused springs to gush forth in it.﴾ ﴿That they may eat of its fruit, and of what their hands have made. Will they not then give thanks?﴾ ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of what they do not know.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness.﴾ ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place; that is the decree of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations, until it returns like the old withered palm-stalk.﴾ ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outrun the day; each floats in an orbit.﴾ ﴿A sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship.﴾ ﴿And We created for them of its like what they ride.﴾ ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry for them, nor are they rescued.﴾ ﴿Except as mercy from Us and enjoyment for a time.﴾

(p-331) He, may He be exalted, informed of the destruction of the people of Habib by one single Cry, which Jibril shouted at them. In this there is a warning to Quraysh that what befell them may befall them too, since they are the ones for whom the parable was struck. He, may He be exalted, also informed that He did not send down against them for their destruction any host from heaven, such as stones, wind, or other things, and they were too insignificant for Him. His saying "after him" (min ba'dihi) indicates the starting point of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning that He did not send a messenger to them, nor did He reproach them after killing him, but hastened their destruction. The apparent reading is that the ma in His saying ﴿وما كُنّا مُنْزِلِينَ﴾ is a negation, so the meaning is close to that of the sentence before it: "It was not valid in Our judgment that We should send down against them a host from heaven for their destruction, because He, may He be exalted, ordained the destruction of every people in some respects and not others, as He said ﴿فَكُلًّا أخَذْنا بِذَنْبِهِ﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 40], and so on." A group said that ma is a noun (ism) conjoined to jund (host). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "That is, a host, and from (p-332) that which We were sending down upon the nations like them." End of quote. This is an unsound interpretation, because the min in min jund is extra (za'idah). According to the Basrans, other than al-Akhfash, the extra min has two conditions: first, that it be preceded by a negation, a prohibition, or an interrogative; second, that it be followed by an indefinite noun. Even if this is so, the conjoined noun after an indefinite cannot be definite. It is not permitted to say: "I did not strike any man, nor Zayd," and it is not permitted to say: "nor from Zayd." Ibn ʿAtiyya took the conjoined word as meaning "the one" (alladhi), which is definite, so it cannot be conjoined to an indefinite noun governed by the extra min. Abu al-Baqa said: "It is permissible for ma to be extra, that is, 'and indeed We were sending down,'" but this is not correct.

He read ﴿إنْ كانَتْ إلّا صَيْحَةً﴾ with the accusative on Sayhah, with kana as a defective (naqisah) verb whose subject (ism) is a pronoun, meaning: "If the seizure or punishment was" (in kanat al-akhdhah aw al-ʿuqubah). Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, and Muʿadh ibn al-Harith al-Qari read sayhatun with the nominative in both places, taking kanat as complete (tammah), meaning: "What happened or occurred was only one Cry." The original rule is that the verb should not take the feminine ending (ta'), because when the verb is attributed to a feminine noun that follows illa, the sign of feminine gender is not attached. One says: "No one stood up but Hind," and it is not permitted to say: "No one stood up but Hind" with the feminine ending attached, according to our companions (the Basran grammarians), except in poetry. Some permitted it in ordinary speech, though rarely. Similar is the reading of al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu Rajaʾ, al-Jahdari, Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, and Abu Bahriyyah: ﴿لا تُرى إلّا مَساكِنُهم﴾ with the ta'. The well-known reading is with the ya'. Also the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

And nothing remained but the ribs, heaving.

And the saying of another:

She is free of suspicion and blame in our war, except the daughters of our paternal uncles.

Abu Hatim and many grammarians rejected this reading because of the attachment of the feminine ending.

﴿فَإذا هم خامِدُونَ﴾: that is, extinction overtook them immediately after the Cry, without delay. He used "extinguished" (khumud) as a metaphor for their silence after their life, like a fire that dies down after it blazed. The address "Alas" (ya hasrah) in this sense means: "This is the time of your presence and manifestation," a supposed address, like this one, according to Sibawayh, and it is an indefinite vocative according to the reading of the majority. Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and al-Hasan read: ﴿يا حَسْرَةَ العِبادِ﴾ with the annexation (idafah). So the regret may be from them over what they missed, and it may be the regret of others over them, for what they missed of following the messengers when they were brought forth for punishment. Human nature is moved when witnessing the punishment of others and grieves over them.

Abu al-Zinad, ʿAbdullah ibn Dhakwan al-Madani, Ibn Hurmuz, and Ibn Jundub read ﴿يا حَسْرَهْ عَلى العِبادِ﴾ with the ha' silent in both states, treating connection like pause, and they paused on the ha' for emphasis in regret, since the ha' contains a sigh like the ta'awwuh (groan). Then they connected in that same state, as stated by the author of al-Lawami. Ibn Khalawayh said: "Ya hasrata ʿala al-ʿibad without tanwin," as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. Its basis is that he dispensed with the fatha in place of the alif, which replaces the ya' of the speaker in vocatives, just as he dispensed with the kasra in place of the ya'. It has also been read: ﴿يا حَسْرَتا﴾ with the alif, meaning "O my regret," and it may be from God in the sense of metaphor, to magnify what they committed against themselves, and to express strong denial and wonder at it. The apparent meaning is that the servants are those who denied the messengers, and the angels grieved over them, as said by al-Dahhak. Al-Dahhak also said: the meaning is "Alas, O regret of the angels over Our servants, the messengers, when faith no longer benefits them." Abu al-ʿAliyah said: the servants here refer to the three messengers, and this regret was from the disbelievers when they saw God's punishment and lamented what they had missed. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "His saying ﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ (no messenger comes to them) refutes this interpretation." End of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: al-hasrah is a state that overtakes a person from excessive regret over what has no end, until he remains exhausted (hasir). It was said: the one addressed is omitted, and ḥasratan is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar), meaning "O people, grieve with grief." It was also said that ﴿يا حَسْرَةً عَلى العِبادِ﴾ is the words of the man who came from the farthest part of the city running, when the people rushed to kill him. It was said: it is the words of the three messengers, who said this when they were killed, and the punishment came down upon them, saying: "Alas for these people," as if they wished that they had believed. End of quote. The alif and lam (in al-ʿibad) are for a known reference (al-ʿahd) if we say the servants meant are the three messengers, or those to whom they were sent, who perished because of their disbelief and denial of them. The apparent meaning is that the definite article here defines the category of the denying disbelievers. In summary, the one who grieves is: the angels, or God, or the believers, or the three messengers, or that man, these are the sayings.

﴿ما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ up to the end of the verse: this is an illustration addressed to Quraysh, who are the people to whom the pronoun in His words ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed﴾ refers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Kam (how many) here is khabariyya (the informative kam), and anna-hum (that they) is a badal (substitute, apposition) for it, and the seeing is ocular seeing." End of quotation. This is not correct, because if it is khabariyya, it is in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by ahlaknā (We destroyed), and nothing else is permissible for it. Given this, it is impossible for anna-hum to be a badal of it, because the badal (substitution) is intended to repeat the governing verb, and if ahlaknā were made to govern anna-hum, it would not be sound. Do you not see that if you said "We destroyed the cessation of their return" or "We destroyed their not returning," it would not be a sentence? But Ibn 'Atiyya imagined that yaraw (they see) has kam as its object, so he imagined that their saying "that they do not return" is a badal, because it is permissible for it to be governed by it, so you say: "Have they not seen that they do not return?" This and its like is evidence of his weakness in the science of Arabic grammar.

al-Zajjaj said: it is a badal from the clause, and the meaning is: "Have they not seen that the generations We destroyed do not return to them? Because non-return and destruction have the meaning of prohibition." What al-Zajjaj said is nothing, because it is not a grammatical badal; he only explained the meaning and did not observe the technical rule of grammar (sina'at al-nahw).

Abu al-Baqa' said: anna-hum ilayhim (that they to them). End of quotation. This is nothing, because kam is not a mu'mal (governed element) of yaraw.

It is transmitted from al-Farra' that he makes yaraw govern in both clauses without badal. His saying "in both clauses" is permissible, because anna-hum and what follows it is not a clause. He did not explain how this governing works.

al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ألم يروا﴾ means "Have they not known?" It is mu'allaq (suspended) from governing kam, because kam is not governed by a verb preceding it, whether it is interrogative or informative, since its origin is interrogation, except that its meaning permeates the sentence, as it permeates in your saying: "Have they not seen that Zayd is indeed departing?" even though you did not govern its wording. And ﴿that they to them do not return﴾ is a badal from (ahlaknā) according to the meaning, not according to the wording. Its estimate: "Have they not seen the multitude of Our destruction of the generations before them, that they are not returning to them?" End of quotation.

So he made yaraw mean ya'lamu (they know) and suspended it from governing kam.
