The pronoun in *lahu* refers to the Messenger, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). One who went far afield said it refers to the Qur'an, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Qur'an, though it has not been mentioned; but he may say: the speech indicates it, and it is clarified by the return of the pronoun to it in His saying: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, meaning: a heavenly book that is read in the sanctuaries, and by reciting it and acting upon it one attains what contains the success of both abodes. How far it is then between it and poetry, most of which is from the prompting of the devils!

Ibn ʿĀmir and Nāfiʿ read *li-tundhira* with the *tā'* of address to the Messenger; the rest of the seven read it with the *yā'* of absence, so it may refer to the Messenger, and it may refer to the Qur'an. Al-Yamānī read *li-yundhara* with a *yā'* in the passive voice, and Ibn Khālawayh related it from al-Jaḥdarī. He said from Abū al-Sammāl and al-Yamānī that they both read *li-yandhara* with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and the *dhāl*, the present of *nadhira* with a *kasra* on the *dhāl*, when one knows of a thing and prepares himself for it.

*Man kāna ḥayyan*: That is, heedless, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, because the heedless is like the dead. By it he means the one upon whom it was sealed with faith, and likewise He contrasted it with His saying: "and the word will be fulfilled" (*wa-yaḥiqqa al-qawl*), that is, the word of punishment, ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, those for whom it is decreed by reaching the end in disbelief.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 36, verses 55–79 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in their enjoyment,﴾ ﴿they and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches,﴾ ﴿for them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for,﴾ ﴿"Peace!" – a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿"And separate yourselves today, O criminals!﴾ ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan – indeed, he is to you a clear enemy?﴾ ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾ ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. So did you not use reason?﴾ ﴿This is Hellfire, which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿Today We seal over their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet testify to what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could have obliterated their eyes, and they would race to the path; but how could they see?﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed or return.﴾ ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation. So will they not reason?﴾ ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him. It is not but a reminder and a clear Qur'an,﴾ ﴿to warn whoever is alive and that the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers.﴾

[p. 342] When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, He followed that with the state of the happy and the wretched. The apparent meaning is that it is a report to us about what they will be in when they arrive at the reward and punishment prepared for them. It has also been said that it is a narration of what will be said on that Day; in such a narration there is an additional depiction of the promised reward in souls, and an encouragement to desire it and to pursue what it produces. The apparent meaning is that *ash-shughl* (busyness) is the bliss that has occupied them away from everything that comes to mind. Mujahid said something close to this. Some scholars restricted this *shughl* to the deflowering of virgins; this was related from Ibn Abbas. Also from him: the hearing of lutes. From al-Hasan: they are occupied away from what the people of the Fire are in. From al-Kalbi: away from their families among the people of the Fire; they do not mention them lest they be disturbed. From Ibn Kaysan: *ash-shughl* is mutual visiting. It has also been said: it is the hospitality of Allah. The singular *ash-shughl* is used because bliss is considered, and it is one insofar as it is bliss.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu Amr read *shughul* with a *damma* on the *shin* and sukun on the *ghayn*; the rest of the seven readers read it with *damma* on both. Mujahid, Abu as-Sammal, and Ibn Hubayra, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh from him, read it with two *fathas*. Yazid an-Nahwi and Ibn Hubayra, as transmitted by Abu al-Fadl ar-Razi, read it with a *fatha* on the *shin* and sukun on the *ghayn*. The majority read *fakihun* with an *alif*. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Qatada, Abu Haywa, Mujahid, Shayba, Abu Raja', Yahya ibn Sabih, and Nafi' in one narration read it without *alif*. Talha and al-A'mash read *fakihin*, with *alif* and *ya'*, in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial state), while *fi shughlin* is the predicate. With the *alif*, it means "people of fruit," as one says *laabin* (possessor of milk), *tamir* (possessor of dates), *shahim* (possessor of fat), and *lahim* (possessor of meat). Without the *alif*, its meaning is "joyful, merry," derived from *al-fukaha*, which is jest. It was also read *fakihin* without *alif* and with *ya'*, and *fakuhun* with a *damma* on the *kaf*. It is said: a man is *fakih* and *fakih*, like *yadus* and *yadis*.

It is permissible for *hum* to be the subject (*mubtada'*) with *fi zilalin* as its predicate, and *muttaki'un* a second predicate; or its predicate is *muttaki'un*, with *fi zilalin* related to it; or it may be an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in *fakihun*, with *fi zilalin* as a *hal*, and *muttaki'un* a second predicate of *inna*; or it may be an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in *shughlin*, shifted to it from the governing word within it.

On this and the preceding possibility, the spouses share in the enjoyment, the busyness, and the reclining on couches, by way of the explicit statement. On the first, they share in the shade and the reclining on couches by way of the explicit statement, and they share in the enjoyment and busyness by way of the meaning.

The majority read *fi zilalin*. Ibn Atiyya said: it is the plural of *zill*, since there is no sun in Paradise, and its air is temperate like the time of dawn before sunrise. End of quote. The plural of *fi'l* in the form *fi'al* is used in the sense of abundance, like *dhi'b* and *dhi'ab* (wolf and wolves). As for the claim that the time of Paradise is like the time of dawn before sunrise, this requires a sound transmission. How could that be? And is there in the hadith something that indicates a *hawra'* (dark-eyed maiden) of Paradise, that if she appeared the world would be illuminated by her light, or something similar to this? He said: it is possible that it is the plural of *zullah* (a canopy). Abu Ali said: like *burmah* and *biram* (cooking pot and pots). Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the plural of *zillah* with a *kasra* on the *za'*; Ibn Atiyya said: this is a dialect of *zullah*. End of quote. Then it would be like *luqhah* and *liqah* (a milch camel and milch camels), and *fi'al* is not regular for *fu'lah* but is preserved by transmission.

Abdullah, as-Sulami, Talha, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read *fi zillin*: the plural of *zillah*. The plural of *fi'lah* on *fi'l* is regular. It refers to the coverings and layers of canopies, curtains, and similar things that provide shade.

Abdullah read *muttaki'in* in the accusative as a *hal*. *Yaddda'una* is the present tense of *idda'a*, which is *if'tala* from *da'a*, and its meaning is: and for them is whatever they wish for. Abu Ubayda said: the Arabs say *ud'u 'alayya ma shi'ta*, meaning "wish upon me whatever you want," and they say, "So-and-so wished in a report." Az-Zajjaj said: it is from *ad-du'a'*, that is, whatever the people of Paradise call for will come to them. It has also been said: they call for it for themselves. It has also been said: they call one another to it, based on the saying *irmuhu* and *taramuhu* (throw it to him, and they threw it to one another).

[p. 343] The majority read *salamun* with *raf'* (nominative). It is an adjective of *ma*, meaning: granted to them and pure. End of quote. This is not valid if *ma* means "that which," because then it would be definite, and *salamun* is indefinite, and a definite noun is not described by an indefinite. If *ma* is an indefinite relative, it is permissible, but then it does not carry generality, as with its status as "that which."

It has also been said: *salamun* is a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is the verb governing *qawlan*, meaning: peace is said, "a word from a Lord, Most Merciful." Or *'alaykum* is omitted, meaning: peace upon you, "a word from a Lord, Most Merciful." It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is peace.

Az-Zamakhshari said: *salamun qawlan* is a substitute (*badal*) for *ma yaddda'un*, as if he said: for them is peace, said to them, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful. The meaning is that Allah greets them with peace through the angels, or without an intermediary, as an exaggeration in their honour. That is what they desire, and they will not be prevented from having it. Ibn Abbas said: and the angels enter upon them with greetings from the Lord of the worlds. End of quote. If *salam* is a substitute for *ma yaddda'un*, it is specifically so. The apparent meaning is that it is general for everything they call for; if it is general, *salam* cannot be a substitute for it.

It has also been said: *salamun* is the predicate of *ma yaddda'un*, and *ma yaddda'un* is the subject, meaning: and for them what they call for is pure peace, and *qawlan* is an emphasizing verbal noun, like His saying, *wa lahum ma yaddda'un salam* ("and for them is what they call for: peace"), meaning a promise from the Merciful. Az-Zamakhshari said: the more correct view is that it is in the accusative by way of specification (*ikhtisas*), and this is one of his figurative usages. End of quote. On this grammatical analysis, *lahum* is related to *salamun*.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read *silmun*, with a *kasra* on the *sin* and sukun on the *lam*, meaning *salam*. Abu al-Fadl ar-Razi said: "peaceful for them," that is, that is peaceful. Ubayy, Abdullah, Isa, and al-Qanawi read *salaman*, in the accusative as a verbal noun. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative as a *hal*, meaning: for them is their desire, pure.

﴿And separate yourselves today﴾: that is, withdraw from the believers, because the place of gathering brings together the righteous and the wicked, so the criminals are commanded to be set apart from the believers. The apparent meaning is that there is an omitted statement here. When Allah mentioned what is said to the believers in His saying, *salamun qawlan min rabbin rahim*, it is said: "And it is said to the criminals: separate yourselves." When they carried out what they were commanded, He said to them, by way of rebuke and reproach, ﴿Did I not charge you?﴾, making them acknowledge His covenant with them and their violation of it. It is related from ad-Dahhak: for every disbeliever there is a house of Fire in which he neither sees nor is seen. According to this, the meaning is that some of them are separated from others. From Qatada: they withdraw from every good. The *'ahd* (covenant) means the charge; *'ahida ilayhi* means he charged him. Allah's covenant with them is what He placed in them of rational proofs and sent down to them of revealed proofs. Worship of Satan means obeying him in what he leads them astray in and adorns for them.

The majority read *a'had* with a *fatha* on the hamza and the *ha'*. Talha and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil al-Kufi read it with a *kasra* on the hamza; Abu al-Lawami said this is the dialect of Tamim, and that this *kasra* on the *nun* and *ta'* is more common than among the letters of the present tense, meaning *ni'had* and *ti'had*. Ibn Khalawayh said: *alam a'had*. Yahya ibn Wathhab: *alam ahad*, the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Atiyya said: al-Hudhayl ibn Wathhab read *alami i'had*, with a *kasra* on the *mim* and hamza and a *fatha* on the *ha'*, and this is according to the dialect of one who puts a *kasra* on the first letter of the present tense except the *ya'*. It was also transmitted from Ibn Wathhab: *alam a'hid*, with a *kasra* on the *ha'*, from *ya'hidu*. End of quote. His saying "with a *kasra* on the *mim* and the hamza" means that the *kasra* on the *mim* indicates a *kasra* on the hamza, because the vowel on the *mim* is the vowel transferred from the hamza with a *kasra*, and the hamza was dropped when its vowel was transferred to the preceding quiescent letter, which is the *mim*. (The reading *a'had* with a cut hamza and a *kasra* is not permissible.) Az-Zamakhshari said: it was read *i'had* with a *kasra* on the hamza, and every verb of the *fa'ila* pattern permits a *kasra* on the letters of its present tense except the *ya'*; *a'hid* with a *kasra* on the *ha'*. Az-Zajjaj permitted that it is of the pattern *na'ama yan'imu* and *darab yadrib*, and *ahad* with *ha'* and *ahid*, which is the dialect of Tamim, and from it their saying: *daha ma'ha* ("leave it with it"). End of quote. His saying "except the *ya'*" is a dialect of some of the tribe of Kalb, who also put a *kasra* on the *ya'*, saying *hal yi'lam* ("does he know?"). His saying *daha maha* means they want *da'ha ma'aha*; they assimilated the *'ayn* into the *ha'*. The reference by "this" is to what He charged them with: disobedience to Satan and obedience to the Merciful.

Nafi' and 'Asim read *jibilan* with a *kasra* on the *jim* and the *ba'* and a shadda on the *lam*. This is the reading of Abu Haywa, Suhayl, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu Raja', and al-Hasan, with a variant from him. The two Arabic readers (Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i?) and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil read it with a *damma* on the *jim* and sukun on the *ba'*. The rest of the seven read it with a *damma* on it and a lightened *lam*. Al-Hasan ibn Abi Ishaq, az-Zuhri, Ibn Hurmuz, Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr, and Hafs ibn Humayd read it with two *dammas* and a shadda on the *lam*. Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli, al-Yamani, and Hammad ibn Maslama from 'Asim read it with a *kasra* on the *jim* and sukun on the *ba'*. Al-A'mash read *jibilan* with two *kasras* and a lightened *lam*. It was also read *jibalan* with a *kasra* on the *jim*, a *fatha* on the *ba'*, and a lightened *lam*, the plural of *jibilah*, like *fitrah* and *fitar*. These are seven dialects in which it was read. Ali ibn Abi Talib and some of the Khurasanis read *jilan*, with a *kasra* on the *jim* and a *ya'* after it, the singular of *ajyal* (generations). *Al-jibl* with a *ba'* and one dot below is the great nation. Ad-Dahhak said: its least number is ten thousand. Allah, exalted is He, addresses the disbelievers with what Satan did with them, as a rebuke to them. The majority read *afalam takunu* with the second-person address; Talha and Isa read it with the third-person *ya'*, referring back to *jibilan*. It is related that they deny and dispute, so their neighbours, tribes, and families testify against them, and they swear that they were not polytheists. Then their mouths are sealed, and their hands and feet speak. In a hadith: "The servant will say on the Day of Resurrection: I do not allow any witness against me except myself. Then his mouth is sealed, and his limbs are told: speak. So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left between himself and speech, and it is said: away with you, and destruction, it was on your account that I was contending."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 55–79 (part 2 of 2):

It was also read: *yukhtamu* in the passive voice, and *tatakallamu aydīhim* with two *tā'*s. It was also read: *wa-li-tukallimunā aydīhim* with two *tā'*s. It was also read: *wa-l-tukallimnā aydīhim wa-l-tashhad* with the *lām* of command and the jussive, on the basis that God commands the limbs to speak and to bear witness. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa related from his father, from his grandfather Ṭalḥa, that he read: *wa-li-tukallimanā aydīhim wa-li-tashhada*, with the *lām* of *kay* (in order that) and the accusative, meaning: "And thus He seals over their mouths." 

The apparent meaning is that *al-aʿyun* (the eyes) are the seeing limbs, and the meaning is: "We would have blinded them, so they could not see how they walk." This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatāda, and the context of the *maskh* (transformation) supports it, for they are within the grip of power and the scope of punishment, if God wills it upon them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: He meant the eyes of insight, and the meaning is: "Had We willed, We would have sealed upon them with disbelief, so that none of them would ever be guided."

*Al-ṭamsh* is the removal of a thing and its trace entirely, to the point that it seems as if it had never existed. If *al-aʿyun* is taken literally, the apparent meaning is that *yaṭmisu* means *yamsakh* (transform) in the literal sense. It is also permissible that *al-ṭamsh* is meant as blindness without the removal of the organ and its trace.

The majority read *fa-stabaqū*, as a past verb conjoined to *la-ṭamasnā*, and this is on the basis of supposition and estimation. *Al-ṣirāṭa* is in the accusative by the assumption of an omitted *ilā* (to), with the verb reaching it directly; the original would be *fa-stabaqū ilā al-ṣirāṭ*. Or it is an object by the *tadmīn* (implication) of *istabaqū* the meaning of *tabādarū* (hasten), and making it "those who are preceded to it." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Or it is in the accusative as an adverb of place, but this is not permissible, because *al-ṣirāṭ* is *al-ṭarīq* (the path), and it is a specific place-adverb. The verb does not reach it except through the mediation of *fī* (in), except in an anomalous usage, as Sībawayh cited:

*Lададн bi-hazzi al-kaffi yaʿsilu matnuhu* / *fīhi kamā ʿasala al-ṭarīqa al-thaʿlabu*

(A supple spear, shaken by the hand, its shaft glides in it as the fox glides along the path.)

The position of Ibn al-Ṭarāwa is that *al-ṣirāṭ*, *al-ṭarīq*, *al-makhram*, and what resembles them of place-adverbs are not specific, so according to his view what al-Zamakhsharī said is permissible."

ʿĪsā read *fa-stabiqū* as an imperative, and it is on the basis of an implied *qawl* (saying), meaning: "It will be said to them: *istabiqū al-ṣirāṭ* (race to the path)." This is by way of incapacitation, for it is not possible for them to race while their eyes are obliterated.

*Fa-annā yubṣirūn* means: how can one who has had his eye obliterated see? The apparent meaning is that the transformation (*al-maskh*) is literal, and it is the changing of their forms into hideous shapes. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *la-maskhnāhum* means into apes and swine, as has been mentioned in the case of the Children of Israel. It was also said: into stones. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and a group said: "We would have made them sit and disabled them, so they could not move at all." The apparent meaning is that this would be in this world. Ibn Salām said: "This entire threat is on the Day of Resurrection."

Al-Ḥasan read *ʿalā makānatihim* in the singular, meaning the place, like *al-maqāma* and *al-maqām*. The majority and Abū Bakr read it in the plural. The majority read *muḍiyyan* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*; Abū Ḥaywa and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr al-Anṭākī, from al-Kisāʾī, read it with a *kasra* on the *mīm* following the vowel of the *ḍād*, like *al-ʿitibiyy* and *al-qitibiyy*, its pattern being *faʿūl*. A silent *wāw* and a *yāʾ* met, so the *wāw* was changed to a *yāʾ*, and it was assimilated into the *yāʾ*, and the letter before it was given a *kasra* to make the *yāʾ* sound correct. It was also read *maḍiyyan* with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm*, in which case it is one of the verbal nouns that come in the pattern *faʿīl*, like *al-rasīm* and *al-wajīf*.

Since the Exalted mentioned the obliteration and the transformation as a supposition of the likened case, He mentioned a proof of His manifest power in reversing the aged, and that this is not done except by Him, Exalted is He. Its reversal (*tankīs*) is: He turned it and made it the opposite of how He created it at first. He created him in weakness of body, devoid of intellect and knowledge, then He made him grow and move from state to state until he reaches his full strength, and his power is completed, and he understands and knows what is for him and what is against him. When he reaches that point, He reverses him in creation, so he diminishes until he returns to a state resembling the state of childhood in the weakness of his body, the scarcity of his intellect, and his lack of understanding, just as an arrow is reversed so that its top becomes its bottom. In all of this there is evidence that the One who did these deeds is able to obliterate them and to do to them what He wills.

The majority read *nunakkisuh* with *tashdīd* (doubled), and ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read it without *tashdīd*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān, and Abū ʿAmr in the narration of ʿAbbās read *taʿqilūn* with the *tā'* of address; the rest of the seven read it with the *yā'* of absence.

*Wa-mā ʿallamnāhu al-shiʿr*: The pronoun in *ʿallamnāhu* refers to the Messenger (ﷺ). They used to say about him: "He is a poet." It is related that the one who said it was ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, and God negated that from him. Their saying about him, "He is a poet," as for one whose nature was poetry, then his saying is obstinacy and a deception for one ignorant of poetry; as for one whose nature was not poetry, then his saying is pure ignorance. Where is he from poetry? Poetry is only metrical, rhymed speech indicating a meaning that poets select from much imagination and embellishment of speech, and other things that the pious person refrains from reciting, let alone composing. He (peace be upon him) did not compose poetry, and when he recited a line he preserved the meaning without its metre, as when he recited:

*Sa-tubdī laka al-ayyāmu mā kunta jāhilan* / *wa-yaʾtīka man lam tuzawwad bi-l-akhbār*

(The days will reveal to you what you were ignorant of, and there will come to you one who was not provisioned with news.)

It was said: "Among the best of poets." So the one who said it said:

*Alam tarayānī kullamā jiʾtu ṭāriqan* / *wajadtu bihā wa-in lam tuṭayyab ṭīban*

(Do you not see me, whenever I come as a night visitor, I find her, even if she is not perfumed, fragrant.)

*Ataj-ʿalu nahbī wa-nahba al-ʿubayd* / *bayna al-aqraʿ wa-ʿuyayna*

(Will you make my plunder and the plunder of ʿUbayd between al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyayna?)

And he recited one day:

*Kafā bi-l-islāmi wa-l-shaybi nāhiyā*

(Sufficient are Islam and grey hair as a restrainer.)

Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said: "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of God." The poet only said: "Sufficient are grey hair and Islam." Sometimes he recited a line perfectly metred, rarely. It is related from him that he recited the line of Ibn Rawāḥa:

*Yabītu yujāfī janbahu ʿan firāshihi* / *idhā istuthqilat bi-l-mushrikīna al-maḍājiʿu*

(He spends the night, his side withdrawn from his bed, when the beds are heavy with the polytheists.)

The fact that a line passed through his tongue metred does not indicate that he knew poetry. Things that accept metre occurred in his speech (peace be upon him), such as his saying:

*Anā al-nabiyyu lā kadhib* / *anā ibnu ʿabd al-muṭṭalib*

(I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.)

Likewise his saying:

*Hal anti illā iṣbaʿun damītī* / *wa-fī sabīli Llāhi mā laqītī*

(Are you anything but a finger that bled, and in the way of God what you suffered?)

This is speech of the same kind as his speech which he uttered by his nature, without artifice in it, nor intention to metre, nor affectation, just as there is found in the Qur'an something metred that is not counted as poetry, such as His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 92], and His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. And in much prose that eloquent people compose, that is not called poetry, nor does it occur to the speaker or the listener that it is poetry.

*Wa-mā yanbaghī lahu*: That is, it is not possible for him, nor valid, nor suitable; because he (peace be upon him) was on the path of pure seriousness, while poetry for the most part is on the path of jest, embellishing what is not beautiful, disparaging what is not ugly, and excessive exaggeration. He (Exalted is He) made him not compose poetry, just as He made him unlettered, not writing, so that the proof would be more firm and the doubt more refuted. It was said: in this verse there is evidence of the baseness of poetry, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I am not a poet, nor does it befit me." Some people went to the view that there is no baseness in it, and that God only prevented His Prophet (peace be upon him) from it. Even if it is a noble adornment, so that the Qur'an would come from his side more wondrously, for if he had the capacity for poetry, it would be said about the Qur'an: "This is from that power."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The matter is not so in my view. He (peace be upon him) had eloquence and clarity in prose at the highest rank, but the speech of God is manifest through its inimitability, and it is distinguished by its description, and the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge removes it from every speech. God only prevented His Prophet from poetry to elevate him above what is in the speech of poets of imagination and embellishment of utterance. As for the Qur'an, it is a reminder with realities and proofs, so it is not the saying of a poet, and this was the style of his speech (peace be upon him), and a single word." End.

The pronoun in *lahu* refers to the Messenger, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). One who went far afield said it refers to the Qur'an, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Qur'an, though it has not been mentioned; but he may say: the speech indicates it, and it is clarified by the return of the pronoun to it in His saying: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, meaning: a heavenly book that is read in the sanctuaries, and by reciting it and acting upon it one attains what contains the success of both abodes. How far it is then between it and poetry, most of which is from the prompting of the devils!

Ibn ʿĀmir and Nāfiʿ read *li-tundhira* with the *tā'* of address to the Messenger; the rest of the seven read it with the *yā'* of absence, so it may refer to the Messenger, and it may refer to the Qur'an. Al-Yamānī read *li-yundhara* with a *yā'* in the passive voice, and Ibn Khālawayh related it from al-Jaḥdarī. He said from Abū al-Sammāl and al-Yamānī that they both read *li-yandhara* with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and the *dhāl*, the present of *nadhira* with a *kasra* on the *dhāl*, when one knows of a thing and prepares himself for it.

*Man kāna ḥayyan*: That is, heedless, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, because the heedless is like the dead. By it he means the one upon whom it was sealed with faith, and likewise He contrasted it with His saying: "and the word will be fulfilled" (*wa-yaḥiqqa al-qawl*), that is, the word of punishment, ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, those for whom it is decreed by reaching the end in disbelief.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 36, verses 55–79 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in their enjoyment,﴾ ﴿they and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches,﴾ ﴿for them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for,﴾ ﴿"Peace!" – a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿"And separate yourselves today, O criminals!﴾ ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan – indeed, he is to you a clear enemy?﴾ ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾ ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. So did you not use reason?﴾ ﴿This is Hellfire, which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿Today We seal over their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet testify to what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could have obliterated their eyes, and they would race to the path; but how could they see?﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed or return.﴾ ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation. So will they not reason?﴾ ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him. It is not but a reminder and a clear Qur'an,﴾ ﴿to warn whoever is alive and that the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers.﴾

[p. 342] When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, He followed that with the state of the happy and the wretched. The apparent meaning is that it is a report to us about what they will be in when they arrive at the reward and punishment prepared for them. It has also been said that it is a narration of what will be said on that Day; in such a narration there is an additional depiction of the promised reward in souls, and an encouragement to desire it and to pursue what it produces. The apparent meaning is that *ash-shughl* (busyness) is the bliss that has occupied them away from everything that comes to mind. Mujahid said something close to this. Some scholars restricted this *shughl* to the deflowering of virgins; this was related from Ibn Abbas. Also from him: the hearing of lutes. From al-Hasan: they are occupied away from what the people of the Fire are in. From al-Kalbi: away from their families among the people of the Fire; they do not mention them lest they be disturbed. From Ibn Kaysan: *ash-shughl* is mutual visiting. It has also been said: it is the hospitality of Allah. The singular *ash-shughl* is used because bliss is considered, and it is one insofar as it is bliss.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu Amr read *shughul* with a *damma* on the *shin* and sukun on the *ghayn*; the rest of the seven readers read it with *damma* on both. Mujahid, Abu as-Sammal, and Ibn Hubayra, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh from him, read it with two *fathas*. Yazid an-Nahwi and Ibn Hubayra, as transmitted by Abu al-Fadl ar-Razi, read it with a *fatha* on the *shin* and sukun on the *ghayn*. The majority read *fakihun* with an *alif*. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Qatada, Abu Haywa, Mujahid, Shayba, Abu Raja', Yahya ibn Sabih, and Nafi' in one narration read it without *alif*. Talha and al-A'mash read *fakihin*, with *alif* and *ya'*, in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial state), while *fi shughlin* is the predicate. With the *alif*, it means "people of fruit," as one says *laabin* (possessor of milk), *tamir* (possessor of dates), *shahim* (possessor of fat), and *lahim* (possessor of meat). Without the *alif*, its meaning is "joyful, merry," derived from *al-fukaha*, which is jest. It was also read *fakihin* without *alif* and with *ya'*, and *fakuhun* with a *damma* on the *kaf*. It is said: a man is *fakih* and *fakih*, like *yadus* and *yadis*.

It is permissible for *hum* to be the subject (*mubtada'*) with *fi zilalin* as its predicate, and *muttaki'un* a second predicate; or its predicate is *muttaki'un*, with *fi zilalin* related to it; or it may be an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in *fakihun*, with *fi zilalin* as a *hal*, and *muttaki'un* a second predicate of *inna*; or it may be an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in *shughlin*, shifted to it from the governing word within it.

On this and the preceding possibility, the spouses share in the enjoyment, the busyness, and the reclining on couches, by way of the explicit statement. On the first, they share in the shade and the reclining on couches by way of the explicit statement, and they share in the enjoyment and busyness by way of the meaning.

The majority read *fi zilalin*. Ibn Atiyya said: it is the plural of *zill*, since there is no sun in Paradise, and its air is temperate like the time of dawn before sunrise. End of quote. The plural of *fi'l* in the form *fi'al* is used in the sense of abundance, like *dhi'b* and *dhi'ab* (wolf and wolves). As for the claim that the time of Paradise is like the time of dawn before sunrise, this requires a sound transmission. How could that be? And is there in the hadith something that indicates a *hawra'* (dark-eyed maiden) of Paradise, that if she appeared the world would be illuminated by her light, or something similar to this? He said: it is possible that it is the plural of *zullah* (a canopy). Abu Ali said: like *burmah* and *biram* (cooking pot and pots). Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the plural of *zillah* with a *kasra* on the *za'*; Ibn Atiyya said: this is a dialect of *zullah*. End of quote. Then it would be like *luqhah* and *liqah* (a milch camel and milch camels), and *fi'al* is not regular for *fu'lah* but is preserved by transmission.

Abdullah, as-Sulami, Talha, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read *fi zillin*: the plural of *zillah*. The plural of *fi'lah* on *fi'l* is regular. It refers to the coverings and layers of canopies, curtains, and similar things that provide shade.

Abdullah read *muttaki'in* in the accusative as a *hal*. *Yaddda'una* is the present tense of *idda'a*, which is *if'tala* from *da'a*, and its meaning is: and for them is whatever they wish for. Abu Ubayda said: the Arabs say *ud'u 'alayya ma shi'ta*, meaning "wish upon me whatever you want," and they say, "So-and-so wished in a report." Az-Zajjaj said: it is from *ad-du'a'*, that is, whatever the people of Paradise call for will come to them. It has also been said: they call for it for themselves. It has also been said: they call one another to it, based on the saying *irmuhu* and *taramuhu* (throw it to him, and they threw it to one another).

[p. 343] The majority read *salamun* with *raf'* (nominative). It is an adjective of *ma*, meaning: granted to them and pure. End of quote. This is not valid if *ma* means "that which," because then it would be definite, and *salamun* is indefinite, and a definite noun is not described by an indefinite. If *ma* is an indefinite relative, it is permissible, but then it does not carry generality, as with its status as "that which."

It has also been said: *salamun* is a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is the verb governing *qawlan*, meaning: peace is said, "a word from a Lord, Most Merciful." Or *'alaykum* is omitted, meaning: peace upon you, "a word from a Lord, Most Merciful." It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is peace.

Az-Zamakhshari said: *salamun qawlan* is a substitute (*badal*) for *ma yaddda'un*, as if he said: for them is peace, said to them, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful. The meaning is that Allah greets them with peace through the angels, or without an intermediary, as an exaggeration in their honour. That is what they desire, and they will not be prevented from having it. Ibn Abbas said: and the angels enter upon them with greetings from the Lord of the worlds. End of quote. If *salam* is a substitute for *ma yaddda'un*, it is specifically so. The apparent meaning is that it is general for everything they call for; if it is general, *salam* cannot be a substitute for it.

It has also been said: *salamun* is the predicate of *ma yaddda'un*, and *ma yaddda'un* is the subject, meaning: and for them what they call for is pure peace, and *qawlan* is an emphasizing verbal noun, like His saying, *wa lahum ma yaddda'un salam* ("and for them is what they call for: peace"), meaning a promise from the Merciful. Az-Zamakhshari said: the more correct view is that it is in the accusative by way of specification (*ikhtisas*), and this is one of his figurative usages. End of quote. On this grammatical analysis, *lahum* is related to *salamun*.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read *silmun*, with a *kasra* on the *sin* and sukun on the *lam*, meaning *salam*. Abu al-Fadl ar-Razi said: "peaceful for them," that is, that is peaceful. Ubayy, Abdullah, Isa, and al-Qanawi read *salaman*, in the accusative as a verbal noun. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative as a *hal*, meaning: for them is their desire, pure.

﴿And separate yourselves today﴾: that is, withdraw from the believers, because the place of gathering brings together the righteous and the wicked, so the criminals are commanded to be set apart from the believers. The apparent meaning is that there is an omitted statement here. When Allah mentioned what is said to the believers in His saying, *salamun qawlan min rabbin rahim*, it is said: "And it is said to the criminals: separate yourselves." When they carried out what they were commanded, He said to them, by way of rebuke and reproach, ﴿Did I not charge you?﴾, making them acknowledge His covenant with them and their violation of it. It is related from ad-Dahhak: for every disbeliever there is a house of Fire in which he neither sees nor is seen. According to this, the meaning is that some of them are separated from others. From Qatada: they withdraw from every good. The *'ahd* (covenant) means the charge; *'ahida ilayhi* means he charged him. Allah's covenant with them is what He placed in them of rational proofs and sent down to them of revealed proofs. Worship of Satan means obeying him in what he leads them astray in and adorns for them.

The majority read *a'had* with a *fatha* on the hamza and the *ha'*. Talha and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil al-Kufi read it with a *kasra* on the hamza; Abu al-Lawami said this is the dialect of Tamim, and that this *kasra* on the *nun* and *ta'* is more common than among the letters of the present tense, meaning *ni'had* and *ti'had*. Ibn Khalawayh said: *alam a'had*. Yahya ibn Wathhab: *alam ahad*, the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Atiyya said: al-Hudhayl ibn Wathhab read *alami i'had*, with a *kasra* on the *mim* and hamza and a *fatha* on the *ha'*, and this is according to the dialect of one who puts a *kasra* on the first letter of the present tense except the *ya'*. It was also transmitted from Ibn Wathhab: *alam a'hid*, with a *kasra* on the *ha'*, from *ya'hidu*. End of quote. His saying "with a *kasra* on the *mim* and the hamza" means that the *kasra* on the *mim* indicates a *kasra* on the hamza, because the vowel on the *mim* is the vowel transferred from the hamza with a *kasra*, and the hamza was dropped when its vowel was transferred to the preceding quiescent letter, which is the *mim*. (The reading *a'had* with a cut hamza and a *kasra* is not permissible.) Az-Zamakhshari said: it was read *i'had* with a *kasra* on the hamza, and every verb of the *fa'ila* pattern permits a *kasra* on the letters of its present tense except the *ya'*; *a'hid* with a *kasra* on the *ha'*. Az-Zajjaj permitted that it is of the pattern *na'ama yan'imu* and *darab yadrib*, and *ahad* with *ha'* and *ahid*, which is the dialect of Tamim, and from it their saying: *daha ma'ha* ("leave it with it"). End of quote. His saying "except the *ya'*" is a dialect of some of the tribe of Kalb, who also put a *kasra* on the *ya'*, saying *hal yi'lam* ("does he know?"). His saying *daha maha* means they want *da'ha ma'aha*; they assimilated the *'ayn* into the *ha'*. The reference by "this" is to what He charged them with: disobedience to Satan and obedience to the Merciful.

Nafi' and 'Asim read *jibilan* with a *kasra* on the *jim* and the *ba'* and a shadda on the *lam*. This is the reading of Abu Haywa, Suhayl, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu Raja', and al-Hasan, with a variant from him. The two Arabic readers (Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i?) and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil read it with a *damma* on the *jim* and sukun on the *ba'*. The rest of the seven read it with a *damma* on it and a lightened *lam*. Al-Hasan ibn Abi Ishaq, az-Zuhri, Ibn Hurmuz, Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr, and Hafs ibn Humayd read it with two *dammas* and a shadda on the *lam*. Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli, al-Yamani, and Hammad ibn Maslama from 'Asim read it with a *kasra* on the *jim* and sukun on the *ba'*. Al-A'mash read *jibilan* with two *kasras* and a lightened *lam*. It was also read *jibalan* with a *kasra* on the *jim*, a *fatha* on the *ba'*, and a lightened *lam*, the plural of *jibilah*, like *fitrah* and *fitar*. These are seven dialects in which it was read. Ali ibn Abi Talib and some of the Khurasanis read *jilan*, with a *kasra* on the *jim* and a *ya'* after it, the singular of *ajyal* (generations). *Al-jibl* with a *ba'* and one dot below is the great nation. Ad-Dahhak said: its least number is ten thousand. Allah, exalted is He, addresses the disbelievers with what Satan did with them, as a rebuke to them. The majority read *afalam takunu* with the second-person address; Talha and Isa read it with the third-person *ya'*, referring back to *jibilan*. It is related that they deny and dispute, so their neighbours, tribes, and families testify against them, and they swear that they were not polytheists. Then their mouths are sealed, and their hands and feet speak. In a hadith: "The servant will say on the Day of Resurrection: I do not allow any witness against me except myself. Then his mouth is sealed, and his limbs are told: speak. So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left between himself and speech, and it is said: away with you, and destruction, it was on your account that I was contending."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 55–79 (part 2 of 2):

It was also read: *yukhtamu* in the passive voice, and *tatakallamu aydīhim* with two *tā'*s. It was also read: *wa-li-tukallimunā aydīhim* with two *tā'*s. It was also read: *wa-l-tukallimnā aydīhim wa-l-tashhad* with the *lām* of command and the jussive, on the basis that God commands the limbs to speak and to bear witness. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa related from his father, from his grandfather Ṭalḥa, that he read: *wa-li-tukallimanā aydīhim wa-li-tashhada*, with the *lām* of *kay* (in order that) and the accusative, meaning: "And thus He seals over their mouths." 

The apparent meaning is that *al-aʿyun* (the eyes) are the seeing limbs, and the meaning is: "We would have blinded them, so they could not see how they walk." This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatāda, and the context of the *maskh* (transformation) supports it, for they are within the grip of power and the scope of punishment, if God wills it upon them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: He meant the eyes of insight, and the meaning is: "Had We willed, We would have sealed upon them with disbelief, so that none of them would ever be guided."

*Al-ṭamsh* is the removal of a thing and its trace entirely, to the point that it seems as if it had never existed. If *al-aʿyun* is taken literally, the apparent meaning is that *yaṭmisu* means *yamsakh* (transform) in the literal sense. It is also permissible that *al-ṭamsh* is meant as blindness without the removal of the organ and its trace.

The majority read *fa-stabaqū*, as a past verb conjoined to *la-ṭamasnā*, and this is on the basis of supposition and estimation. *Al-ṣirāṭa* is in the accusative by the assumption of an omitted *ilā* (to), with the verb reaching it directly; the original would be *fa-stabaqū ilā al-ṣirāṭ*. Or it is an object by the *tadmīn* (implication) of *istabaqū* the meaning of *tabādarū* (hasten), and making it "those who are preceded to it." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Or it is in the accusative as an adverb of place, but this is not permissible, because *al-ṣirāṭ* is *al-ṭarīq* (the path), and it is a specific place-adverb. The verb does not reach it except through the mediation of *fī* (in), except in an anomalous usage, as Sībawayh cited:

*Lададн bi-hazzi al-kaffi yaʿsilu matnuhu* / *fīhi kamā ʿasala al-ṭarīqa al-thaʿlabu*

(A supple spear, shaken by the hand, its shaft glides in it as the fox glides along the path.)

The position of Ibn al-Ṭarāwa is that *al-ṣirāṭ*, *al-ṭarīq*, *al-makhram*, and what resembles them of place-adverbs are not specific, so according to his view what al-Zamakhsharī said is permissible."

ʿĪsā read *fa-stabiqū* as an imperative, and it is on the basis of an implied *qawl* (saying), meaning: "It will be said to them: *istabiqū al-ṣirāṭ* (race to the path)." This is by way of incapacitation, for it is not possible for them to race while their eyes are obliterated.

*Fa-annā yubṣirūn* means: how can one who has had his eye obliterated see? The apparent meaning is that the transformation (*al-maskh*) is literal, and it is the changing of their forms into hideous shapes. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *la-maskhnāhum* means into apes and swine, as has been mentioned in the case of the Children of Israel. It was also said: into stones. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and a group said: "We would have made them sit and disabled them, so they could not move at all." The apparent meaning is that this would be in this world. Ibn Salām said: "This entire threat is on the Day of Resurrection."

Al-Ḥasan read *ʿalā makānatihim* in the singular, meaning the place, like *al-maqāma* and *al-maqām*. The majority and Abū Bakr read it in the plural. The majority read *muḍiyyan* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*; Abū Ḥaywa and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr al-Anṭākī, from al-Kisāʾī, read it with a *kasra* on the *mīm* following the vowel of the *ḍād*, like *al-ʿitibiyy* and *al-qitibiyy*, its pattern being *faʿūl*. A silent *wāw* and a *yāʾ* met, so the *wāw* was changed to a *yāʾ*, and it was assimilated into the *yāʾ*, and the letter before it was given a *kasra* to make the *yāʾ* sound correct. It was also read *maḍiyyan* with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm*, in which case it is one of the verbal nouns that come in the pattern *faʿīl*, like *al-rasīm* and *al-wajīf*.

Since the Exalted mentioned the obliteration and the transformation as a supposition of the likened case, He mentioned a proof of His manifest power in reversing the aged, and that this is not done except by Him, Exalted is He. Its reversal (*tankīs*) is: He turned it and made it the opposite of how He created it at first. He created him in weakness of body, devoid of intellect and knowledge, then He made him grow and move from state to state until he reaches his full strength, and his power is completed, and he understands and knows what is for him and what is against him. When he reaches that point, He reverses him in creation, so he diminishes until he returns to a state resembling the state of childhood in the weakness of his body, the scarcity of his intellect, and his lack of understanding, just as an arrow is reversed so that its top becomes its bottom. In all of this there is evidence that the One who did these deeds is able to obliterate them and to do to them what He wills.

The majority read *nunakkisuh* with *tashdīd* (doubled), and ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read it without *tashdīd*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān, and Abū ʿAmr in the narration of ʿAbbās read *taʿqilūn* with the *tā'* of address; the rest of the seven read it with the *yā'* of absence.

*Wa-mā ʿallamnāhu al-shiʿr*: The pronoun in *ʿallamnāhu* refers to the Messenger (ﷺ). They used to say about him: "He is a poet." It is related that the one who said it was ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, and God negated that from him. Their saying about him, "He is a poet," as for one whose nature was poetry, then his saying is obstinacy and a deception for one ignorant of poetry; as for one whose nature was not poetry, then his saying is pure ignorance. Where is he from poetry? Poetry is only metrical, rhymed speech indicating a meaning that poets select from much imagination and embellishment of speech, and other things that the pious person refrains from reciting, let alone composing. He (peace be upon him) did not compose poetry, and when he recited a line he preserved the meaning without its metre, as when he recited:

*Sa-tubdī laka al-ayyāmu mā kunta jāhilan* / *wa-yaʾtīka man lam tuzawwad bi-l-akhbār*

(The days will reveal to you what you were ignorant of, and there will come to you one who was not provisioned with news.)

It was said: "Among the best of poets." So the one who said it said:

*Alam tarayānī kullamā jiʾtu ṭāriqan* / *wajadtu bihā wa-in lam tuṭayyab ṭīban*

(Do you not see me, whenever I come as a night visitor, I find her, even if she is not perfumed, fragrant.)

*Ataj-ʿalu nahbī wa-nahba al-ʿubayd* / *bayna al-aqraʿ wa-ʿuyayna*

(Will you make my plunder and the plunder of ʿUbayd between al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyayna?)

And he recited one day:

*Kafā bi-l-islāmi wa-l-shaybi nāhiyā*

(Sufficient are Islam and grey hair as a restrainer.)

Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said: "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of God." The poet only said: "Sufficient are grey hair and Islam." Sometimes he recited a line perfectly metred, rarely. It is related from him that he recited the line of Ibn Rawāḥa:

*Yabītu yujāfī janbahu ʿan firāshihi* / *idhā istuthqilat bi-l-mushrikīna al-maḍājiʿu*

(He spends the night, his side withdrawn from his bed, when the beds are heavy with the polytheists.)

The fact that a line passed through his tongue metred does not indicate that he knew poetry. Things that accept metre occurred in his speech (peace be upon him), such as his saying:

*Anā al-nabiyyu lā kadhib* / *anā ibnu ʿabd al-muṭṭalib*

(I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.)

Likewise his saying:

*Hal anti illā iṣbaʿun damītī* / *wa-fī sabīli Llāhi mā laqītī*

(Are you anything but a finger that bled, and in the way of God what you suffered?)

This is speech of the same kind as his speech which he uttered by his nature, without artifice in it, nor intention to metre, nor affectation, just as there is found in the Qur'an something metred that is not counted as poetry, such as His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 92], and His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. And in much prose that eloquent people compose, that is not called poetry, nor does it occur to the speaker or the listener that it is poetry.

*Wa-mā yanbaghī lahu*: That is, it is not possible for him, nor valid, nor suitable; because he (peace be upon him) was on the path of pure seriousness, while poetry for the most part is on the path of jest, embellishing what is not beautiful, disparaging what is not ugly, and excessive exaggeration. He (Exalted is He) made him not compose poetry, just as He made him unlettered, not writing, so that the proof would be more firm and the doubt more refuted. It was said: in this verse there is evidence of the baseness of poetry, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I am not a poet, nor does it befit me." Some people went to the view that there is no baseness in it, and that God only prevented His Prophet (peace be upon him) from it. Even if it is a noble adornment, so that the Qur'an would come from his side more wondrously, for if he had the capacity for poetry, it would be said about the Qur'an: "This is from that power."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The matter is not so in my view. He (peace be upon him) had eloquence and clarity in prose at the highest rank, but the speech of God is manifest through its inimitability, and it is distinguished by its description, and the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge removes it from every speech. God only prevented His Prophet from poetry to elevate him above what is in the speech of poets of imagination and embellishment of utterance. As for the Qur'an, it is a reminder with realities and proofs, so it is not the saying of a poet, and this was the style of his speech (peace be upon him), and a single word." End.

The pronoun in *lahu* refers to the Messenger, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). One who went far afield said it refers to the Qur'an, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Qur'an, though it has not been mentioned; but he may say: the speech indicates it, and it is clarified by the return of the pronoun to it in His saying: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, meaning: a heavenly book that is read in the sanctuaries, and by reciting it and acting upon it one attains what contains the success of both abodes. How far it is then between it and poetry, most of which is from the prompting of the devils!

Ibn ʿĀmir and Nāfiʿ read *li-tundhira* with the *tā'* of address to the Messenger; the rest of the seven read it with the *yā'* of absence, so it may refer to the Messenger, and it may refer to the Qur'an. Al-Yamānī read *li-yundhara* with a *yā'* in the passive voice, and Ibn Khālawayh related it from al-Jaḥdarī. He said from Abū al-Sammāl and al-Yamānī that they both read *li-yandhara* with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and the *dhāl*, the present of *nadhira* with a *kasra* on the *dhāl*, when one knows of a thing and prepares himself for it.

*Man kāna ḥayyan*: That is, heedless, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, because the heedless is like the dead. By it he means the one upon whom it was sealed with faith, and likewise He contrasted it with His saying: "and the word will be fulfilled" (*wa-yaḥiqqa al-qawl*), that is, the word of punishment, ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, those for whom it is decreed by reaching the end in disbelief.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 36, verses 55–79 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in their enjoyment,﴾ ﴿they and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches,﴾ ﴿for them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for,﴾ ﴿"Peace!" – a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿"And separate yourselves today, O criminals!﴾ ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan – indeed, he is to you a clear enemy?﴾ ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾ ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. So did you not use reason?﴾ ﴿This is Hellfire, which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein today for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ ﴿Today We seal over their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet testify to what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could have obliterated their eyes, and they would race to the path; but how could they see?﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could have transformed them in their places, so they would not be able to proceed or return.﴾ ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation. So will they not reason?﴾ ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him. It is not but a reminder and a clear Qur'an,﴾ ﴿to warn whoever is alive and that the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers.﴾

[p. 342] When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, He followed that with the state of the happy and the wretched. The apparent meaning is that it is a report to us about what they will be in when they arrive at the reward and punishment prepared for them. It has also been said that it is a narration of what will be said on that Day; in such a narration there is an additional depiction of the promised reward in souls, and an encouragement to desire it and to pursue what it produces. The apparent meaning is that *ash-shughl* (busyness) is the bliss that has occupied them away from everything that comes to mind. Mujahid said something close to this. Some scholars restricted this *shughl* to the deflowering of virgins; this was related from Ibn Abbas. Also from him: the hearing of lutes. From al-Hasan: they are occupied away from what the people of the Fire are in. From al-Kalbi: away from their families among the people of the Fire; they do not mention them lest they be disturbed. From Ibn Kaysan: *ash-shughl* is mutual visiting. It has also been said: it is the hospitality of Allah. The singular *ash-shughl* is used because bliss is considered, and it is one insofar as it is bliss.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu Amr read *shughul* with a *damma* on the *shin* and sukun on the *ghayn*; the rest of the seven readers read it with *damma* on both. Mujahid, Abu as-Sammal, and Ibn Hubayra, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh from him, read it with two *fathas*. Yazid an-Nahwi and Ibn Hubayra, as transmitted by Abu al-Fadl ar-Razi, read it with a *fatha* on the *shin* and sukun on the *ghayn*. The majority read *fakihun* with an *alif*. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Qatada, Abu Haywa, Mujahid, Shayba, Abu Raja', Yahya ibn Sabih, and Nafi' in one narration read it without *alif*. Talha and al-A'mash read *fakihin*, with *alif* and *ya'*, in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial state), while *fi shughlin* is the predicate. With the *alif*, it means "people of fruit," as one says *laabin* (possessor of milk), *tamir* (possessor of dates), *shahim* (possessor of fat), and *lahim* (possessor of meat). Without the *alif*, its meaning is "joyful, merry," derived from *al-fukaha*, which is jest. It was also read *fakihin* without *alif* and with *ya'*, and *fakuhun* with a *damma* on the *kaf*. It is said: a man is *fakih* and *fakih*, like *yadus* and *yadis*.

It is permissible for *hum* to be the subject (*mubtada'*) with *fi zilalin* as its predicate, and *muttaki'un* a second predicate; or its predicate is *muttaki'un*, with *fi zilalin* related to it; or it may be an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in *fakihun*, with *fi zilalin* as a *hal*, and *muttaki'un* a second predicate of *inna*; or it may be an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in *shughlin*, shifted to it from the governing word within it.

On this and the preceding possibility, the spouses share in the enjoyment, the busyness, and the reclining on couches, by way of the explicit statement. On the first, they share in the shade and the reclining on couches by way of the explicit statement, and they share in the enjoyment and busyness by way of the meaning.

The majority read *fi zilalin*. Ibn Atiyya said: it is the plural of *zill*, since there is no sun in Paradise, and its air is temperate like the time of dawn before sunrise. End of quote. The plural of *fi'l* in the form *fi'al* is used in the sense of abundance, like *dhi'b* and *dhi'ab* (wolf and wolves). As for the claim that the time of Paradise is like the time of dawn before sunrise, this requires a sound transmission. How could that be? And is there in the hadith something that indicates a *hawra'* (dark-eyed maiden) of Paradise, that if she appeared the world would be illuminated by her light, or something similar to this? He said: it is possible that it is the plural of *zullah* (a canopy). Abu Ali said: like *burmah* and *biram* (cooking pot and pots). Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the plural of *zillah* with a *kasra* on the *za'*; Ibn Atiyya said: this is a dialect of *zullah*. End of quote. Then it would be like *luqhah* and *liqah* (a milch camel and milch camels), and *fi'al* is not regular for *fu'lah* but is preserved by transmission.

Abdullah, as-Sulami, Talha, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read *fi zillin*: the plural of *zillah*. The plural of *fi'lah* on *fi'l* is regular. It refers to the coverings and layers of canopies, curtains, and similar things that provide shade.

Abdullah read *muttaki'in* in the accusative as a *hal*. *Yaddda'una* is the present tense of *idda'a*, which is *if'tala* from *da'a*, and its meaning is: and for them is whatever they wish for. Abu Ubayda said: the Arabs say *ud'u 'alayya ma shi'ta*, meaning "wish upon me whatever you want," and they say, "So-and-so wished in a report." Az-Zajjaj said: it is from *ad-du'a'*, that is, whatever the people of Paradise call for will come to them. It has also been said: they call for it for themselves. It has also been said: they call one another to it, based on the saying *irmuhu* and *taramuhu* (throw it to him, and they threw it to one another).

[p. 343] The majority read *salamun* with *raf'* (nominative). It is an adjective of *ma*, meaning: granted to them and pure. End of quote. This is not valid if *ma* means "that which," because then it would be definite, and *salamun* is indefinite, and a definite noun is not described by an indefinite. If *ma* is an indefinite relative, it is permissible, but then it does not carry generality, as with its status as "that which."

It has also been said: *salamun* is a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is the verb governing *qawlan*, meaning: peace is said, "a word from a Lord, Most Merciful." Or *'alaykum* is omitted, meaning: peace upon you, "a word from a Lord, Most Merciful." It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is peace.

Az-Zamakhshari said: *salamun qawlan* is a substitute (*badal*) for *ma yaddda'un*, as if he said: for them is peace, said to them, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful. The meaning is that Allah greets them with peace through the angels, or without an intermediary, as an exaggeration in their honour. That is what they desire, and they will not be prevented from having it. Ibn Abbas said: and the angels enter upon them with greetings from the Lord of the worlds. End of quote. If *salam* is a substitute for *ma yaddda'un*, it is specifically so. The apparent meaning is that it is general for everything they call for; if it is general, *salam* cannot be a substitute for it.

It has also been said: *salamun* is the predicate of *ma yaddda'un*, and *ma yaddda'un* is the subject, meaning: and for them what they call for is pure peace, and *qawlan* is an emphasizing verbal noun, like His saying, *wa lahum ma yaddda'un salam* ("and for them is what they call for: peace"), meaning a promise from the Merciful. Az-Zamakhshari said: the more correct view is that it is in the accusative by way of specification (*ikhtisas*), and this is one of his figurative usages. End of quote. On this grammatical analysis, *lahum* is related to *salamun*.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read *silmun*, with a *kasra* on the *sin* and sukun on the *lam*, meaning *salam*. Abu al-Fadl ar-Razi said: "peaceful for them," that is, that is peaceful. Ubayy, Abdullah, Isa, and al-Qanawi read *salaman*, in the accusative as a verbal noun. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative as a *hal*, meaning: for them is their desire, pure.

﴿And separate yourselves today﴾: that is, withdraw from the believers, because the place of gathering brings together the righteous and the wicked, so the criminals are commanded to be set apart from the believers. The apparent meaning is that there is an omitted statement here. When Allah mentioned what is said to the believers in His saying, *salamun qawlan min rabbin rahim*, it is said: "And it is said to the criminals: separate yourselves." When they carried out what they were commanded, He said to them, by way of rebuke and reproach, ﴿Did I not charge you?﴾, making them acknowledge His covenant with them and their violation of it. It is related from ad-Dahhak: for every disbeliever there is a house of Fire in which he neither sees nor is seen. According to this, the meaning is that some of them are separated from others. From Qatada: they withdraw from every good. The *'ahd* (covenant) means the charge; *'ahida ilayhi* means he charged him. Allah's covenant with them is what He placed in them of rational proofs and sent down to them of revealed proofs. Worship of Satan means obeying him in what he leads them astray in and adorns for them.

The majority read *a'had* with a *fatha* on the hamza and the *ha'*. Talha and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil al-Kufi read it with a *kasra* on the hamza; Abu al-Lawami said this is the dialect of Tamim, and that this *kasra* on the *nun* and *ta'* is more common than among the letters of the present tense, meaning *ni'had* and *ti'had*. Ibn Khalawayh said: *alam a'had*. Yahya ibn Wathhab: *alam ahad*, the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Atiyya said: al-Hudhayl ibn Wathhab read *alami i'had*, with a *kasra* on the *mim* and hamza and a *fatha* on the *ha'*, and this is according to the dialect of one who puts a *kasra* on the first letter of the present tense except the *ya'*. It was also transmitted from Ibn Wathhab: *alam a'hid*, with a *kasra* on the *ha'*, from *ya'hidu*. End of quote. His saying "with a *kasra* on the *mim* and the hamza" means that the *kasra* on the *mim* indicates a *kasra* on the hamza, because the vowel on the *mim* is the vowel transferred from the hamza with a *kasra*, and the hamza was dropped when its vowel was transferred to the preceding quiescent letter, which is the *mim*. (The reading *a'had* with a cut hamza and a *kasra* is not permissible.) Az-Zamakhshari said: it was read *i'had* with a *kasra* on the hamza, and every verb of the *fa'ila* pattern permits a *kasra* on the letters of its present tense except the *ya'*; *a'hid* with a *kasra* on the *ha'*. Az-Zajjaj permitted that it is of the pattern *na'ama yan'imu* and *darab yadrib*, and *ahad* with *ha'* and *ahid*, which is the dialect of Tamim, and from it their saying: *daha ma'ha* ("leave it with it"). End of quote. His saying "except the *ya'*" is a dialect of some of the tribe of Kalb, who also put a *kasra* on the *ya'*, saying *hal yi'lam* ("does he know?"). His saying *daha maha* means they want *da'ha ma'aha*; they assimilated the *'ayn* into the *ha'*. The reference by "this" is to what He charged them with: disobedience to Satan and obedience to the Merciful.

Nafi' and 'Asim read *jibilan* with a *kasra* on the *jim* and the *ba'* and a shadda on the *lam*. This is the reading of Abu Haywa, Suhayl, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu Raja', and al-Hasan, with a variant from him. The two Arabic readers (Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i?) and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil read it with a *damma* on the *jim* and sukun on the *ba'*. The rest of the seven read it with a *damma* on it and a lightened *lam*. Al-Hasan ibn Abi Ishaq, az-Zuhri, Ibn Hurmuz, Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr, and Hafs ibn Humayd read it with two *dammas* and a shadda on the *lam*. Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli, al-Yamani, and Hammad ibn Maslama from 'Asim read it with a *kasra* on the *jim* and sukun on the *ba'*. Al-A'mash read *jibilan* with two *kasras* and a lightened *lam*. It was also read *jibalan* with a *kasra* on the *jim*, a *fatha* on the *ba'*, and a lightened *lam*, the plural of *jibilah*, like *fitrah* and *fitar*. These are seven dialects in which it was read. Ali ibn Abi Talib and some of the Khurasanis read *jilan*, with a *kasra* on the *jim* and a *ya'* after it, the singular of *ajyal* (generations). *Al-jibl* with a *ba'* and one dot below is the great nation. Ad-Dahhak said: its least number is ten thousand. Allah, exalted is He, addresses the disbelievers with what Satan did with them, as a rebuke to them. The majority read *afalam takunu* with the second-person address; Talha and Isa read it with the third-person *ya'*, referring back to *jibilan*. It is related that they deny and dispute, so their neighbours, tribes, and families testify against them, and they swear that they were not polytheists. Then their mouths are sealed, and their hands and feet speak. In a hadith: "The servant will say on the Day of Resurrection: I do not allow any witness against me except myself. Then his mouth is sealed, and his limbs are told: speak. So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left between himself and speech, and it is said: away with you, and destruction, it was on your account that I was contending."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 36, verses 55–79 (part 2 of 2):

It was also read: *yukhtamu* in the passive voice, and *tatakallamu aydīhim* with two *tā'*s. It was also read: *wa-li-tukallimunā aydīhim* with two *tā'*s. It was also read: *wa-l-tukallimnā aydīhim wa-l-tashhad* with the *lām* of command and the jussive, on the basis that God commands the limbs to speak and to bear witness. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa related from his father, from his grandfather Ṭalḥa, that he read: *wa-li-tukallimanā aydīhim wa-li-tashhada*, with the *lām* of *kay* (in order that) and the accusative, meaning: "And thus He seals over their mouths." 

The apparent meaning is that *al-aʿyun* (the eyes) are the seeing limbs, and the meaning is: "We would have blinded them, so they could not see how they walk." This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatāda, and the context of the *maskh* (transformation) supports it, for they are within the grip of power and the scope of punishment, if God wills it upon them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: He meant the eyes of insight, and the meaning is: "Had We willed, We would have sealed upon them with disbelief, so that none of them would ever be guided."

*Al-ṭamsh* is the removal of a thing and its trace entirely, to the point that it seems as if it had never existed. If *al-aʿyun* is taken literally, the apparent meaning is that *yaṭmisu* means *yamsakh* (transform) in the literal sense. It is also permissible that *al-ṭamsh* is meant as blindness without the removal of the organ and its trace.

The majority read *fa-stabaqū*, as a past verb conjoined to *la-ṭamasnā*, and this is on the basis of supposition and estimation. *Al-ṣirāṭa* is in the accusative by the assumption of an omitted *ilā* (to), with the verb reaching it directly; the original would be *fa-stabaqū ilā al-ṣirāṭ*. Or it is an object by the *tadmīn* (implication) of *istabaqū* the meaning of *tabādarū* (hasten), and making it "those who are preceded to it." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Or it is in the accusative as an adverb of place, but this is not permissible, because *al-ṣirāṭ* is *al-ṭarīq* (the path), and it is a specific place-adverb. The verb does not reach it except through the mediation of *fī* (in), except in an anomalous usage, as Sībawayh cited:

*Lададн bi-hazzi al-kaffi yaʿsilu matnuhu* / *fīhi kamā ʿasala al-ṭarīqa al-thaʿlabu*

(A supple spear, shaken by the hand, its shaft glides in it as the fox glides along the path.)

The position of Ibn al-Ṭarāwa is that *al-ṣirāṭ*, *al-ṭarīq*, *al-makhram*, and what resembles them of place-adverbs are not specific, so according to his view what al-Zamakhsharī said is permissible."

ʿĪsā read *fa-stabiqū* as an imperative, and it is on the basis of an implied *qawl* (saying), meaning: "It will be said to them: *istabiqū al-ṣirāṭ* (race to the path)." This is by way of incapacitation, for it is not possible for them to race while their eyes are obliterated.

*Fa-annā yubṣirūn* means: how can one who has had his eye obliterated see? The apparent meaning is that the transformation (*al-maskh*) is literal, and it is the changing of their forms into hideous shapes. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *la-maskhnāhum* means into apes and swine, as has been mentioned in the case of the Children of Israel. It was also said: into stones. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and a group said: "We would have made them sit and disabled them, so they could not move at all." The apparent meaning is that this would be in this world. Ibn Salām said: "This entire threat is on the Day of Resurrection."

Al-Ḥasan read *ʿalā makānatihim* in the singular, meaning the place, like *al-maqāma* and *al-maqām*. The majority and Abū Bakr read it in the plural. The majority read *muḍiyyan* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*; Abū Ḥaywa and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr al-Anṭākī, from al-Kisāʾī, read it with a *kasra* on the *mīm* following the vowel of the *ḍād*, like *al-ʿitibiyy* and *al-qitibiyy*, its pattern being *faʿūl*. A silent *wāw* and a *yāʾ* met, so the *wāw* was changed to a *yāʾ*, and it was assimilated into the *yāʾ*, and the letter before it was given a *kasra* to make the *yāʾ* sound correct. It was also read *maḍiyyan* with a *fatḥa* on the *mīm*, in which case it is one of the verbal nouns that come in the pattern *faʿīl*, like *al-rasīm* and *al-wajīf*.

Since the Exalted mentioned the obliteration and the transformation as a supposition of the likened case, He mentioned a proof of His manifest power in reversing the aged, and that this is not done except by Him, Exalted is He. Its reversal (*tankīs*) is: He turned it and made it the opposite of how He created it at first. He created him in weakness of body, devoid of intellect and knowledge, then He made him grow and move from state to state until he reaches his full strength, and his power is completed, and he understands and knows what is for him and what is against him. When he reaches that point, He reverses him in creation, so he diminishes until he returns to a state resembling the state of childhood in the weakness of his body, the scarcity of his intellect, and his lack of understanding, just as an arrow is reversed so that its top becomes its bottom. In all of this there is evidence that the One who did these deeds is able to obliterate them and to do to them what He wills.

The majority read *nunakkisuh* with *tashdīd* (doubled), and ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read it without *tashdīd*. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Dhakwān, and Abū ʿAmr in the narration of ʿAbbās read *taʿqilūn* with the *tā'* of address; the rest of the seven read it with the *yā'* of absence.

*Wa-mā ʿallamnāhu al-shiʿr*: The pronoun in *ʿallamnāhu* refers to the Messenger (ﷺ). They used to say about him: "He is a poet." It is related that the one who said it was ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, and God negated that from him. Their saying about him, "He is a poet," as for one whose nature was poetry, then his saying is obstinacy and a deception for one ignorant of poetry; as for one whose nature was not poetry, then his saying is pure ignorance. Where is he from poetry? Poetry is only metrical, rhymed speech indicating a meaning that poets select from much imagination and embellishment of speech, and other things that the pious person refrains from reciting, let alone composing. He (peace be upon him) did not compose poetry, and when he recited a line he preserved the meaning without its metre, as when he recited:

*Sa-tubdī laka al-ayyāmu mā kunta jāhilan* / *wa-yaʾtīka man lam tuzawwad bi-l-akhbār*

(The days will reveal to you what you were ignorant of, and there will come to you one who was not provisioned with news.)

It was said: "Among the best of poets." So the one who said it said:

*Alam tarayānī kullamā jiʾtu ṭāriqan* / *wajadtu bihā wa-in lam tuṭayyab ṭīban*

(Do you not see me, whenever I come as a night visitor, I find her, even if she is not perfumed, fragrant.)

*Ataj-ʿalu nahbī wa-nahba al-ʿubayd* / *bayna al-aqraʿ wa-ʿuyayna*

(Will you make my plunder and the plunder of ʿUbayd between al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyayna?)

And he recited one day:

*Kafā bi-l-islāmi wa-l-shaybi nāhiyā*

(Sufficient are Islam and grey hair as a restrainer.)

Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said: "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of God." The poet only said: "Sufficient are grey hair and Islam." Sometimes he recited a line perfectly metred, rarely. It is related from him that he recited the line of Ibn Rawāḥa:

*Yabītu yujāfī janbahu ʿan firāshihi* / *idhā istuthqilat bi-l-mushrikīna al-maḍājiʿu*

(He spends the night, his side withdrawn from his bed, when the beds are heavy with the polytheists.)

The fact that a line passed through his tongue metred does not indicate that he knew poetry. Things that accept metre occurred in his speech (peace be upon him), such as his saying:

*Anā al-nabiyyu lā kadhib* / *anā ibnu ʿabd al-muṭṭalib*

(I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.)

Likewise his saying:

*Hal anti illā iṣbaʿun damītī* / *wa-fī sabīli Llāhi mā laqītī*

(Are you anything but a finger that bled, and in the way of God what you suffered?)

This is speech of the same kind as his speech which he uttered by his nature, without artifice in it, nor intention to metre, nor affectation, just as there is found in the Qur'an something metred that is not counted as poetry, such as His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 92], and His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. And in much prose that eloquent people compose, that is not called poetry, nor does it occur to the speaker or the listener that it is poetry.

*Wa-mā yanbaghī lahu*: That is, it is not possible for him, nor valid, nor suitable; because he (peace be upon him) was on the path of pure seriousness, while poetry for the most part is on the path of jest, embellishing what is not beautiful, disparaging what is not ugly, and excessive exaggeration. He (Exalted is He) made him not compose poetry, just as He made him unlettered, not writing, so that the proof would be more firm and the doubt more refuted. It was said: in this verse there is evidence of the baseness of poetry, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I am not a poet, nor does it befit me." Some people went to the view that there is no baseness in it, and that God only prevented His Prophet (peace be upon him) from it. Even if it is a noble adornment, so that the Qur'an would come from his side more wondrously, for if he had the capacity for poetry, it would be said about the Qur'an: "This is from that power."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The matter is not so in my view. He (peace be upon him) had eloquence and clarity in prose at the highest rank, but the speech of God is manifest through its inimitability, and it is distinguished by its description, and the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge removes it from every speech. God only prevented His Prophet from poetry to elevate him above what is in the speech of poets of imagination and embellishment of utterance. As for the Qur'an, it is a reminder with realities and proofs, so it is not the saying of a poet, and this was the style of his speech (peace be upon him), and a single word." End.

The pronoun in *lahu* refers to the Messenger, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). One who went far afield said it refers to the Qur'an, meaning: poetry is not befitting for the Qur'an, though it has not been mentioned; but he may say: the speech indicates it, and it is clarified by the return of the pronoun to it in His saying: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, meaning: a heavenly book that is read in the sanctuaries, and by reciting it and acting upon it one attains what contains the success of both abodes. How far it is then between it and poetry, most of which is from the prompting of the devils!

Ibn ʿĀmir and Nāfiʿ read *li-tundhira* with the *tā'* of address to the Messenger; the rest of the seven read it with the *yā'* of absence, so it may refer to the Messenger, and it may refer to the Qur'an. Al-Yamānī read *li-yundhara* with a *yā'* in the passive voice, and Ibn Khālawayh related it from al-Jaḥdarī. He said from Abū al-Sammāl and al-Yamānī that they both read *li-yandhara* with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and the *dhāl*, the present of *nadhira* with a *kasra* on the *dhāl*, when one knows of a thing and prepares himself for it.

*Man kāna ḥayyan*: That is, heedless, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, because the heedless is like the dead. By it he means the one upon whom it was sealed with faith, and likewise He contrasted it with His saying: "and the word will be fulfilled" (*wa-yaḥiqqa al-qawl*), that is, the word of punishment, ﴿against the disbelievers﴾, those for whom it is decreed by reaching the end in disbelief.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 36, verses 55–79 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in their enjoyment,﴾ ﴿they and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches,﴾ ﴿for them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for,﴾ ﴿"Peace!" – a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿"And separate yourselves today, O criminals!﴾ ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan – indeed, he is to you a clear enemy?﴾ ﴿And that you worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾ ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude.
